articles.title_zh: IMB传教士使用家庭、咖啡馆、应用程序为西班牙的福音对话敞开大门
articles.content: Men and women gather to discuss spiritual topics with Caleb and Carina Beaty, International Mission Board missionaries who serve in Madrid. IMB Photo Across Spain, people looking for connection and meaningful conversation turn to the internet to find groups where they can meet others. At a café by the river, Caleb and Carina Beaty engage in conversations about finding purpose, beauty and “what’s wrong with the world.” A website called Meetup allows people to search for groups to meet in person. The description of the Beatys’ group indicates that it discusses spiritual topics. People come expecting to talk about faith, so it’s not a surprise when they arrive. Caleb said he always has a list of questions that begin broadly and funnel into questions such as, “If there were a God …” or “What do you think Christians believe about that?” or “Why do you think religions have such different perspectives?” The Beatys’ goal in these conversations is to work toward deeper worldview questions within 45 minutes to an hour. Most of the people who attend their Meetup group are from Madrid, but they also have conversations with people from other countries. During one Meetup, Caleb and Carina shared how creation was perfect, but sin led to a world separated from the Father. God offers salvation through the death and resurrection of Jesus, they explained. “There are times we’re able to get to a clear gospel presentation with a group of people, and sometimes we’re doing pre-evangelism.” Caleb said. Some repeat attendees who have been attending for more than a year quickly jump to the heart of the discussion. “All right, Caleb, what’s the Bible say about suffering?” they’ll ask. Caleb and Carina then have the opportunity to share the Christian perspective. IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty and their children pose for a photo in a park in Madrid, Spain.  IMB Photo Spain has secularized rapidly since the 1990s, Caleb said. While many may think of it as a Catholic nation, many people do not know the basic tenets of Christianity. “We’ve got all the churches, we’ve got the cathedrals, and they do processions, but the average person on the street does not know anything about the gospel and does not know anything about Jesus,” Caleb said. Younger Spaniards are drawn to their group and are receptive to the gospel because they don’t have a spiritual foundation or know anyone who does. “There’s just this curiosity because, for a lot of them, they’ve never met someone who actually believes that God exists, and that changes your life,” Carina said. “I’ve had people completely shocked that we believe in God. ‘You really believe that God exists?’ They can’t wrap their mind around that.” During one Meetup, a man contrasted Protestant and Catholic beliefs by saying Protestants focus on Jesus’ suffering and Catholics on Mary’s grief. Caleb responded that evangelicals focus on the resurrection. When Caleb said Jesus rose from the dead, the man replied that he needed to look into that. Caleb said encounters like that reveal how little many Spaniards know about the gospel. Caleb noted the irony of the man’s sharing the Catholic perspective without truly understanding it. He is not the only person the Beatys have met who has missed the heart of the gospel. A friend of the Beatys told them she’d heard Jesus died, but she hadn’t heard he rose from the dead. A man reads a passage of Scripture during a Bible study hosted by IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty at their family’s apartment in Madrid, Spain. Five atheists began attending their Bible study after attending the couple’s Meetup group. IMB Photo The Beatys also host seasonal outreach events through the Meetup. Members from their church in Madrid have started attending the Meetup to learn how the Beatys lead discussions. Their group has become so popular, a waitlist has formed. Caleb and Carina host a small-group Bible study in their home. Five atheists who joined their Meetup now attend the Bible study.

articles.content: IMB Graphic NASHVILLE – As the books closed on the latest fiscal year, receipts for the two Southern Baptist national annual missions offerings underscored the value Southern Baptist churches place on reaching the world with the gospel. The Lottie Moon Christmas Offering® (LMCO) totaled $212.5 million to support International Mission Board (IMB) missionaries, and the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering® (AAEO) reached $73.6 million to support the North American Mission Board’s (NAMB) church planting, compassion ministry and other evangelistic efforts to reach North America. IMB President Paul Chitwood said he celebrates what God did in the 2025-26 season and what He is doing now to lead Southern Baptists toward historic generosity. “I thank God for Southern Baptists! With giving through the Lottie Moon offering at an all-time high, churches and individual givers continue to display a heart for the gospel to be proclaimed to every nation, all tribes, peoples and languages,” Chitwood said. The Annie total marked the second highest in NAMB’s history. The record Lottie Moon offering total surpassed last year’s total by more than $5 million and is the best offering in IMB history. “God is giving our generation unprecedented opportunity to send missionaries to the most unreached peoples and places,” Chitwood continued. “Though the challenges faced by our missionaries are enormous, the generosity of Southern Baptists ensures they have what they need to face those challenges and continue in the work while we hold the ropes with our support.” IMB missionary Landon Williams (center) walks with a Chilean pastor and a U.S. pastor on a remote island in Chile. Cooperation and generosity among Southern Baptists fuels the work to reach the uttermost parts of the world with the gospel. IMB Photo National goals for both offerings are set in partnership with Woman’s Missionary Union (WMU) each year. In response to the offering totals, Sandy Wisdom-Martin, executive director-treasurer of WMU, said: “As Southern Baptists, we are all in for His mission. When we give sacrificially, we prioritize the mission of God. Together our fervent prayers, our faithful generosity and our wholehearted obedience become channels for the gospel to reach our neighbors as well as the nations.” For the last 10 years, Southern Baptists have increasingly supported the Annie offering, setting records in seven of the last 10 years. Totals in each of the last four years have surpassed $70 million. “I am so grateful to the pastors and churches for the faithfulness and generosity they have demonstrated through this offering,” said NAMB president Kevin Ezell. “As I travel and speak in churches of all sizes, I love seeing the posters in the hallways showing their offering goals. For some it is a few hundred dollars, for others several thousand.” The Annie Armstrong offering supports more than 3,000 missionaries in North America, including the ongoing work of church planting in the U.S. and Canada. In 2025, Southern Baptists planted the largest number of churches, 699, since 2016. Including church plants and replants, Southern Baptists have surpassed 700 new churches in four of the last five years. More than 12,000 churches have been planted since 2010. To go along with the increased giving totals to the SBC’s missions offerings, Southern Baptists have also increased their local outreach efforts, indicating that the focus is not just on giving but on sending. Baptism totals have increased in each of the last five years, recovering from the pandemic-year low in 2020 to surpass the 2017 total. The five consecutive years of increase marked the first such streak in approximately 75 years. To Jordan Adams, unheard of things like 38 baptisms in one worship service have become “heard of” for his congregation. articles.content: Staff members at First Baptist Church in Wagoner, Oklahoma, evaluate their church’s involvement with missions and missionary support. IMB Photo The chapel at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City turned into a science lab on Oct. 5-6. Microscopes, beakers and test tubes weren’t in the room, but this Sending Church Lab drew nearly 40 people representing 12 Oklahoma Baptist churches committed to send and care for international missionaries well. The Sending Church Lab, facilitated by the International Mission Board, brought pastors, church leaders and missionaries together for two days of discussion, self-assessment and planning centered on one question: What does it mean for a church to truly be a sending church? For Mike Wall, a global missions ministry partner of Oklahoma Baptists, the answer begins with churches reclaiming responsibility for the Great Commission. Wall first attended a Sending Church Lab last year in Tulsa with few expectations. He left convinced more churches needed the training. “When I went there, I thought, ‘You’ve got to do this in Oklahoma City,’” Wall said, “because of the content and how much our churches need something just like this.” After observing churches work through the exercises in the lab, Wall said he was encouraged by an emphasis on local church ownership in missions. “We can’t just send our people and say, ‘OK, now this is your job, IMB,’” he said. “We have to do our job in sending, preparing and training the best ‘sent ones’ so that when they get to the field, they can already hit the ground running.” Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement specialist, leads a Sending Church Lab at Council Road Baptist Church in Oklahoma City. He is emphasizing the importance of sending churches assessing and equipping future IMB missionaries. IMB Photo Leading the lab was Bryan Wooten, IMB senior church engagement strategist, who developed the concept after seeing the need for stronger relationships between missionaries and local churches. “A Sending Church Lab is our attempt to raise up a host of IMB sending churches,” Wooten said, crediting the North American Mission Board for doing similar events and having successful results. The lab helps churches understand what Wooten calls the church engagement pathway: praying, cooperating, partnering and sending. While many churches faithfully pray, give and go, he said sending requires something more intentional. “Sending includes taking responsibility for an IMB missionary by providing ongoing encouragement, accountability and soul care throughout their term of service,” he explained. During the two-day event, participants gathered around whiteboards to evaluate their church’s missions practices, identify strengths and weaknesses and develop plans for improvement. “We don’t just need to deliver content,” Wooten said. “We need to invite churches to do some work on their own.” Rather than simply listening to presentations, attendees worked through practical questions about prayer, giving, short-term missions, missionary assessment and long-term care. Wooten said churches consistently tell him the greatest benefit is clarity. “They are thankful for clarity on what an IMB sending church is and what our roles and responsibilities are,” he said. For IMB missionaries Peter and Katie Weeks, that clarity is especially valuable. They participated in the lab alongside church leaders. Their real names have been changed to protect their work in Southeast Asia. “There’s no other place I’d rather be during these few days than here,” Peter said. Katie appreciated the interactive nature of the training. “I really appreciate the way they’re actually requiring information from the different churches and encouraging dialogue about how they can go through the steps,” she said. From a missionary perspective, she believes the lab addresses a common challenge. “It’s hard to know sometimes as churches how to be a good sending church and how to support missionaries,” she sa

articles.title_zh: 数字化之门为东南亚岛民打开福音之门
articles.content: Just as young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than in person, the same is true for people in Southeast Asia. IMB missionaries are creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content to connect with the lost through the internet. IMB Photo Recently, an International Mission Board team in Southeast Asia asked a young woman if she had heard the story of Jesus. She replied that, yes, she had heard about Him through a video online! “Back in the day,” shared Amanda Clarkston, an IMB missionary who has served in Southeast Asia for 33 years, “when I first came on the field, you’d go somewhere and gather all the people together in the village to watch the JESUS film.” Now, face-to-face conversations about Christ on the Southeast Asian islands are harder to accomplish. While teams travel to these remote islands often, living in a sparsely populated, animistic background culture as a foreigner creates suspicion and make long-term ministry difficult. Furthermore, young people today have become more comfortable with talking online than they are in person, Clarkston said, which is true of the islanders as well. Attempting to have a spiritual conversation face-to-face has become “too much” for locals, Clarkston shared. So, how do you share the gospel with multiple people groups who are constantly online and less comfortable with in-person interactions? For these Southeast Asia teams, digital engagement — the use of social media platforms to share a message — has become a plausible and effective entry point. The social media agency We Are Social confirmed this, revealing that 82.4% of Southeast Asia’s population uses the internet. “No matter where they go, how far they go, how remote it is, people have phones,” Clarkston and her team realized, “And though sometimes they do have to climb up the highest peak to get reception, people do it.” Clarkston’s team has begun creating and publishing Jesus-focused ads, videos and other digital content in hopes of building bridges to the islanders through the internet. Viewers can click on the ad to message back and forth with a responder, a local believer or missionary who is available to pray, build relationships and answer spiritual questions. “It seems like locals are more open to watching those things in the privacy of their own cell phones,” Clarkston said. Clarkston intends to use digital engagement as a means for initial contact with people with animistic backgrounds, evangelism and, eventually, discipleship. She said that this new ministry has the potential to open doors with individuals across these islands who would normally never reach out on their own or respond to the gospel in person. “Maybe they’ll respond this way,” Clarkston said, “I know without a shadow of a doubt that God is calling people to Himself.” Now, more than ever, technology has a grip on society. Many spend hours each day mindlessly scrolling, searching for meaning, for happiness. And now, more than ever, there is an incredible opportunity to plant seeds across Southeast Asian islands through digital engagement. The IMB Southeast Asia team gives praise to the Lord that He has provided a creative way to reach the lost and plant seeds. Pray the people among the Southeast Asian islands would see these ads and engage with responders boldly, even though they may face persecution or harm because of it. Names were changed for security. Mikah Young is serving overseas with the IMB. The work of the IMB is sustained through faithful giving to the Cooperative Program and the Lottie Moon Christmas Offering ® . articles.title_zh: Alliance寻求下一任执行董事
articles.content: God’s Word transforms lives, strengthens churches and brings hope across generations. Bible translation is part of that story, as communities around the world encounter God’s Word in their own languages. Its future calls for leaders who listen deeply, build trust across cultures and empower others. Within this context, the Wycliffe Global Alliance is searching for its next Executive Director. Could this be your next calling? The Wycliffe Global Alliance is seeking its next Executive Director to serve a worldwide community of more than 100 organisations united in God’s mission through Bible translation. Th e opportunity : Bring our global community together around a shared vision, strengthen local leadership and help a diverse global movement respond to new opportunities with faith and wisdom. The challenge : Lead through change. Articulate a compelling shared vision, strengthen the support the Alliance offers its organisations, and engage support organisations and financial partners in advancing the work. This calls for leadership that honours local autonomy while strengthening global unity, trust, mutual accountability and financial sustainability. We are looking for a leader who brings: A deep commitment to Jesus Christ and a humble, prayerful approach to leadership. At least five years of senior leadership experience and a relevant master’s degree. Proven ability to lead across cultures, develop leaders and empower local churches. Strategic vision, significant fundraising experience and the ability to turn plans into meaningful outcomes. Emotional maturity, integrity and resilience through change. Feel called—or know someone who might be? Expressions of interest, or candidate recommendations, are welcomed confidentially by 30 November 2026 . More info: full profile and how to respond

articles.content: Communication staff at 18 Bible translation organizations across Africa need professional training to tell God’s stories well. In November 2026, a one-week workshop in Ruiru, Kenya will teach practical skills like writing, photography, design and video. Then, six months of follow-up support will continue to strengthen networks and create a collaborative culture of sharing God’s stories widely and effectively. Project Name: Africa Area Communication Capacity Building Workshop Implementing Organization: Wycliffe Global Alliance – Africa Area Contact: Phil Prior Director for Communication Wycliffe Global Alliance phil_prior@wycliffe.net Matthew Bore Project Funding Manager Wycliffe Global Alliance matthew_bore@wycliffe.net Start date: September 2026 End date: March 2027 Summary Across Africa, God is moving. Communities are receiving the Bible in their own language for the first time. Lives are being transformed. But too often, these stories never become known beyond the place where they happen. Why? Because not enough people are trained to recognise and report these stories to a wider audience. Among 18 Bible translation organisations across Africa, communication staff are doing their best—but without formal training in news writing, interviewing, photography, video and social media. Many also work in relative isolation without the chance to exchange ideas and collaborate on stories. The result: Amazing stories remain untold, and the people who could be praying, giving or getting involved never learn about the opportunities. This project changes that. For one week (2-6 November 2026) in Ruiru, Kenya, communication staff from those 18 Wycliffe Global Alliance organisations will come together — not just to sit in a classroom, but to actually create. Using smartphones and free tools, they will learn to capture the moments that matter: local communities and churches collaborating; a translation team’s challenges and creative solutions, groups engaging with Scripture, lives being transformed. Attendees also will build plans for how their organisations will keep telling these types of stories long after the workshop ends. Then, over the ensuing six months, this same group will keep coaching, encouraging, and learning from each other — turning 18 separate voices into one strong, unified story of what God is doing across Africa. articles.summary: This project seeks to equip trainers who can contextualise and deliver OBT training within Latin America
articles.summary_zh: 该项目旨在为培训师提供能够在拉丁美洲范围内提供OBT培训的背景知识
articles.title_zh: 在东南亚培训口译员
articles.content: A three-year training program will prepare local translators across Southeast Asia to put the Bible into spoken forms—like storytelling and song—for communities that share knowledge by voice, not writing. Three workshops will build translators’ skills from basic to advanced to mentoring, so at least 20 participants gain local expertise. Project Name: Training Oral Translators Across Southeast Asia Implementing Organization: Wycliffe Global Alliance Contact: Evelyn Gan Consultant for Oral Translation Programmes Wycliffe Global Alliance evelyn_gan@wycliffe.net Start date: FY 2026 End date: FY 2028 Summary Across Southeast Asia, many communities pass along their culture through spoken word—storytelling, song, and drama—rather than through reading and writing. For them, hearing the Bible in these natural forms often connects more deeply than a printed text. Oral Bible Translation is expanding rapidly in Southeast Asia, but the region lacks enough trained people to sustain it. Seminary graduates know the Bible but not oral translation. Practitioners already working need a path to advance their skills. And almost no one is ready to step into consultant roles. Without urgent, structured training, this shortage could stall Oral Bible Translation projects across the region. This three-year project will trains local translators and seminary students in oral Bible translation. Participants move through three stages: a foundation workshop, an advanced workshop and consultant-level training, with only those who show strong skills advancing to the next stage. Our goal is for at least 20 participants, with a smaller group becoming fully qualified to guide future translation projects. Half of the trainers will themselves be new, gaining experience so the program can continue and grow after this project ends. By working in collaboration with Wycliffe Thai Foundation, Wycliffe Malaysia, YWAM Chiang Mai, FCBH, Spoken Worldwide and CRU, the project is rooted in strong partnerships that will ensure sustainability and local ownership. articles.title: Training Oral Translators in Indonesia
articles.summary: This project seeks to equip trainers who can contextualise and deliver OBT training within Latin America

articles.title_zh: 在印尼培训口译员
articles.content: Indonesia has hundreds of languages still without Scripture in natural, spoken forms. This three-year program will train 20 local translators and seminary students to fill that gap, building skills from basic to advanced to mentoring. Working with local partners, it aims to grow into a lasting, homegrown training network. Project Name: Training Oral Translators in Indonesia Implementing Organization: Wycliffe Global Alliance Evelyn Gan Consultant for Oral Translation Programmes Wycliffe Global Alliance evelyn_gan@wycliffe.net Start date: FY 2026 End date: FY 2028 Summary Indonesia is home to hundreds of languages whose speakers pass on knowledge through spoken word rather than writing. Most still lack the Bible in a form that feels natural to hear. Oral Bible Translation is expanding quickly in Indonesia, but training hasn’t kept up—seminary graduates lack oral translation skills, and working practitioners have no path to grow or reach consultant-level readiness. Without urgent, structured training, projects across the country risk stalling. This three-year project trains local translators and seminary students to close that gap. Participants move through three stages—foundational, advanced and consultant-level training—with those who show strong skills advancing to the next stage. Our goal is for at least 20 participants, with a smaller group becoming fully qualified to guide future translation projects on their own. The project partners with several Indonesian organizations, including seminaries, so that this training becomes part of local theological education rather than a one-time effort. That partnership is central to the goal: building lasting, Indonesian-led capacity so that projects no longer depend on outside experts. articles.title: Bible translation’s future is diverse … and local
articles.summary: The ultimate metric of success is no longer just the distribution of physical books, but measurable transformation of lives through deep, culturally authentic understanding.
articles.summary_zh: 衡量成功的最终标准不再仅仅是实体书籍的分发，而是通过深刻的文化真实理解对生活进行可衡量的转变。
articles.title_zh: 圣经翻译的未来是多元化的……和本地
articles.content: Yaoundé, Cameroon — The landscape of global Bible translation is undergoing a paradigm shift, moving away from traditional, agency-led book printing and toward multimodal translations driven by local communities. At a June 2026 gathering in Yaoundé, translation partners and members of Wycliffe Global Alliance organisations spanning Africa, Europe and Latin America reflected on how Scripture is delivered in the 21st century. Their consensus: The ultimate metric of success is no longer just the distribution of physical books, but measurable transformation of lives through deep, culturally authentic understanding. Community-led translation Dr. Paul Kimbi, the Alliance’s Consultant for Bible Translation Programmes, said Bible translation’s future belongs to community dialogue rather than isolated translation agencies. This emerging approach, known as conversational translation, prioritises localised, grassroots work: listening intimately to communities, engaging them in active storytelling and using locally adapted communication channels. As multiple translation agencies increasingly operate within the same borders, global leaders are urging a shift toward radical collaboration. ‘The multiplicity of agencies is not a hindrance; however, harmony and unity are essential,’ Kimbi said. ‘Unity does not mean uniformity. Each agency, according to its unique strengths, approaches Bible translation as a collaborative piece of God’s global mission.’ Multimodal translations will better serve people from different contexts . Beyond the Book: Multimodal and AI Integration Because cultural contexts vary wildly across the globe, the Alliance’s Africa Area gathering highlighted the urgent need for ‘embodied and multimodal’ translations. This means managing multiple streams of communication simultaneously—integrating oral storytelling, vibrant illustrations, written text and digital media. ‘We do not communicate only with words; we communicate with colours, images, and multimedia,’ Kimbi said. ‘We can no longer consider translation strictly as a written book, but rather as a dynamic multimodal experience.’ This digital evolution naturally intersects with the rise of artificial intelligence. While delegates recognised AI’s immense potential to increase translation speed, optimise efficiency and lower operational costs for minority languages, attendees maintained a stance of strategic caution. ‘Technology accelerates the advancement of Bible translation and language development, but it also creates new strategic responsibilities for leaders and organisations,’ said Etienne Ondoa, a language technology consultant. Staff capacity building, therefore, remains the greatest investment, he said. As technology evolves, the skills required to support it in ministry also evolve. ‘Technological leadership should have a voice in strategic decision-making processes, Ondoa said. ‘Technological decisions increasingly influence ministry outcomes, sound financial resource management, cybersecurity, AI adoption and organisational resilience.’ Etienne Ondoa A Symphony for the Global Church Ultimately, leaders at the event reaffirmed that translation organisations do not operate in a vacuum. They exist to serve the church, which remains God’s primary vehicle for global mission. Kimbi likened the future of the movement to a grand, global arrangement. ‘The particularity of modern Bible translation is that it is a diverse ensemble—an orchestra of varied influences interpreting a magnificent symphony titled ‘Scriptures’ for every language community,’ he said. ‘And in this orchestra, we need everyone: local churches, oral communicators, media creators, literacy specialists and technology partners.’ Story: Lune Prudence Mvondo and Isaac Forchie Photos: Isaac Forchie
articles.content_zh: 喀麦隆雅温得 全球圣经翻译的地貌正在发生范式转变,从传统的、机构主导的书籍印刷转向由当地社区驱动的多模式翻译。 在2026年6月的雅温得集会上,翻译伙伴和遍布非洲、欧洲和拉丁美洲的维克利夫全球联盟组织的成员反思了21世纪如何交付《圣经》。 他们的共识: 衡量成功与否的终极尺度不再仅仅是物理图书的发行,而是通过深刻,文化上真实的理解,对生活进行可测量的转变. 联盟的圣经翻译方案顾问Paul Kimbi博士说,圣经翻译的未来属于社区对话而不是孤立的翻译机构。 这种新兴方法被称为对话翻译、地方化优先化、基层工作:密切听取社区的意见,让他们参与积极讲故事,并使用适合当地情况的交流渠道。 随着多个翻译机构越来越多地在同一边界内运作,全球领导人正在敦促向根本合作转变。 Kimbi说 : “ 机构繁多并非障碍, `团结并不意味着统一。 每个机构都根据其独特的长处,将圣经翻译视为上帝全球使命的合作作品。 多式联运将更好地为来自不同背景的人服务。 除了《书:多式联运和人工智能一体化》之外,由于世界各地的文化背景大相径庭,联盟的非洲地区会议强调迫切需要 " 健全和多模式 " 翻译。 这意味着同时管理多种通信流——将口头讲故事、活泼的插图、书面文字和数字媒体结合起来。 Kimbi说 : “ 我们不只用文字沟通, 我们不能再严格地认为翻译是一本书, 这种数字演变自然地与人工智能的兴起相交. 虽然代表们承认大赦国际在提高翻译速度、优化效率和降低少数民族语言的业务费用方面具有巨大潜力,但与会者保持战略谨慎的立场。 语言技术顾问Etienne Ondoa说, “技术加速了圣经翻译和语言发展的进步, 因此,他说,工作人员的能力建设仍然是最大的投资。 随着技术的发展,部内支持技术所需的技能也随之而来. Ondoa说,“技术领导在战略决策进程中应有发言权。 “技术决定日益影响部委的成果、健全的财政资源管理、网络安全、人工智能的采用和组织复原力。” Etienne Ondoa是全球教会的交响乐团, 它们的存在是为了为教会服务,而教会仍然是上帝执行全球任务的主要工具。 金比把运动的未来比作一个宏伟的全球安排. 他说,“现代圣经译本的特殊性在于它是一个多样化的合唱团——由各种影响组成的管弦乐团,为每个语言群体解释一首名为 " 脚本 " 的宏伟交响乐。 “在这个管弦乐团中,我们需要每个人:地方教会、口头宣传者、媒体创造者、扫盲专家和技术伙伴。” 故事:吕恩·普鲁登斯·姆冯多和艾萨克·福奇相片:艾萨克·福奇相片

articles.title: No Mask, Simply Jesus
articles.summary: In ancient Greece, actors on stage would portray the emotions of their characters by wearing masks that either expressed tragedy or comedy. Masks also allowed the same actor to play multiple roles in the same production. They weren’t permanent, nor were they representative of the real person.

articles.title: Prison Didn’t Mean Paul Was Wrong
articles.summary: Steven Morales explains why following Jesus is worth every sacrifice, even when faithfulness leads to suffering and imprisonment.
articles.summary_zh: 史蒂文·莫拉莱斯（ Steven Morales ）解释了为什么即使忠诚导致痛苦和监禁，跟随耶稣也是值得的。
articles.title_zh: 监狱并不意味着保罗错了
articles.content: “I therefore, a prisoner for the Lord, urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling to which you have been called.” (Eph. 4:1) Those are weighty words. And they’re weighty not because Paul is writing from a quiet study or a place of comfort, but because he is writing them from a prison cell. Paul isn’t sending this letter from a position of safety or success as the world defines it. He’s writing as a man in chains—arrested for preaching the gospel and planting churches. To his critics, he was a troublemaker. A dangerous agitator. To God, he was a faithful servant . That matters. Paul is suffering for the very message he’s urging the church in Ephesus to remember and live out. His words carry weight because his life backs them up. He’s not asking them to do anything he himself isn’t already doing—at great personal cost. And here’s the remarkable thing about Paul: there is no scenario in which he loses. Let him go free, and he’ll travel to the ends of the earth preaching Christ and starting churches. Lock him up, and he’ll become “a prisoner for the Lord,” turning his suffering into a living testimony of the worth of the gospel. Execute him? Fine. As he says elsewhere, “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:21, ESV). There is no situation where Paul says, “The gospel isn’t enough anymore.” There is no moment where he concludes, “This just isn’t worth it.” Instead, Paul’s entire life—especially his suffering—testifies to this truth: no matter your circumstances, trusting in the gospel is never wasted. Paul wasn’t in prison because his ministry failed. He was in prison because he believed the message was worth suffering for. And that’s an important distinction. If a message isn’t worth suffering for, it’s probably not worth believing in. Christianity doesn’t promise a life without pain. What it promises is something better: a suffering that is not meaningless. A hope that suffering does not get the final word. That’s why Paul can say this in 2 Corinthians: “For this light momentary affliction is preparing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison, as we look not to the things that are seen but to the things that are unseen. For the things that are seen are transient, but the things that are unseen are eternal.” (2 Co. 4:17–18) The gospel gives us a framework for enduring temporary suffering because it anchors us in permanent promises. We can endure hardship now because we know it won’t last forever. Our pain has an expiration date . Why? Because Jesus has already suffered fully in our place. He took sin, death, and judgment upon himself—and walked out of the grave victorious. Because of him, not even death has the final say over us. So when Paul urges believers to “walk in a manner worthy of the calling,” he’s not laying a burden on their shoulders. He’s inviting them into a life shaped by hope—a life that knows that whatever it costs to follow Jesus, it will never be in vain. articles.content_zh: 因此,我为主而遭俘虏,求你按照你们被召唤的礼仪而行走。 (第4:1页) 这些话很重 他们的体重不是因为保罗从安静的书房或舒适的地方写作,而是因为他从监狱牢房里写作。 保罗不会像世界所定义的那样, 他在写作时, 对他的批评者来说,他是一个麻烦制造者. 一个危险的煽动者。 对上帝来说,他是一个忠实的仆人。 这很重要。 他敦促以弗所的教会记住并活下来。 他的话很重,因为他的生活支持他们。 他并没有要求他们做他自己没有做的事, 保罗的惊人之处是:他没有失败的可能。 他将前往地底, 宣扬基督, 将他关起来,他将成为“主的俘虏”,将他的痛苦变成福音价值的活生生的见证。 处决他? 精细。 正如他在别处所说的那样,“对我来说,是基督,而死亡是利益”(Phil. 1:21,ESV)。 保罗说,“福音已经不够了。 ” 他没有一刻可以得出结论,“这不值得。 ” 相反,保罗的整个生活,特别是他的痛苦,证明了这一真理:无论你的情况如何,相信福音永远不会白白浪费。 保罗并未入狱, 他入狱是因为他认为这个消息值得忍受. 这是一个重要的区别。 如果信息不值得痛苦, 基督教不会保证没有痛苦的生活。 它所许诺的是更好的事情:没有意义的痛苦。 希望苦难得不到最终结果。 这就是为什么保罗可以在两个科林斯语中说:“由于这种短暂的灾难,我们准备了一种永恒的光荣之分,超越一切的比喻,因为我们不看所见的事物,而看所见的事物。 所见之物是短暂的,而所见之物是永恒的。” 福音为我们提供了一个忍受暂时痛苦的框架,因为它将我们置于永久的承诺中。 现在我们可以忍受苦难, 我们的疼痛有结束期 为什么? 因为耶稣已经在我们的位置上遭受了完全的痛苦。 他自受其害、死亡、判决。他从坟墓中走出, 因为他,连死亡都无法战胜我们 当保罗敦促信徒们“以值得召唤的方式行走”时, 他邀请他们过着充满希望的生活, 这篇文章首次刊登在委员会的双周通讯《激进》上, 今日订阅.

articles.content: Congregations around the world will set aside Sunday, Nov. 1 for the International Day of Prayer for the Persecuted Church, and this year Open Doors, the Christian ministry that tracks persecution, is asking them to start with Syria. Its 2026 World Watch List moved Syria from 18th place to sixth, a 12-point jump in its score and the largest in the top 10. Open Doors says Syria is now at its most dangerous for Christians since the Islamic State group occupied significant parts of the country. About 300,000 Christians live in Syria. Since the fall of the Assad government in December 2024, the country has been mostly controlled by forces led by Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham, an Islamic extremist group with roots in al-Qaeda. The group has made overtures toward moderation and held talks with representatives of Syria’s traditional Christian communities, but it is too soon to know what will come of the new leadership. Widespread instability has produced deadly clashes that have affected Druze and Alawites in particular, with Christians caught in the crossfire, and Islamic State attacks have resumed, including the deadly attack on a church in Damascus in June 2025. “The trauma of what happened hit us all hard,” said “Mourad,” who is responsible for the work of Open Doors’ local partner in Syria. “We thought getting rid of the previous regime would give us some sense of freedom, yet it seems there are still people who only believe in killing.” The interim Syrian constitution adopted in March 2025 makes Islamic law the main source of legislation, and it offers insufficient protection for religious minorities. Pressure on Christians is greatest in Damascus and Aleppo, while the northeast is generally safer. The World Watch List ranks the 50 countries where Christians face the most extreme persecution, using a points system built on data from experts on the ground in 100 countries. North Korea is first with a score of 97 out of 100, followed by Somalia, Yemen, Sudan and Eritrea. Syria is sixth with 90, ahead of Nigeria, Pakistan, Libya and Iran. Open Doors counts more than 388 million Christians worldwide facing high levels of persecution and discrimination for their faith, about one in seven, and in the top 50 countries alone, more than 315 million face very high or extreme persecution. In its 2026 report it recorded 4,849 Christians killed, 4,712 detained and 3,632 churches and Christian properties attacked. For more than 1,600 years Christians have set aside early November to remember believers who suffered for their faith. Open Doors’ free toolkit for churches and small groups includes guided prayer points, videos, sermon material and social images, and this year’s focus is the Middle East, beginning with Syria. Open Doors’ prayer points for Syria ask for three things: that believers would lean on God as their “Rock eternal” (Isaiah 26:4), that converts from Islam would find love and fellowship even when family and friends reject them, and that the victims of the Damascus church attack would feel God’s closeness.
articles.content_zh: 世界范围内的教会将预留11月1日为受迫害教会国际祈祷日, 今年追踪迫害的基督教部也要求他们从叙利亚开始。 其2026年世界观察榜将叙利亚从第18名提升到第6名,比分跳出12分,位列前10名. 叙利亚现在对基督徒来说是最危险的, 约30万基督徒居住在叙利亚. 自2024年12月阿萨德政府倒台后,该国多由伊斯兰极端主义团体"基地"(Hay'at Tahrir al-Sham)所领导的势力所控制. 这个团体向着温和的态度,并与叙利亚传统基督教社区的代表举行了会谈,但现在还不知道新领导人会怎样。 普遍的不稳定导致了致命的冲突,尤其影响到德鲁兹人和阿拉维人,基督徒陷入了交火中,伊斯兰国又恢复了袭击,包括2025年6月大马士革一教堂被致命袭击. Mourad对叙利亚当地合作伙伴的工作负责。 “我们认为摆脱前政权会给我们一些自由感, 2025年3月通过的叙利亚临时宪法将伊斯兰法作为立法的主要来源,对宗教少数群体的保护不足. 大马士革和阿勒颇对基督徒的压力最大,而东北部一般比较安全. 世界观察列表将基督徒面临最极端迫害的50个国家排行榜,使用基于100个国家当地专家数据建立的分数系统. 朝鲜以97胜100负的分数排名第一,其次是索马里,也门,苏丹和厄立特里亚. 叙利亚以90分位列第六,领先尼日利亚,巴基斯坦,利比亚和伊朗. 开放门人数超过3.88亿,全世界因信仰而面临严重迫害和歧视的基督教徒约有七分之一,仅在前50个国家,就有3.15亿多基督教徒面临极高或极端迫害。 它在2026年的报告中记录了4 849名基督徒被杀死,4 712人被拘押,3 632所教堂和基督教财产被袭击。 1600多年以来,基督徒在11月上旬留作纪念因信仰而受苦受难的信徒. 开放的门对教堂和小团体免费的工具包包括导游的祈祷要点、录像、布道材料和社会形象,今年的重点是中东,首先是叙利亚。 开放的门对叙利亚的祈祷点要求三件事:信徒们倚靠上帝作为他们的"永生"(Isaiah 26:4),从伊斯兰教皈依的人即使家人和朋友拒绝也会找到爱和友谊,大马士革教堂袭击的受害者也会感受到上帝的亲切.

articles.content: In my weekly Works & Wonders column, I combine a brief devotional with other interesting and uplifting bits and pieces I gleaned throughout the week. I hope you enjoy this week’s collection! It includes: When God Acts in Power Wikipop Weather Photographer of the Year Bring on the Dawn Big Words Men Sing 1. When God Acts in Power No element of God’s character can be separated from any other. You or I may use the power available to us recklessly, imperfectly, or sinfully—we may act forcefully yet unwisely, or authoritatively yet with evil motives and immoral outcomes. We may act impulsively, on the basis of false information, or in ways that foster prejudice or injustice. In this way, power can be used to bring about great good or great harm. But God never acts in such a way that he diminishes any part of his character. Hence, when God acts in power, he invariably exercises that power in ways that are wise, holy, just, good, and true. I think Jen Wilkin says this well: “The truth of God’s limitless power would be absolutely terrifying were it not paired with the truth of His limitless goodness.” God’s power separated from his other attributes would mean there is nothing that would withhold or restrain him. Yet God’s power paired with his other attributes is tremendously comforting, for we know he will use his power only in ways that are ultimately for our good and his glory. 2. Wikipop Wikipop is a microsite that offers the answer to just one question: What Wikipedia page was everyone looking at yesterday? You probably won’t be shocked to know that on Saturday, when I finalized this article, it told me that everyone had been looking for Patrick Stewart, who died a few days prior. (Note: I add this site with a bit of trepidation because I can’t predict what article will be featured on the day you click the link, so hopefully it’s nothing bad!) 3. Weather Photographer of the Year I know I keep sharing photography contests, but as I said last week, this is the time of year when many of them announce the winners. But this one is different from others I have shared since it features weather. In the Weather Photographer of the Year shortlist, you’ll find exactly what you’d expect—a stunning collection of photos of the weather. 4. Bring on the Dawn I know many people who have appreciated Douglas McKelvey’s Every Moment Holy books, which offer liturgies and prayers for all of life’s moments. Anchor Hymns recently collaborated with McKelvey on an album titled Bring on the Dawn that was inspired by his books. I’m pretty sure that if you appreciate the books, you’ll also like the music. 5. Big Words Sometimes the best apps are the simplest—the ones that do just one thing, but do it well. That’s the case with Big Words . What does it do? It lets you use your phone (or iPad or other screen) to display big words. “Make a full-screen sign, timer or message from a link. Hold up your phone at arrivals, put a countdown on the TV, or show the Wi-Fi password at the front desk. No account, no app, nothing stored on a server. The link is the whole display, so you can share it or bookmark it.” There is nothing to download, so you can just go ahead and bookmark it to use when the need arises. 6. Men Sing I love this delightfully countercultural “Men Sing” trend that’s happening among Dutch Reformed churches, and would love to see it spread. What is it? It’s just men getting together to sing hymns. I had hoped to attend the recent one in Hamilton, but was on the road at the time. Hopefully I can make it to the next one. You can find videos from churches in Hamilton , Grand Rapids , and Chilliwack . I assume it’s happening in other places where there are lots of Dutch Reformed churches. Well done, Dutch guys! See Also Works & Wonders: October 25 Works & Wonders (Oct 11) Works & Wonders (August 2)

你或我可能会莽撞地、不完美地、或罪恶地使用我们所拥有的权力——我们可能会以邪恶的动机和不道德的结果,采取强而不明智或权威的行动。 我们可能根据虚假信息或以助长偏见或不公正的方式采取冲动行动。 这样,权力可以用来带来巨大的好坏.

articles.title: Develop Healthy Tech Habits with Your Teen
articles.summary: ‘Scroll Less, Live More’ helps teens and parents develop the tech skills they need to live a life rooted in reality and steeped in wisdom.
articles.summary_zh: “少滚动，多活”可以帮助青少年和家长培养他们所需的技术技能，从而过上扎根于现实、充满智慧的生活。
articles.title_zh: 与青少年一起养成健康的科技习惯
articles.content: Each Sunday night at youth group, our time of worship through singing is followed by a short sermon then small-group discussion. The high school kids in the group I lead know the routine. Before we open the Scriptures, we pull our chairs into a circle. Then we take out our phones and stack them in a pile on the floor in the middle of the ring. We won’t touch those screens again until the Bible-study hour is done. The phone stack is a simple habit. But it’s helped the students in our group pay closer attention to both one another and the Bible text. In his practical new book, Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Healthy Tech Habits for Teens , Samuel James commends a number of similar practices. His goal is to give teenagers “a vivid picture of what it looks like to apply [biblical] wisdom to technology usage in today’s digital age” (155). James recognizes that simple, repeatable practices can help young people resist the foolishness today’s tech promotes so they can instead grow in the fear of the Lord. Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More builds on the foundation James laid in his previous book for adults, Digital Liturgies: Rediscovering Christian Wisdom in an Online Age . One of his main premises is that technology isn’t neutral. Rather, it’s a powerful force that “shapes and influences us in ways we aren’t always aware of” (30). One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. To illustrate this truth, James points to tech invented in the 19th century: Before the telephone . . . people just accepted that if they weren’t in the same room as somebody, they couldn’t communicate with that person in the moment. After the telephone was introduced, being able to communicate with someone in a different place at any time became not only possible but also important. (125) Similarly, 21st-century tech such as generative AI brings with it both new possibilities and greater expectations: “AI’s capability to produce an amazing variety of work and art with very little direct human involvement creates an expectation that using it regularly for these purposes is normal” (127). The more we off-load our creativity and effort to it, the more we believe we should do so. One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. Digital technology changes us in other ways too. James draws on the work of tech realists such as Neil Postman , Nicholas Carr , and Marshall McLuhan , but he makes their perspective accessible for adolescents. James repeatedly shows young people how poor digital habits affect their cognition, emotions, and relationships. Living on a phone will slow down thinking, leaving teens feeling anxious, or even angry, amid daily interactions that then become more awkward and strained. Way of Wisdom: Guard Your Heart How do we help young people avoid this path? James gives teens some practical encouragements, telling them to charge their phones somewhere other than in their bedrooms overnight. He also provides a list self-examination questions to help them grow in self-awareness and he appeals to family rules such as only using devices in open areas of the home. But ultimately, James is convinced that using technology well involves more than simply following a list of dos and don’ts. He writes, We don’t need a huge list of rules that will have to be updated every time Apple releases a new phone or a new social media app; we need something that will help us determine how to use technology well in any circumstance. We need wisdom. (16–17) Proverbs says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight” (9:10). James is clear that growing in wisdom and the knowledge of the Lord requires more than adjusting one’s screen-time settings; it takes guarding one’s heart. James encourages teens to think of their hearts as a palace where a king or queen lives. He says, “In any royal palace, you’re sure to find soldiers keeping watch over who and what has access to the very importa
articles.content_zh:
每个星期天晚上,在青年团体,我们通过唱歌进行礼拜的时间,接着是简短的布道,然后是小组讨论。 我带领的高中生们都懂规矩 在打开"圣经"前,把椅子拉入一圈. 然后我们拿出我们的电话 把它们堆在地上 戒指中间。

我们不会再碰那些屏幕, 电话堆是一个简单的习惯。 这帮助了我们团体的学生更密切地关注彼此和圣经文本。 在他实用的新书"Scroll Less"(Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Health Tech Habits for Teens)中,塞缪尔·詹姆斯称赞了一些类似的做法.

他的目标是让青少年 " 生动地了解在当今数字时代将[圣经上 智慧应用于技术应用的外表 " (155)。 詹姆斯认识到简单、可重复的做法可以帮助年轻人抵制当今技术推广的愚蠢,让他们在上帝的恐惧中成长。

Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More 在他的前作中为成年人奠定的基础上, 科技并非中立。 而是一股强大的力量, “塑造并影响我们,

技术改变我们的方法之一是改变我们的期望。 为了说明这个事实,詹姆斯指出19世纪发明的技术: 在电话之前, 人们刚刚接受, 如果他们不和别人在同一间屋子里,

在电话引入后,能够随时与另一个地方的某个人通信不仅成为可能,而且非常重要.

(125) 同样地,21世纪的技术,如基因人工智能,也带来了新的可能性和更大的期望: " 人工智能在人类很少直接参与的情况下生产出惊人的作品和艺术的能力,使人们期望经常用于这些目的是正常的 " (127)。 我们越是放弃我们的创造力和努力,我们就越相信我们应该这样做。

技术改变我们的方法之一是改变我们的期望。 数字技术也以其他方式改变我们。 James借鉴了Neil Postman、Nicholas Carr、Marshall McLuhan等科技现实主义者的作品, 詹姆斯反复地向年轻人展示,不良的数字习惯如何影响他们的认知,情感和关系.

生活在电话里会减缓思考, 让青少年感到焦虑甚至愤怒, 智慧之道:守护你的心 我们如何帮助年轻人避免这条道路? 詹姆斯给青少年一些实际的鼓励,让他们在一夜之间在卧室以外的地方充电电话.

他还提供了一份自查问题清单,帮助他们提高自我意识,他呼吁遵守家庭规则,例如只在家庭的空地使用装置。 但最终,詹姆斯相信,使用良好的技术不仅仅涉及遵循一个做和不做的清单。

他写道, 我们不需要一连串的规则, 每次苹果公司发布新手机或新社交媒体应用时, 我们需要智慧。 (16-17) 普罗活佛说:"对耶和华的恐惧是智慧的开始,对圣者的知识是洞察力"(9:10).

詹姆斯明白,智慧和上帝的知识的不断增长,不仅需要调整一个人的屏幕时间设置,还需要守护一个人的心。 詹姆斯鼓励青少年将心想成一个国王或女王所居住的宫殿. 他说,“在任何皇家宫殿里,你肯定能找到士兵来监视谁和谁能进入这个宫殿。

articles.title: Praying for Answers
articles.summary: When Monica’s son Augustine wanted to leave home for a city known for its immorality, she pleaded with God not to let him go. But he went anyway, which greatly grieved his mother, yet it was there that God transformed his life. In his Confessions, Augustine later prayed, “Yet in your deep counsel you heard the central point of her longing . . . [so] that you would make me what she continually prayed for.”

articles.title: Discerning Between Godly and Worldly Grief
articles.summary: Godly grief leads to mourning over sin, not simply its consequences.   The post  Discerning Between Godly and Worldly Grief  appeared first on  9Marks .
articles.summary_zh: 敬虔的悲伤会导致对罪的哀悼，而不仅仅是对罪的后果的哀悼。文章《辨别虔诚与世俗的悲伤》首次出现在九分榜上。
articles.title_zh: 分辨虔诚与世俗的悲伤
articles.content: Abstract: Sam Crites offers three ways to help pastors distinguish between worldly grief and godly grief based on Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians 7:10. Only godly grief produces true repentance, and such grief can be discerned by mourning over sin, not merely its consequences; a genuine desire for reconciliation, no matter the cost; and an earnest desire to please God, not the world. The fruit of godly grief usually becomes evident over time through ongoing repentance and faith in Christ. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . I was discipled by a man named Steve Tucker. He was a simple man full of simple lessons, and one of those simple lessons has stuck with me: a true mark of genuine conversion and its effects is how willing someone is to repent of their sin. However, genuine repentance is a tricky thing. When I catch my children doing something wrong, they are more than willing to “repent,” especially when punishment is imminent. They go from enjoying their wrongdoing to shedding tears. But it’s not always easy to tell if they are grieved over upsetting me or because they know there will be consequences for their actions. Pastors have to make a similar determination when a member is confronted for their sin. Is this person shedding tears only because they were caught in sin, or are they truly repenting? Both kinds of grief can look the same, at least on the surface, but only one leads to life. Those who refuse to repent give evidence that they haven’t been converted. So how can we tell the difference? Three Marks of Godly Grief Since we cannot see the heart of a man, we must look at the fruit of his life—the marks of repentance that accompany genuine conversion. Heart change, not behavior modification, is always the aim. Therefore, we must discern the external evidences of the Spirit’s internal work. This is where Paul’s words to the Corinthians can help us out. He says, “For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Cor. 7:10). Notice that genuine repentance is produced by “godly grief.” Allow me, then, to put forward three marks of repentance from 2 Corinthians 7 that are evidence of godly grief. This list is not meant to be exhaustive but merely a helpful tool for discerning true repentance and, therefore, genuine conversion. 1. Godly Grief Leads to Mourning over Sin, Not Simply Its Consequences In 2 Corinthians 7, Paul describes how restless and anxious he was as he awaited the Corinthians’ response to his previous letter. But when Titus came, Paul was comforted because his report brought news of the grief of the Corinthians—not grief over the harshness of Paul’s letter but grief over their own sin. We’re reminded that godly grief is first and foremost a response to sin and not merely its consequences. David says to God in Psalm 51:4, “Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight.” How could David be so insensitive? What about Uriah and Bathsheba? Or the child who died? David was aware of how the consequences of his sin affected others, but he felt greater anguish in his heart over how he had offended the Lord. And this should be true for all who repent: they should care most about how their sin has offended their Lord. This is the fruit of understanding the gospel, as the sufferings of Christ on the cross were the payment due for our sin. On the other hand, a preoccupation with the sin of others, a tendency to shift the blame to someone else, or grief that is only short-lived—all these are indications that an individual is not mourning because they have offended the Lord, but instead because of the consequences of their sin. 2. Godly Grief Leads to a Genuine Desire for Reconciliation, No Matter the Cost The Corinthians were grieved that their sin had ruptured their relationship with Paul. articles.content: Shelf Life , a new comedy from the producers of The Promised Land , follows a pastor who loses his pulpit and ends up working at a grocery store. Jim O’Heir ( Parks and Recreation ) and Zachary Levi ( Shazam! ) lead the cast, and the series is set to premiere exclusively on the Angel platform in 2027. Shelf Life is created, written and directed by Brian Cates and produced by Milk & Honey Studios. It is currently in production. The premise is a former pastor who is kicked out of the pulpit takes a job at a local grocery store, where he realizes his calling to care for others can’t be shelved while surrounded by quirky coworkers. The cast also includes Wesam Keesh, Donna Biscoe, Tommy Woodard, Jonathan Charles, Leilany Celeste, Jazelle Villanueva and Brittany Visser. Richie Johns produces. Mitch Hudson, an executive producer on the series, shared the news on Instagram. “It’s official – I’m executive producing a comedy series starring Jim O’Heir and Zachary Levi!” he wrote. He said Cates has “an incredible vision” as creator and director, that his business partner Johns is leading the producing team, and that Milk & Honey Studios is adding “another comedy show to our lineup” with Angel as a partner. “More info coming soon!” he added. Cates said he has spent 20 years working in the faith and comedy space and believes “if you make people laugh, you can make people listen.” He described the show as something families can watch together, “genuinely funny, but also honest about life, faith, failure and second chances.” The message, he said, is that “we all reach moments when we think we’ve passed our expiration date. But God isn’t finished with us yet.” O’Heir said that with Shelf Life “you come for the laughs, but you end up genuinely caring about these people.”

Christian music has its own version of this tradition, and her name is Lauren Daigle. While nobody has to thaw her—she’s been out here the whole…
articles.summary_zh: 每年11月，在一个安全设施的某个地方，一个专业团队会温柔地解冻Mariah Carey ，这样她就可以为整个星球唱“All I Want for Christmas Is You”。基督教音乐有自己的传统，她的名字叫劳伦·戴格尔（ Lauren Daigle ）。虽然没有人需要解冻她，但她一直在这里……
articles.title_zh: Lauren Daigle发布圣诞音乐，圣诞季正式开放
articles.content: Every November, somewhere in a secure facility, a team of professionals gently thaws Mariah Carey so she can sing “All I Want for Christmas Is You” for the entire planet. Christian music has its own version of this tradition, and her name is Lauren Daigle. While nobody has to thaw her—she’s been out here the whole time—this weekend she released two more holiday songs, this time with the Preservation Hall Jazz Band: “Sleigh Ride” and “Go Tell It on the Mountain.” If you feel like it is too early for this, please know that the paperwork has been filed. Halloween is over, the candy has been marked down to 50 percent, and the Christmas music season has legally begun. For anyone keeping score at home, this is not a new hobby for her. Daigle’s first Christmas album, Behold , came out in 2016 and climbed to No. 29 on the Billboard 200. It also started a tradition: the Behold Christmas Tour, which returns this December for its 10th annual run. That is the real Mariah comparison. A holiday arrives, and so does Lauren Daigle, with a setlist and a very good coat. The new songs are a pair of old favorites with a New Orleans accent. “Sleigh Ride” is the one that has been running through department stores since before you were born, and “Go Tell It on the Mountain” is the spiritual that has been spreading the Good News even longer than that. Preservation Hall brings the brass, the swing, and the general feeling that a very good party has broken out in a church basement. They also joined her last December for a holiday medley at the CMA Country Christmas special, so the chemistry was already on the record. There is also a business angle, if you like those. It is her first release on Capitol, Interscope and CCMG, which is a lot of letters to put on one sleigh. The songs will come out on a 7-inch vinyl on Nov. 27, the day after Thanksgiving, so you can be a person who owns a Christmas record while also being a person who is still full of pie. And if recorded music is not enough, the 10th annual Behold Christmas Tour opens Dec. 2 at the Ryman in Nashville, with stops in New Orleans and Orlando to follow. It is a beautiful room that was built for exactly this kind of evening, and it will probably smell like cinnamon candles and good intentions. The thaw has happened, the songs are out, and the season has officially been declared open. Please enjoy your holidays responsibly, which in this case means having “Sleigh Ride” on rotation.
articles.content_zh:
每年11月,在一个安全的设施里,一群专业人士轻轻地解冻了Mariah Carey,这样她就能为整个地球唱出“我渴望的只有你”。 基督教音乐有它自己的这种传统版本,她叫劳伦·戴格.

这个周末她又发行了两首节日歌曲, 如果你觉得现在为时尚早,请知道文件已经归档。

万圣节结束,糖果被标记为50%,圣诞音乐季合法开始. 对于任何在家记分的人来说,这不是她的新爱好. Daigle的首张圣诞专辑"Beye"于2016年出道并登上"Billboard 200"的29号. 它也开创了传统: 圣诞之旅,

这是真正的Mariah比较。 节日到来 Lauren Daigle也来了 里面有固定名单 外衣很好看 新歌是一对有"新奥尔良口音"的旧相声. " 雪橇骑 " 是自你出生前就一直在百货公司跑来跑去的一款,而 " 在山上说吧 " 是传播 " 好消息 " 的时间甚至更长的精神。

保存 霍尔带来了青铜器,秋千,以及一般感觉一个非常好的聚会在教堂地下室爆发了. 他们去年12月也加入她,参加CMA乡村圣诞特辑会的节日梅德利会,因此化学已经录制了. 也有一个商业角度,如果你喜欢这些。

这是她首次在Capitol,Interscope和CCMG上发布,这是许多要放上雪橇的信. 歌曲会在感恩节后第二天的11月27日以7英寸的花花筒出道,这样你就可以成为拥有圣诞唱片的人,同时也是仍然充满了派的人. 如果录制的音乐还不够的话,第10届年度"看圣诞之旅"(Book Christmas Tour)将于12月开通.

2个在纳什维尔的雷曼车站,在新奥尔良和奥兰多停站后再跟进. 这是一个美丽的房间, 建造的正是这种夜晚, 它可能闻起来像肉桂蜡烛和良好意图。 冰冻已出,歌曲已出道,赛季正式宣布开播.

请以负责任的方式享受假期,这意味着轮回“雪橇骑”。

articles.title: Inside Indie Tribe’s Plan to Disrupt Christian Hip-Hop
articles.summary: On 'Who Do You Say I Am?', the Christian hip-hop collective reads the Bible's villains with empathy — and asks the church to do the same for everyone it writes off.
articles.summary_zh: 在《你说我是谁？》（ Who Do You Say I Am? ）一文中，这位基督教嘻哈乐队以同理心解读了《圣经》中的恶棍，并要求教会为它所注销的每一个人做同样的事情。
articles.title_zh: 探索独立部落颠覆基督教嘻哈的计划
articles.content: Somewhere in the middle of talking about Scripture, Indie Tribe starts arguing about how to describe someone getting kicked in the groin. nobigdyl., Jon Keith, Mogli the Iceburg and DJ Mykael V are mid-sentence about the theological weight of community when the conversation collapses into a bit about their bandmate, Torey D’Shaun, who has stepped out and, per group tradition, is simply “in the bathroom.” The jokes runs a full minute before anyone remembers what they were talking about. This is more or less Indie Tribe’s operating system: theology, friendship, music and dumb jokes occupying the same room. Their new album, Who Do You Say I Am? , works the same way. They didn’t set out to make a concept record. nobigdyl., Jon Keith, Mogli and Mykael V have been a unit for years, joined more recently by D’Shaun, who folded into the group in 2024 in the middle of an album cycle. Their process has never looked like a studio session. It looks like a household. “We live together and eat together, pray together, we do Bible studies, all that kind of stuff, and we make music for a week,” Jon Keith says. They don’t start with a concept. They start with proximity, then look back at what they made and find the thread already running through it. “We kind of look at the range of the songs that we’re making,” Jon Keith says. “We’re like, ‘Okay, it kind of feels like God is moving this in a certain direction.’” Who Do You Say I Am? happened that way. Written and recorded in December 2024 and released March 27 this year, it’s the first project to feature D’Shaun from the ground up, and the group says his arrival changed the chemistry entirely. “This is really the first time to me that it feels like — I love our previous albums, but the way that this album has a heart and a story to it and a concept, it makes the other albums feel like mixtapes,” Jon Keith says. “This joint is easily the longest album we’ve done. It really feels like our first album album.” The title eventually gave them the question holding the record together: What does it actually feel like to be the person history remembers as the villain? “It’s the product of a lot of introspection that we’ve had,” Mogli says. “We’ve gone through the Bible together multiple times through different lenses, at different times in life when we’re going through different things.” The goal wasn’t to defend bad behavior. It was to stop flattening biblical figures into cautionary tales and start reading them like people, asking how it feels to be the character everyone’s quick to condemn. nobigdyl. pushes it further. The discomfort people feel toward Scripture’s messier figures, he argues, says more about a failure of imagination than a failure of faith. Take David, a man the Bible treats as a hero despite a life that would read as chaos by modern standards. “If you take David’s context and put it now, he sounds like Future,” nobigdyl. says. “How many baby moms he got? OK, you’re Nick Cannon.” The Bible’s heroes, he says, were “tripping the same way” as the people society is quick to write off today. For Keith, that cuts both directions. articles.title_zh: 法律的美丽
articles.content: This week, the blog is sponsored by Zondervan . This article is taken from The Jesus Bible , from Passion Publishing and Zondervan. The Lord called Joshua to be strong and courageous as Joshua replaced Moses as Israel’s leader and led the people into the promised land. This calling was based on his obedience and submission to the Word of God. As the Creator, God knows how life is meant to be lived and the way for people to experience life to the full ( Jn 10:10). The gift of the law was a gracious act of God to instruct his people in his ways. It was never intended to be a moralistic plan to earn God’s favor. Rather, the law was given to those who had already experienced God’s redeeming grace. In the law, God provided instructions for how his children can love him and other people. This law is not a collection of arbitrary dictates from a malevolent deity, but instead it is the wisdom of God distilled in human language. It is a path to joy and life — the way people were meant to live. The Bible continually portrays the law of God in this fashion. For example, in the longest psalm in the Bible, Psalm 119, the author says that he loves, treasures, delights in and longs for the law. It is a source of hope, peace, joy and direction. In Psalm 19, the psalmist says the law refreshes the soul, makes wise the simple, gives joy to the heart and gives light to the eyes (Ps 19:7 – 8). The law is a beautiful gift from a gracious God. Jesus testified to the lasting value of the law when he said that he did not come to abolish the law (Mt 5:17). Instead, Jesus amplified the law, explaining the transformation that should result as a proper response to his work. In his masterful Sermon on the Mount in Matthew 5 through 7, Jesus called people to a far greater standard of obedience than mere conformity to external regulations. Instead of simply condemning murder, Jesus unmasked the anger that fueled this act. Adultery is not the prime culprit, but lust rooted in the human heart is the real problem. Jesus methodically outlined the heart-level change that the law relied upon. Rather than rendering the law obsolete, Jesus showed that the law continued to provide an authoritative standard and guidance for God’s people. Now, because of the finished work of Christ, believers have hope that the price for their disobedience of the law has been paid and that they have God’s Spirit dwelling within them, providing them the power to live the life God intends. 博客由Zondervan赞助, 这篇文章取自"耶稣圣经","激情出版"和"赞德凡". 耶和华召约书亚为强而勇敢,因为约书亚取代了摩西成为以色列领导人并带领人民进入所应许之地. 这个召唤是基于他的服从和顺从上帝之道.

作为造物主,上帝知道生命的本意,知道人们如何体验到生命的完全(Jn 10:10). 法律的天赋是上帝的恩惠行为,以指示他的人民如何行事. 这从来就没有打算成为赢得上帝恩惠的道德计划。 相反,法律是给予那些已经经历过上帝赎回恩惠的人的。

在法律中,上帝为他的孩子如何能爱他和其他人提供了指示. 这部法则并不是从邪恶的神灵中任意地指令的集合,而是用人类语言来提炼出上帝的智慧. 这是通往快乐和生活的道路——人们本该生活的方式。 圣经以这种方式不断地描绘出上帝的法则.

耶稣作证了法律的持久价值,他说他不是来废除法律的(Mt 5:17). 相反地,耶稣放大了律法,解释了应该因适当回应他的工作而导致的转变. 在他精通马太福音5号到7号的"山上赛蒙"中,耶稣把人们称为服从的标准远远高于单纯遵守外规.

耶稣不是简单地谴责谋杀,而是揭发了激起这一行为的愤怒. 通奸不是罪魁祸首,但植根于人心的欲望才是真正的问题. 耶稣有条不紊地概述了法律所依赖的心脏层面的变化. 耶稣没有使法律过时,而是表明法律继续为上帝的人民提供权威的标准和指导.

现在,由于基督的完成,信徒们希望他们违抗法律的代价已经付出,他们心中有上帝的精神,给他们以神想要的生活的力量。 另见12月自由聚会(Zondervan反省会)12月自由聚会(Zondervan反省会)自由聚会(Zondervan反省会)的基督教新书。

articles.title_zh: 解决婚姻冲突的技巧
articles.content: It is inevitable that lives lived in deep intimacy will generate conflict. We wish this weren’t so, but sadly, it is. Therefore, wise couples learn to anticipate conflict and learn to resolve it well. I was recently asked to provide some thoughts on conflict resolution, and thought I’d share what I came up with. Yet as I have sat with couples and tried to help them work through various issues, it has shocked me to find how many have never learned to settle conflict well. Many set habits and patterns in their early years that become hard to break or overcome. I have met with couples who have only ever tried to resolve conflict by raising their voices, and with others who have only ever tried to resolve it by going silent. I have met with some who have only ever relied on text messaging instead of speaking face to face, and with others who have long since given up and don’t even bother trying anymore. Much of this stems from their first years and their failure to get well grounded in conflict resolution. To that end, here are a few suggestions on resolving conflict well. First, borrowing from Robert Murray M’Cheyne, follow this pattern: For every one look at your spouse’s sin, take ten at your own. It’s easy enough to become an expert in the way your spouse sins against you, but it’s far more important to become an expert in the ways you sin against your spouse. It concerns me when I see someone who seems adamantly committed to his spouse’s holiness but seemingly not very interested in his own. Your first calling before the Lord is to deal with your own sin so you can put it to death and come alive to righteousness. Second, invite your spouse to identify your sin. Because of the sheer quantity of the time and intimacy you share, you will inevitably sin against your spouse more than you will sin against anyone else. Not only that, but married life lets your spouse see the kinds of sins that no one else will. Only he or she sees how you sin in the bedroom, for example, or when you’re running late and nobody else is around. What’s more, your spouse sees deeper into your soul than anyone else and, therefore, knows more about you. In a healthy marriage, if you are truly committed to holiness, it only makes sense that you will ask your spouse to speak into your life. It is wise to provide a safe setting to do this where you won’t be a baby or a bully, and won’t sulk or lash out. Set aside some time, tell your spouse that you’d like to hear what sins you are committing, then listen patiently and calmly, without showing anger or being defensive. Having done that, go away, think about it, pray about it, and don’t respond until a day later. This could be a great means of grace in your life. Third, identify times when you won’t try to resolve conflict. Aileen and I, for example, have a long-established 10 o’clock rule, which means we won’t try to fix anything after 10 p.m. We are well aware that Ephesians 4:26 says, “Do not let the sun go down on your anger,” but we have also learned that some issues simply cannot be neatly resolved by bedtime. (Married folk will know that some of the most common conflicts tend to happen between the time you get into bed together and the time you actually fall asleep.) The later the day gets, the more we tend to operate out of emotion rather than reason. And some things seem way worse in the evening when we’re tired than in the morning when we’re fresh. So if we haven’t worked it out by 10, we will call a halt, kiss one another, pray with one another, say something like “I love you and we are going to be all right,” and then go to sleep. Then we can try to work it out at a better time, when we are in a better frame of mind. And honestly, in the light of day, we often realize the situation wasn’t nearly as dire as we thought and that it can be covered by love (1 Peter 4:8). Fourth, invite others in when necessary. Sometimes the most helpful thing you can do in a time of conflict is invite some friends or so

It’s also worth browsing the monthly sales . Recommended Reading A Candy Shop Owner, a Customs Officer, and a Beloved Family. I like this illustration. “Anyone traveling to another country knows that customs officers don’t mess around. They might grill you about what you are bringing into the country, who you are visiting, where you are going, and what your intentions are in the country. I’ve been asked all of those questions. I’ve never felt warmly welcomed by a customs officer. Currently our daughter lives in Southern California. We look forward to those sweet times she can come home. When she arrives home for Christmas, will we grill her? ‘What are the purposes of your stay at our home?’ ‘Who do you plan to visit?’ ‘What are you bringing into our home?’ Certainly not! We will throw the door open, wrap her in our arms, and welcome her in. She is family!” Your Definition of Blessing Is Too Small. “How do we square the Bible’s unblushing promises of blessing for the faithful with its theology of suffering? Put another way, how does Psalm 128 fit with a passage like Psalm 88, where the faithful one seems utterly abandoned to the darkness? One way to answer this question succinctly is to realize that the Bible, first, expands the meaning of blessing in this life, and second, eternalizes it.” These are helpful categories when we consider a difficult topic. 5 Ways Retirees Can Serve the Church. I am not yet a retiree, but when the time comes, this article lists some of the ways I will want to serve my church. “‘Retirement at last! Now I can sleep as late as I want to. Now I get to do nothing all day.’ Such is a popular description of how retirement looks to many people. I know some who would even add, ‘Now I get to play golf every day.’ Obviously, this does not reflect the Christian perspective of someone who understands that his chief end is ‘to glorify God and enjoy Him forever.’ This is not to say that sleeping later and playing golf are anti-Christian. However, there are some significant ways that retirees can still serve the church.” You Can See Everything: On Masks, Performing, and Holiness. Joseph Whitenton explains that the movie provokes the question of whether you can ever truly know someone, then says “I can’t help but feel a deep sense of dread. Is this really all we can say about our relationships to one another? That it might be impossible to really know someone? To even know ourselves? Are our lives just a string of performances? I can’t help but think about how a social media centered age might further contribute to this feeling of constantly performing, as Bo Burnham, another comedian/prophet has observed.” The Straightest Path to Happiness. articles.title_zh: 第一人称：伟大的使命—我们主人的月球射击
articles.content: Jeff Ginn, IMB's senior ambassador for U.S. and global relations, speaks to a crowd gathered to discover new ways to partner in God's mission. Ginn is available to speak in churches on behalf of the IMB. IMB Photo Portrait of Jeff Ginn, IMB senior ambassador of U.S. and global relations. IMB Photo I was born in 1961. The U.S. president at that time was John F. Kennedy. In that year he issued a challenge to our nation. It was that we build a rocket ship, put men in it, send it to the moon, have them walk on the surface, plant our flag, then return them safely to earth. He called on the nation to accomplish this within a decade. This extraordinary, demanding, costly endeavor is known to history as Kennedy’s “moon shot.” The nation rose to the challenge. I still remember watching in 1969 a grainy, black-and-white broadcast as Neil Armstrong stepped on the surface of the moon and declared, “One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.” We often think of the astronauts with admiration. And rightly so. They were courageous. However, let’s note that the Apollo mission employed some 400,000 additional people to fulfill the mission. Team members included mission controllers, metal fabricators, communication specialists, caterers, engineers, scientists, nurses, doctors, mathematicians and computer programmers. Beyond these, all U.S. taxpayers contributed! It took a nation to get two astronauts to the moon and safely return them! That term, “moon shot,” has made its way into our vocabulary. It can be used for other daring, costly, and valuable undertakings. It is fair, then, to say that the Lord Jesus, our Master, has a moon shot of His own! His mission merits our lives and resources. His mission includes all who name Christ as Lord collaborating to fulfill it. At the International Mission Board, all our plans, strategies and decisions center around this biblical idea that we all must work together to fulfill Christ’s mission. We all must pray. We all must give. We all must go. We all must send. Matthew 28:18-20 is one passage, perhaps the best known, that gives us the details for our mission. The name that evangelicalism has given to this passage is “The Great Commission.” The word “commission” is not one that we use commonly. It simply means a command. How interesting that, with hundreds of commands in Scripture, this is this one that gets the definitive article, “the,” and the adjective, “great.” Does it merit that moniker? I say that it does, and I offer three reasons why. Because it makes a great claim When quoting the Great Commission, it is common for folks to omit verse 18 and simply begin with verse 19. But to do so undercuts the weight that Jesus’ claim in verse 18 adds. There He claims to have all authority in heaven and on earth. That essentially is a claim to divinity — to supremacy. He is saying that He is the King above all kings and the Lord above all lords. When we consider His claim, we all have a choice to make. To borrow from C. S. Lewis, we could decide that He is a liar or a lunatic. Following liberal theologians or Muslim theology, we could decide that much of what is taught about Him in the New Testament is the stuff of legend — that the disciples exaggerated and “created” the Christ of faith. Jeff and Nell Ginn served with the International Mission Board in Colombia. Jeff currently serves churches as IMB senior ambassador. IMB Photo But the decision that I have made (and on which I’ve staked my eternal destiny) is that He is not a liar, nor a lunatic, nor a legend. He is, in fact, Lord! My prayer is that all will decide similarly. As such, He has the authority to issue any commission and our only right response is, “Yes, Lord!” His authority is why, 35 years ago, my wife, Nell, and I said “yes” when He called us to serve with the IMB in Cali, Colombia.  It was under His authority that we planted churches and taught future leaders in the seminary there. Because it gives a great command Not only is it the Gr

我还记得1969年在尼尔·阿姆斯特朗踏上月球时,我还观看了一场粗糙的、黑白的广播,并宣布“为人类迈出一小步,为人类迈出一大步”。 我们常常以钦佩的眼光来看待宇航员. 没错 他们很勇敢 然而,让我们注意到,阿波罗任务又雇用了大约40万人来完成这一任务。

articles.title: Your Church May Know Less Bible Than You Think (And What to Do About It)
articles.summary: A new survey indicates Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it.
articles.summary_zh: 一项新的调查显示，基督徒已经屈服于该文化的普遍识字危机。“书中的人”不读它。
articles.title_zh: 你的教会可能知道的圣经比你想象的要少（以及该怎么做）
articles.content: In November 1900, Mark Twain delivered a speech titled “The Disappearance of Literature” to the students at Connecticut Wesleyan University. With signature slyness, he told them , “I don’t believe any of you have ever read Paradise Lost , and you don’t want to. That’s something that you just want to take on trust. It’s . . . the definition of a classic—something that everybody wants to have read and nobody wants to read.” Twain was noting the beginning of the illiteracy rockslide that we now witness as an avalanche. The statistics we see in the age of smartphones and social media bear out our eroded literacy: In 2003, average Americans older than age 15 read 21.9 minutes on a given day. By 2010, the number had dropped to 18.3 minutes, and in 2025, it had sunk to 16.2 minutes a day. Imagine how ChatGPT will gut that number even further in the next few years. America is moving rapidly into a postliterate reality, a sort of new Dark Ages, one in which we consume information in images and sound bites, all predigested for us by others. Consider the implications for a system of belief whose transmission from one generation to the next is staked on a book. Christian Literacy Crisis A new survey from Lifeway Research throws into stark relief the chasm between Christian commitment to and knowledge of the Bible. More than 2,000 Christians who attend church in a typical month were surveyed across eight categories of Bible knowledge: major people, passages, events, divisions of Scripture, and more. The researchers designed questions around what would be typically well known rather than obscure. Two out of three respondents scored less than 60, a failing grade. Fifty-five percent could not correctly name the first king of Israel. Only 11 percent could correctly order four major Old Testament events, and only 27 percent could correctly order four major New Testament events. Forty-four percent failed to identify the book of Mark as belonging to the Gospels. Two out of three respondents wrongly believed Hezekiah was a book of the Bible, and 44 percent believed the Gospel of Thomas was as well. Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The “people of the Book” don’t read it. The Bible itself, the classic of all classics, has apparently become a book that every Christian wants to have read, and few Christians want to read. If we do read to sustain our faith, we’re more likely to read books about the Bible than the Bible itself. We may consume sermons or podcasts or use devotional resources that cherry-pick verses to give us a positive emotion in 10 minutes or less, but largely, we’ve become curators of other people’s opinions about a book we don’t read ourselves. Failure of Discipleship I believe these results show a failure of discipleship strategies, one with massive implications: We cannot pass along to someone else what we ourselves don’t know. How can the church fulfill the Great Commission if it’s incapable of teaching others to observe everything Jesus commanded? The numbers show we haven’t taught even the basics. If the church were a local public school responsible for teaching basic math and reading, we would receive a failing grade and face funding sanctions. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it. Yet, according to a 2024 Lifeway Research survey of 2,620 Protestant pastors, 52 percent are satisfied with the state of discipleship and spiritual formation in their churches. Twenty-nine percent report that they regularly evaluate discipleship progress among their congregations. When asked their first priority in discipleship, the largest number responded that it be “biblical knowledge focused.” And in response to the question “What approaches does your church specifically use to disciple and encourage the spiritual development of adults in your congregation?” 89 percent responded the sermon, the top answer by a 20-point gap, with adult Sunday school listed second.
