articles.summary_zh: 伊恩· H ·穆雷（ Iain H. Murray ）的《艾米·卡迈克尔：灰烬之美》（ Amy Carmichael: Beauty for Ashes ）是对爱尔兰传教士前往印度的非凡生活的简短复述。接下来是该标题的第4章， “艰难的日子和黄金岁月。“如果说艾米·卡迈克尔的生活有任何模式的话，那就是令人耳目一新的时代，然后是考验的时代，令人兴奋的‘攀登’的时代[…]艾米·卡迈克尔的帖子：令人耳目一新的时代和考验的时代首先出现在真理美国的旗帜上。
articles.title_zh: 艾米·卡迈克尔：令人耳目一新的时代和审判的时代
articles.content: Iain H. Murray’s Amy Carmichael: Beauty for Ashes is a short retelling of the remarkable life of the Irish missionary to India. What follows is Chapter 4 of that title, ‘Hard Days and Golden Years.’ If there was any pattern to Amy Carmichael’s life it was of times of refreshing then of trials, of exhilarating ‘climbing’ then of walking in dark ravines. In part her explanation was that demonic activity follows the work of the Holy Spirit. As she quoted from George Bowen, When Christianity assumes an aggressive attitude the first result is a great exhibition of Satanic power. Satan’s power to be manifested must be assaulted. 1 Such an understanding does not come so readily to us who do not live, as she did, within sight of demon possession, or within hearing of tom-tom drums calling devotees to idols. Shortly before Walker 2 had left on his last mission, he had been sitting with Amy and others in deck chairs under the stars. ‘We had been talking’, she later wrote, of work and workers, and of those (to me) most wonderful women, who seemed perfectly self-reliant, needing no strong arm alongside. I remember how, suddenly startled at the bare thought of working alone, in the sense of all the burden of responsibility, I exclaimed that I never could do it. Mr Walker laughed. ‘Well, you don’t have to’, he said. 3 Amy was the weaker when her ‘strong arm’ died at the age of fifty-four. What she owed to Walker’s ‘courageous championship’ of the children’s work, ‘through its first very difficult years, no words can tell, nor can words tell how he is missed’. 4 At times, as she faced her loss, she would need to say to herself, ‘Don’t give up, don’t be afraid: go on.’ Prayer for ‘fortitude’ entered her life. There were unsympathetic neighbours who observed the work at Dohnavur who supposed that Amy would now be more vulnerable. One of these was a lawyer who, soon after Walker’s death, wrote with the demand that current work on the building of a wall around the compoundbe stopped, and that a half-built nursery should be pulled down. They were using ground, he claimed, to which they did not have legal title. ‘He had waited till Mr Walker’s death had left us, as he thought, defenceless, almost desolate, and sure to be easily cowed by threats of court trouble.’ The wall building had been prompted by the passage of a tiger through the compound at night; and the new nursery was necessitated by the growing numbers of children for whom Dohnavur had become home. Amy ignored the letter and heard nothing more of the threat. The Dohnavur family of seventy children and grown-ups in 1906, had doubled itself by this date, and the need of more helpers was pressing. Mrs Catherine Carmichael was never able to return. She died on July 14, 1913. A few weeks earlier a letter from her to Amy began with the words, ‘My own most precious earthly possession’. While Amy did not lament her mother’s death—for no Christian death was to be ‘lamented’—in the days ahead she needed to preach to herself, ‘I must remind myself to live in the joy of those gone, not grovel in the sense of my loss.’ Mrs Carmichael had been a constant supporter and representative for Dohnavur in Britain. She acted as the home secretary to whom gifts could be sent, and helped to make her daughter’s books more widely known. In 1912 those books had been noted by Queen Mary, wife of King George V, who expressed her thanks for them. While Amy was busy in 1913 writing Walker of Tinnevelly , there came the possibility of the loss of her closest female friend and helper, Ponnammal, who had been with her ever since, as a young widow, she had come to new life through Walker’s preaching. She now needed surgery for cancer and Amy went with her to a Salvation Army Hospital at Neyyoor for a period. In their absence from Dohnavur (forty-six miles away), and the absence of Mabel Wade who was on furlough, 70 of the children were ill. The need for more medical facilities at Dohnavur itself was evident. After much s
articles.content_zh: 伊恩·H·默里所著的"艾米·卡迈克尔:爱希斯的美人"(Amy Carmichael: Beautiful for Ashes)是爱尔兰传教士到印度的出众生的短篇回忆. 下面是该标题的第4章: " 艰难的日子和黄金年 " 。 如果Amy Carmichael的生活有任何规律的话, 她的部分解释是,妖魔活动遵循了圣灵的工作. 正如她从乔治·博文所引述的那样,当基督教采取侵略态度时,第一个结果就是撒旦力量的伟大展览. 必须攻击撒旦的力量。 1 对我们来说,这种理解并不像她那样活在恶魔拥有的目光下,或者在听到汤姆·通鼓呼唤献给偶像的人面前。 在行走者2号执行上个任务前不久,他一直和艾米等人坐在星空下的甲板椅上. 她后来写道:‘我们谈过了',内容是工作和工人,以及那些似乎完全自力更生、不需要任何坚强的手臂的妇女。 我记得,我突然对独自工作的赤裸裸的想法感到惊奇,因为我肩负着所有的责任,我感到惊叹,我永远做不到。 华克先生笑了 他说,你不必这么做。 3 Amy在54岁时死亡, 她对沃克的“勇敢的冠军”儿童工作所负的责任是,“在第一个非常困难的岁月里,言语无法分辨,言语也无法分辨他是如何被错过的”。 页:1 有时,当她面临损失时,她需要对自己说: " 不要放弃,不要害怕:继续吧。 " 祈求`宽恕'进入她的生活。 有不同情的邻居在多赫纳武尔观察作品,他们认为艾米现在会更加脆弱. 其中一个是一位律师,他在Walker死后不久写道,他要求停止目前在大院周围建造一堵墙的工作,应当拆除一个半建的托儿所。 他声称,他们使用了他们没有合法所有权的地盘。 他一直等待着沃克先生的死像他所想的那样离开我们,他手无寸铁,几乎是荒凉的,而且肯定很容易被法庭麻烦的威胁吓倒了。 墙上建筑的动因是一只老虎在夜间穿过大院;新的托儿所是因越来越多的儿童成为家而必需的。 艾米无视信件,没有听到更多的威胁. 1906年有70个孩子和成年人的多赫纳武尔家族,到这时已使自己翻了一番,迫切需要更多的帮助. 凯瑟琳·卡迈克尔夫人一直没能回来 她于1913年7月14日去世. 几周前,她给艾米的一封信开头写道,“我拥有自己最珍贵的地产”。 Amy没有为她母亲的死感到悲哀——因为没有一个基督徒的死是`在她需要为自己传道的几天里感到悲伤',`我必须提醒自己生活在那些死去的人的欢快中,而不是在我失去的意义上的忧郁'。 卡迈克尔夫人一直是英国多赫纳武尔的支持者和代表。 她担任家庭秘书,可以向她寄送礼物,并帮助使她女儿的书更广为人知。 1912年,这些书被乔治五世国王的妻子玛丽王后所注意到,玛丽王后对之表示感谢. 在1913年艾米忙于写作"Tinnevelly"的Walker(Walker of Tinnevelly)时,出现了失去她最亲密的女性朋友和助手Ponnammal(Ponnammal)的可能性,她从那时起就一直与她在一起,作为一个年轻的寡妇,她通过Walker的传道而来到了新的生活. 她现在需要手术治疗癌症,艾米和她一起去内约尔的救世军医院住了一段时间. 在他们离开多克纳武尔(相距四十六里外),而当时在放假的马贝尔·韦德(英语:Mabel Wade (film))不在的情况下,70个孩子生病了. Dohnavur本身显然需要更多的医疗设施。 这么多之后

articles.summary_zh: 六个帖子中的第二个帖子包含了阿尔伯特· N ·马丁（ Albert N. Martin ）在1984年旗帜青年大会（ Banner Youth Conference ）上给出的教学内容，展示了基督教生活的基本圣经神学。原则2 ：基督徒的生活无法摆脱紧张和冲突。我并不是说基督徒的生活就是这样[…]在基督徒的生活中，《没有逃脱的张力》这篇文章最初出现在美国真理的旗帜上。
articles.title_zh: 在基督徒的生活中，没有摆脱紧张的途径
articles.content: The second of six posts containing the substance of teaching given by Albert N. Martin at the 1984 Banner Youth Conference, presenting a basic biblical theology of the Christian life. Principle 2: There is no escape from tension and conflict in living the Christian life. I do not say that the Christian life is all tension and all conflict. The kind of teaching I am attempting to expose as fallacious is as follows: At a conference a speaker takes a text out of context to which he attaches or from which he extracts a shibboleth – perhaps the shibboleth of Christ living his life through us, or the saving life of Christ, or the abiding life. Then the preacher, having expounded his theory of the Christian life, gives an appeal like this: ‘Child of God, are you weary of the tension of wrestling with your remaining sin? Are you tired of struggling in prayer? Are you weary of having to battle with impure thoughts and thoughts of envy and pride and jealousy? Are you tired of this incessant conflict?’ And every true Christian sits there with his fangs dripping, saying, ‘Oh God, you know I am tired, I would give anything to have one day, one day in which I did not have to battle with dullness of heart and distraction of mind and the seductions to sin that come from without and from within’. And the speaker then says ‘Ah, if you are tired of the tension, weary of the conflict, if you will but take these steps, then Christ will so live his life through you that it will be a life marked by the negation of tension and conflict. You will be so filled with the Spirit, so taken up in the Spirit, that tension and conflict for all intents and purposes will be a thing of the past as long as you maintain the posture of the abiding life. The moment you feel tension and conflict, it is because you slipped out of that life, back to your old ways.’ Now that is not a caricature, that is spelled out in page after page, book after book. Beware of the writings of Watchman Nee! Beware of some of the writings of such as Norman Grubb and Hannah Whithall Smith. Beware of these writings, because if you take them seriously they could drive you either into a world of unreality or into a world of scepticism. Now what proof do I offer from the word of God for that proposition? 1. Because of the reality of indwelling sin with its incessant and powerful actions upon us. Galatians 5:17: ‘The flesh is lusting against the Spirit and the Spirit against the flesh and these two are contrary the one to the other, so that you may not do the things that you would’. And Paul does not go on to say that there is a way to be utterly, totally delivered from that conscious­ness of tension and conflict. He does tell us that we need not be dominated by the flesh: ‘Walk in the Spirit and you shall not fulfil the lusts of the flesh’. But he nowhere says that the consciousness of the flesh’s lusting will be negated, and where flesh is lusting against Spirit, there is conflict. I hold to the time-proven exegesis of Romans 7:14 I do not say that the Christian life is all tension and all conflict. The kind of teaching I am attempting to expose as fallacious is as follows: At a conference a speaker takes a text out of context to which he attaches or from which he extracts a shibboleth – perhaps the shibboleth of Christ living his life through us, or the saving life of Christ, or the abiding life. Then the preacher, having expounded his theory of the Christian life, gives an appeal like this: ‘Child of God, are you weary of the tension of wrestling with your remaining sin? Are you tired of struggling in prayer? Are you weary of having to battle with impure thoughts and thoughts of envy and pride and jealousy? Are you tired of this incessant conflict?’ And every true Christian sits there with his fangs dripping, saying, ‘Oh God, you know I am tired, I would give anything to have one day, one day in which I did not have to battle with dullness of heart and distraction of mind and the seduction

articles.title: Building a Workplace Where People Flourish (with Landon Hobson)
articles.summary: What happens when a seminary-trained economist takes over a pet-products plant? Landon Hobson, CEO of Cosmos Corporation, shares how paid mission days, a book club, and a ‘make the coffee’ ethic help ordinary workers flourish.
articles.summary_zh: 当受过神学院培训的经济学家接管宠物产品工厂时会发生什么？ Cosmos Corporation首席执行官兰登·霍布森（ Landon Hobson ）分享了带薪传教日、读书俱乐部和“制作咖啡”伦理如何帮助普通工人蓬勃发展。
articles.title_zh: 打造让人们茁壮成长的工作场所（与Landon Hobson一起）
articles.content: Landon Hobson is the CEO of Cosmos Corporation, a family business outside St. Louis that makes pet care and household cleaning products sold in 70 countries. With degrees in theology and economics, Landon never expected to run a 250,000-square-foot manufacturing plant—until his father-in-law asked him to take over the company, and he sensed that God had been preparing him for exactly that. Landon describes how his faith shapes Cosmos’s culture: tuition support for any degree an employee wants to pursue, a “Better Book Club” that pays people to read, five paid mission days a year, and a core value of being “willing to make the coffee” for the person behind you. He answers hard questions about whether making dog shampoo really matters to God, and he speaks candidly about the hard years—supply chain disruptions, a drop in sales, and layoffs of people he cared about. He also explains why CEOs need pastors who aren’t passive, and what he has gained from a group of believing business leaders who share the same struggles. Resources Mentioned: To Change the World by James Davison Hunter Every Good Endeavor by Timothy Keller A Public Faith by Miroslav Volf Work in the Spirit by Miroslav Volf
articles.content_zh:
兰登·霍布森(Landon Hobson)是宇宙公司(Cosmos Corporation)的首席执行官,该公司是圣路易斯以外的一家企业,在70个国家销售宠物护理和家庭清洁产品. 凭借神学和经济学的学位,兰登从未预期会经营25万平方英尺的制造厂——直到岳父要求他接管公司,他感到上帝一直在为他做好完全这样的准备.

Landon描述了他的信仰如何塑造宇宙文化:为雇员想要追求的任何学位提供学费支持,一个支付人们阅读费的“更好的书社”,每年有5个付薪的任务日,以及为背后的人“愿意煮咖啡”的核心价值。

他直言不讳地说, 连锁供应中断、销售量下降、以及他所关心的人被解雇。 他也解释了为什么CEO需要不是被动的牧师,

articles.title: The Missing Piece in John Mark Comer’s Quiet Time
articles.summary: ‘Into the Quiet’ effectively critiques the ills of our hectic cultural moment, but it also promotes a spirituality that could quickly become disconnected from Scripture.
articles.summary_zh: “进入宁静”有效地批评了我们忙碌的文化时刻的弊端，但它也促进了一种可能很快与圣经脱节的灵性。
articles.title_zh: 约翰·马克·科默安静时光中缺失的部分
articles.content: According to a recent Pew Research study, more than half of U.S. adults report spending too much time on their smartphones. Even those who acknowledge the negative effects of smartphone addiction find it incredibly difficult to cut back. Excessive screen time isn’t just harming our productivity and connection with other people; it also makes practicing spiritual disciplines more challenging. In his latest book, Into the Quiet: Following Jesus in a World of Noise , John Mark Comer argues that “nurturing a practice of solitude, silence, and stillness is utterly indispensable to a flourishing spiritual life” (26). This timely book addresses important issues in a lively, engaging, and accessible manner. And though the staccato prose style sometimes borders on gimmicky, it’s never dull. Comer dons three hats, appearing as technoskeptic, therapist, and mystic. I responded differently to each: cheering the first, querying the second, and rejecting the third. Into the Quiet effectively critiques the ills of our hectic cultural moment, but it also makes questionable claims about the spiritual value of silence and promotes a spirituality that could quickly become disconnected from Scripture. Comer as Technoskeptic Comer’s consistent message is that readers need to intentionally disconnect from an increasingly noisy world. By “noise,” he means both literal sounds and the ever-present flood of distraction enabled by digital devices. The result is that “it is now possible to go through our entire lives and never be alone ” (18, emphasis original). Channeling secular authors like Jonathan Haidt and Johann Hari, Comer argues that constant noise threatens our well-being, whether we’re religious or not. But this dynamic is especially harmful for Christians. “Are we really surprised that . . . when we sit down to pray, we can barely even pay attention?” he asks (20). Our always-on lives differ greatly from the example of Jesus, who models a strategy of “retreat and return” (30). He ministers to the crowds and then withdraws to solitary places to pray (e.g., Matt. 14:23). This is the book’s strongest material, a timely warning with which I wholeheartedly agree. Comer as Therapist But then Comer moves in another direction. He advances therapeutic claims that may be helpful to some people but that aren’t clearly grounded in Scripture. According to Comer, solitude forces a confrontation with pain that serves an essential psychological purpose: All of this stuff is in you . . . leaking out like toxic pollution into the water supply of your relational world . . . it’s asking to be dealt with. To be given a moment to speak, say its piece. To be healed. Released. (85) While the imprecatory psalms and the psalms of lament certainly model honest prayer before the Lord, and self-examination is clearly a biblical imperative, Comer’s specific claims seem more informed by extrabiblical therapeutic practices than by Scripture itself. Is it actually true that “naming our feelings out loud allows our bodies to process and discharge pain without it getting lodged in our cores” (100)? That doesn’t sound like Scripture. According to Comer, solitude forces a confrontation with pain that serves an essential psychological purpose. The primary biblical support he gives for the practice of naming feelings to discharge pain is Jesus’s prayer in the garden of Gethsemane, an incident that provides the “template” for “the moments of our own Golgothas” (101). The problem is that Jesus in the garden isn’t surfacing old “toxic pollution” from “the water supply of [his] relational world” with an eye toward therapeutic healing (85). He’s facing an imminent crisis and asking the Father for either deliverance from or strength to face the trial set before him. Whatever the value of surfacing past trauma, Gethsemane doesn’t establish Comer’s claims on that point. John Mark Comer在其最新著作《静默:在噪音的世界中追随耶稣》中认为,“折磨一种孤独、沉默和静静的习俗对于繁荣的精神生活是绝对不可或缺的”(26)。 这本及时的书以活泼、参与和无障碍的方式处理了重要问题。 虽然这种散文风格有时会与 gi相接,

来者会戴三顶帽子 以技术怀疑者、治疗师和神秘主义者的身份出现 我对每一个都作出了不同的反应:欢呼第一个,询问第二个,拒绝第三个.

articles.title: What Does It Mean to Be Human?: 12 Theses Answer a Pressing Question
articles.summary: Learning about a Christian theological anthropology is no mere academic exercise. It gets to the heart of who we are, explains our daily experience, and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good.
articles.summary_zh: 学习基督教神学人类学不仅仅是学术练习。它触及我们的核心，解释我们的日常经历，并推动我们朝着爱邻居和公共利益的方向前进。
articles.title_zh: 做人意味着什么？ ： 12篇论文回答了一个紧迫的问题
articles.content: No question today is more pertinent than this: What does it mean to be human? With declining belief in God and rising secularization come renewed debates concerning human nature. Culture now seems to hold to two contradictory beliefs: Either that we’re entirely material beings, meaningless clumps of matter in an endless void; or that we’re sovereign masters who determine our own meaning, with an internal sense of who we are that we dare not defy. It’s no surprise that rejections of God lead to confusion concerning the image of God and the biblical teaching that we’re humbly related to this material cosmos and yet dignified as the crown of creation. With the advent of artificial intelligence and ongoing debates about race, gender, and sexuality, it’s all the more important to be clear about what we are and who we’re made to be. Learning about a Christian theological anthropology is no mere academic exercise. It gets to the heart of who we are, explains our daily experience, and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. A Christian theological anthropology gets to the heart of who we are and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. In my book, For Us and for Our Salvation , I seek to address these issues by providing a biblical, theological, and practical introduction to the doctrines of humanity and sin. In this article, I present 12 theses that summarize a biblical and Reformed-catholic theological anthropology that I explain throughout the book. These 12 theses, I hope, can ground us as we stand in culture’s ever-changing landscape. 1. All human beings are made in the image of the triune God and are thus called to represent, enjoy, and glorify God forever. God creates each individual according to his image. The first-person plural in Genesis 1:26 indicates that the whole triune God is the archetype for the human being, for each person of the Trinity shares a singular divine substance (see also Col. 1:15–17). Humans are created as representatives of God and are thus religious creatures made to have communion with their Origin. Therefore, each human being as such is created good, with dignity and agency. Our religiosity, corrupted by the fall, doesn’t lead us to cease being religious but rather causes us to elevate and idolize one aspect of creation over others, as we prefer the creature over the Creator (Rom. 1:18–23). We refuse to acknowledge God as the end for which we were made, and we seek enjoyment in other things—we idolize good, created reality and render it ultimate. 2. The doctrine of the image of God entails both ontological and ethical affirmations. God creates humans as embodied souls with intellectual and volitional capacities, and he calls humans to represent him by a proper exercise of those faculties in righteousness, holiness, and true knowledge. Human beings are endowed with capacities for wisdom and righteousness. A twofold metaphysical concept is important here: act and potency. Potency refers to the natural power that distinguishes a particular kind of thing from other kinds, and act refers to the exercise of that power. Humans, for instance, are the kinds of beings endowed with the potency to think rationally, but the actualization of those potencies is a distinct matter. Edward Feser clarifies , In arguing for the existence of active potencies or causal powers, Scholastic writers emphasize the point that a cause is not always bringing about its characteristic effect. . . . My power to write must therefore be distinguished from this or that actual, particular action of writing, as a standing precondition of the latter. Infants or those in a comatose state due to some serious injury, therefore, continue to be image-bearers, even while the potency for wisdom or will isn’t actualized in any way. Similarly, those who are cognitively impaired still have the potency or essential capacity of reason and volition even though it manifests differently than in others, and even if th
articles.content_zh:
今天的问题莫过于: 何谓为人. 随着对上帝信仰的下降和世俗化的不断加深,关于人性的辩论又再度出现。 文化现在似乎持有两种相互矛盾的信念: 要么我们完全是物质生物,

或者我们是决定自己意义的主权主人, 对上帝的拒绝导致对上帝形象和圣经教义的困惑, 即我们与这个物质宇宙有着神圣的关系,

随着人工智能的出现和关于种族、性别和性问题的持续辩论的到来,更需要弄清楚我们是什么人,我们是谁。 学习基督教神学人类学不仅仅是学术实践. 它触及我们是谁的心脏, 解释我们的日常经历, 并把我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。

一个基督教神学人类学 得到了我们的心脏 我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。 在我《为了我们和我们的救世主》一书中,我试图通过提供一本圣经、神学和关于人类和罪恶理论的实际介绍来解决这些问题。

在这篇文章中,我提出了12篇论文,总结了一本圣经和改革天主教神学人类学,我在整个书中都对此作了解释. 我希望这12篇论文能让我们在文化不断变化的地貌中落脚。 1. 所有的人都是以三月神的形象塑造的,因此被召唤来代表、享受和永远颂扬上帝。

上帝根据他的形象创造每个人。 创世纪1:26中的第一人称复数表示,整个三角神是人类的原型,对于三位一体的每个人来说,都有一个独特的神性物质(另见1:15-17). 人类是作为上帝的代表而创造的,因此是宗教的生物,被赋予与他们的起源有共性.

因此,每个人都是善良、有尊严和有作用的。 我们的信仰被堕落所腐蚀, 并不导致我们不再信奉宗教,

我们拒绝承认真主是我们的末日,我们寻求享受,我们崇拜善神,创造现实,使它达到极点。 2. 关于上帝形象的理论包括本体论和伦理论。

上帝以智慧和意志能力创造人性,他号召人通过正确行使正义、圣洁和真正知识的才能来代表他。 人类拥有智慧和正义的能力。 这里有两个元概念很重要:行为和效力。

强力(potency)是指将某种特定事物与其他类型区分开来的自然力量,行为是指行使这种力量. 例如,人类是具有理性思考能力的生物,但是,这些能力的实现是一个独特的问题。

Edward Feser澄清说,在主张存在主动的力量或因果力量时,学术作家强调一个原因并不总是能产生其特征效应。  . 因此,我的写作能力必须与这种或那种实际的、特别的写作行动区分开来,作为后者的长期先决条件。

因此,婴儿或因严重伤害而处于昏迷状态的人继续是形象的持有者,即使智慧或意志的力量根本没有实现。 同样,那些在认知上受损的人仍然具有理智和意志的能力或基本能力,尽管这种能力的表现与其他人不同,而且即使存在这种能力。

articles.title: Praying for Hindus during Diwali
articles.summary: Jamie Dean provides four prayer points for reaching Hindu communities with the hope of the gospel during Diwali.
articles.summary_zh: 杰米·迪恩（ Jamie Dean ）提供了四个祈祷点，以帮助印度教社区在排灯节期间获得福音的希望。
articles.title_zh: 排灯节期间为印度教徒祈祷
articles.content: On Sunday, Nov. 8, nearly 1.2 billion Hindus worldwide will celebrate Diwali, the most significant holiday in Hinduism each year. More than a billion of those Hindus live in India , making Diwali a massive festival in the world’s most populous (and most Hindu) nation. India also has the world’s largest diaspora population, with an estimated 35 million people living outside the country. During the holiday known as “the festival of lights,” here are a few ways for Christians to pray for the light of Christ to break through Hinduism’s spiritual darkness, whether in India, other nations, or in the lives of our own neighbors: 1. Pray for opportunities to hear and respond to the gospel in India. Many people in India live and die without ever hearing the gospel clearly explained. Pray more Indians will be exposed to the good news of redemption in Christ, and that God will draw many to himself. 2. Pray for Christ-centered churches in India. Though Christians make up only 2 percent of India’s population, that’s still about 28 million people. Pray for faithful, Christ-centered churches to preach the gospel faithfully and reach those around them. 3. Pray for Christians facing persecution to be a faithful witness. Christians in many parts of India face increasing opposition and persecution for their faith in Christ. Pray the Lord will protect these believers and help them to be a faithful witness—including during Diwali, when many Christians stand out for not participating in the holiday. 4. Pray for Hindus in other nations, and in your own neighborhood. Diwali is also a major holiday in other countries, including Nepal , where the majority of the population is Hindu. Pray for Nepalese living in spiritual darkness to hear the gospel of Christ, even as they continue recovering from devastating floods . Pray also for the Indian diaspora. Pray the Lord will give Hindus living in other nations the opportunity to hear the gospel, perhaps for the first time. Pray and look for opportunities in your own city or neighborhood to build friendships that might lead to gospel conversations with Hindu neighbors.

articles.title_zh: 你就不能爱所有人吗？
articles.content: “Love one another.” This is one of the undeniable imperatives of Christianity. God is love (1 John 4:8, 16). We must love one another (1 John 4:11). By this love all men know that we are Christ’s disciples (John 13:35). Love fulfills the law (Romans 13:10). So why not just love one another? Why build walls, make distinctions, establish boundaries, and draw lines? Why confront sins? Why not welcome all equally? Can ’ t you just love everyone? The impulse and the argument “just to love everyone” is superficially attractive, even apparently compelling. However, the argument uses Bible language the way Satan does — selectively and deceptively. When tempting Christ, the devil selectively quoted Scripture but twisted the whole sense (cf. Matthew 4:5–7; Psalm 91:11–12). It is possible to use Bible language while ignoring the context, imposing a different meaning on the words and drawing false conclusions based on faulty assumptions. This regularly happens with the meaning of love . Does it really matter? Yes . Churches are disrupted and even destroyed by the confusion created by such shallow reading and reasoning. The language of love is thoroughly scriptural, but we need to handle our Bibles carefully. We need to understand the true definition and the proper direction and order of love. Love Defined and Established Think of love’s definition and foundation. Love does not appear in a vacuum, a sort of glowing, amorphous cloud of feeling which we can press into any mold. Rather, God defines it carefully. God’s love sets the standard for our love: In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him. In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. (1 John 4:9–11) God’s love, which we reflect and replicate by the Spirit’s power, is not a generic niceness but a determined act of the divine will, directed toward the utterly unlovely. It does not at all diminish or dilute the reality of sin. It faces sin’s pollution, punishment, and power head-on, fully honoring divine justice as well as divine mercy. It is love manifested in sacrifice, love determined to do heavenly good to its object, to make the unlovely lovely through whatever righteous means necessary. Christian people show a similar Godlike and Christlike love toward one another. Anticipating his sacrifice, our Lord says, A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another. By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. (John 13:34) Christlike love for other believers is a mark of a true disciple. Because God in Christ sets the standard for what love looks like, we cannot collapse Christian love into mere sentimentality, a kind of anodyne sweetness that overlooks or dismisses sin and downplays righteousness. Love Directed and Ordered Think also of love’s direction and order. Our love for our brothers demonstrates our love for God himself (1 John 4:20–21). Our Lord goes to the cross for his beloved people out of love to his Father. The structure of the greatest commandment reveals both direction and order: First , love the Lord your God entirely, and second , love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37–40; Mark 12:29–31). While not denying a proper love of affinity, Christ calls us to a crowning love of supremacy: We are to love Christ more than father or mother, son or daughter (Matthew 10:37). Love for our nearest and dearest might even be considered hatred in comparison to the love that we have for him (Luke 14:26)! We must not, then, think of love first in its horizontal dimension toward men. Love must first be directed vertically toward God, in response to his love to us, before it spills over horizontally toward others. “Love” toward men at the expense of love t

为什么不平等地欢迎大家? 你就不能只爱每个人吗? 冲动和“仅仅爱每个人”的论点表面上具有吸引力,甚至显然具有说服力。 然而,这一论点使用与撒旦一样的圣经语言——有选择和欺骗. 当诱惑基督时,恶魔有选择地引用了圣经,但扭曲了整个意义(参见马太福音4:5–7;诗篇91:11–12).

可以同时使用圣经语言而忽略上下文,将不同的含义强加于词上,并根据错误的假设得出错误的结论. 这经常发生在爱的意义。 这真的重要吗? 对 教会被这种浅浅的阅读和推理造成的混乱所扰乱甚至摧毁。

爱的语言是彻头彻尾的文字,但我们需要仔细处理我们的圣经. 我们需要了解真正的定义,以及爱的正确方向和秩序. 爱的定义和基础。 爱情不会出现在真空中, 一种发光的,无形态的感受云, 我们可以压进任何模具。 相反的,上帝是精心定义的。

上帝的爱为我们的爱设定了标准: 在这件事情中,上帝的爱在我们中间被显现出来,上帝把他唯一的儿子送入了世界,以便我们通过他而生存. 爱不是我们爱上帝 而是他爱我们 派他儿子来为我们的罪孽辩护 被爱,如果上帝如此爱我们, 我们也应该相爱。

(1 John 4:9-11)上帝的爱,我们用精神的力量来反映和复制,不是一种一般的善意,而是神意志的坚定行为,直接对准完全不爱的人。 它丝毫没有削弱或淡化罪恶的现实。 它面临着罪恶的污染、惩罚和权力,完全尊重神圣的正义和神圣的慈悲。

爱表现在牺牲中,爱决心为它的目标做天上的好事,通过任何必要的正义手段使不爱的人变得可爱. 基督教徒对彼此的爱 表现出类似上帝和基督的爱

我们的主说,在期待他的牺牲时,我给你新的戒律,即你们彼此相爱:正如我一直爱你们一样,你们也要彼此相爱。 由此一切众生悉知汝等为我弟子,若有相爱. (约翰13:34) 基督爱其他信徒是真正的门徒的标志.

因为上帝在基督中为爱的外表设定了标准, 我们不能把基督教的爱 变成单纯的多愁善感, 一种忽视或否定罪孽和贬低正义的厌倦的甜言蜜语。 Love Directed and Ordered 想想爱的方向和秩序。 我们对我们兄弟的爱显示了我们对上帝本人的爱(1 John 4:20–21).

我们的主为了他敬爱的百姓去十字架 为了他父亲 最伟大的戒律结构揭示了方向和秩序:第一,完全爱主你的神,第二,像爱自己一样爱邻居(Matthew 22:37–40;Mark 12:29–31).

基督在不否认亲情的同时, 要求我们拥有至高无上的爱: 我们比父亲或母亲、儿子或女儿更爱基督(Matthew 10:37)。 相较于我们对他的爱,对亲近和最亲近的爱甚至可能被视为仇恨(公爵14:26)! 那么,我们决不能在对男人的横向层面首先想到爱情。

爱必须首先垂直地向上帝倾斜,以应对他对我们的爱,然后横向地向他人倾斜。 "爱"对男人 牺牲爱T

articles.title_zh: 任务对儿童来说是否太昂贵？
articles.content: Are my children also called to this ? As a mama missionary, I wonder about our fitness for the task when our family of eight clogs airport security and labors in language study and ministry like a well-meaning circus. Will my kids catch a deadly virus from the airport carpet? Will beans be lunch every day ? How can we possibly replace years spent with grandparents and a vibrant children’s church? Will they become healthy adults when this calling cuts not only us but them? Are the unreached regions of the Joshua Project map reserved for singles? Our family’s plane-ticket prices alone might argue that case. Does the church only send the strong? In the world’s economy, our crew is inefficient and slow to get the job done. Risk Worth Reward The missionary call may cost our precious children extra bouts of food poisoning, power outages, awkward cultural moments, and loneliness. It may even, like Perpetua Broten and Ezra, Violet, and Calvin Pals , require their lives. When Jesus called his followers, he asked for painful, costly sacrifice. He reminded them that though foxes and birds return each day to their burrows and nests, he had no place to lay his head (Matthew 8:20). He called his disciples to take no change of clothes or spare coin for their ministry (Matthew 10:9–10). And yet he said, “There is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold” both now and in eternity (Mark 10:29–30). God’s economy is not man’s. Jesus calls kids to go with moms and dads to serve the nations because God’s kingdom advancement is for families too, and the risk is worth its reward. The forward momentum of God’s kingdom does not exclude our children. The garden mandate to be fruitful and multiply now expands spiritually, and we take our kids along. We aren’t disqualified from overseas ministry if we’re changing diapers on the hour. God is the author of life and the genius behind the family design. Our dominion over the earth as image-bearers includes those in our care, even if they look too small to slay dragons. The risks of going with kids in tow are many; only the rewards of trust and obedience eclipse their reality. If we pursued mere adventure or greater cultural appreciation, we would be the “most to be pitied” (1 Corinthians 15:19). But if God calls us to glory in Christ in dungeon-like places, teaching our children to cup their hands around their mouths and cry to prisoners, “Come out!” then we offer them diamond-quality joy (Isaiah 49:9, 61:1). We weep with our kids over the cost they see and feel in their own lives, helping them gather the broken pieces of their hearts to hand to Jesus, teaching them firsthand that Christ’s flesh and blood satisfy. Shepherding Your Flock Before my two oldest children were dunked in the cold mountain water of our village in baptism, they testified to God’s grace in their lives. God had shown them his best at their worst. I flinched inwardly as I heard them recall dangerous accidents and desperate emotions in our time overseas. But when it turned darkest, God shone brightest. If it were up to me, I would have taken an eraser to God’s plan of pain for them. If I had, I would also have unknowingly rubbed out his intimate deliverances. The pleasure of following God to the farthest reaches of the planet with your kids is finding that God is there too. All that said, our family just moved ministry locations overseas due to prolonged isolation and our kids’ growing need for friends and community. Missions is a family affair and worth the risk, while at the same time, God does not depend on our presence in a place to accomplish his purposes, and he cares specifically for our kids. Our kids’ particular needs are not at odds with our calling but can direct our feet and make us wise shepherds of our flock. God is not biting his nails on the sidelines of our missionary service, hoping we’ll perform well enou

我的孩子也被叫来了吗? 作为一位母亲传教士,我想知道我们是否适合完成这项任务,当我们这个8个堵塞的机场保安和劳工家庭在语言学习和像一个善意的马戏团一样的部委工作时。 我的孩子会从机场地毯上感染致命病毒吗? 每天吃豆子吃午饭吗? 我们怎样才能取代在祖父母和充满活力的儿童教堂度过的岁月?

他们会不会成为健康的成年人 当这个呼吁不仅削减我们,而且削减他们? 约书亚计划图中未进入的地区是否为单人保留? 我们家族的飞机票价本身就可能证明这一点。 教会只派强者吗? 在世界经济中,我们的船员效率低下,完成任务的速度缓慢。

值得回报的风险 传教士的召唤可能使我们珍贵的孩子们额外损失食物中毒、断电、尴尬的文化时刻和孤独。 它甚至可能像Perpetua Broten和Ezra、Violet和Calvin Pals一样需要他们的生命。 当耶稣召唤他的追随者时,他要求痛苦,昂贵的牺牲.

他提醒他们,虽然狐狸和鸟儿每天返回他们的洞穴和巢穴,但他没有地方安顿头颅(Matthew 8:20). 他叫门徒们不要为他们的部会换衣服或多余的硬币(Matthew 10:9-10).

然而,他却说,“没有人离开过家,也没有人离开过兄弟姐妹,也没有人离开过母亲、孩子或土地,为了我和福音,现在和永远都得不到一百倍”(Mark 10:29-30)。 上帝的经济不是人类的经济。

因为上帝的王国进步也是为了家庭, 上帝王国的前进势头并不排除我们的孩子。 花园的任务富有成果,倍增,现在精神上有所扩展,我们带着我们的孩子一起走.

如果我们换尿布, 上帝是生命的作者,也是家庭设计背后的天才. 我们作为形象持有者对地球的统治权包括那些受我们照顾的人,即使他们看起来太小,不能杀死龙。 和孩子一起被拖走的风险是很多的;只有信任和服从的回报掩盖了他们的现实。

如果我们仅仅追求冒险或更大的文化欣赏,我们将“最可怜”(科林斯15:19)。 但是,如果上帝在类似地牢的地方召唤我们在基督中荣耀,教我们的孩子用手握住嘴,向囚犯喊叫,“出来吧!”那么我们给他们提供钻石质量的快乐(以赛亚49:9,61:1)。

我们和孩子们一起为他们自己生活中所看到和感受到的代价而哭泣,帮助他们收集心碎的碎片交给耶稣,并亲身教他们基督的血肉满足。 在我两个年长的孩子 被浸在村里的寒冷山水里之前 他们证明了上帝的恩惠

上帝在他们最坏的时候 给他们展示了他最好的一面 当我听到他们回想起我们海外时代的危险事故和绝望情绪时,我内向退缩。 但当它变得最黑暗时,上帝会闪耀 如果由我决定的话,我本来会用一个抹除器去完成上帝给他们的痛苦计划。 如果我有的话,我也会不知不觉地 抹去他的亲切奉献。

和你们的孩子一起跟随上帝到达地球最远的地方的乐趣 就是发现上帝也在那里 我们的家人因为长期孤立和孩子对朋友和社区的日益需求,刚刚将部属迁往海外。

使命是一种家庭事务,值得冒风险,与此同时,上帝并不依赖我们的存在来实现他的目的,他特别关心我们的孩子. 我们的孩子的特殊需求与我们的召唤并不矛盾,

articles.title: A Daring Suggestion for Netflix
articles.summary: Netflix appears to have fallen on hard times and I have some suggestions that I'd like to think would help it: cut the sex, nudity, and profanity, and gain back the viewers it's long been alienating. See Also A La Carte (April 28) A La Carte (October 22) Netflix’s Biggest Competition
articles.summary_zh: Netflix似乎陷入了困境，我提出了一些我认为会有所帮助的建议：减少性、裸露和亵渎，并赢回长期以来一直疏远的观众。另请参阅点菜（ 4月28日）点菜（ 10月22日） Netflix最大的比赛
articles.title_zh: 对Netflix的大胆建议
articles.content: Netflix appears to have fallen on hard times. The company’s co-CEOs recently announced they would be laying off around 1,000 employees, the deepest round of cuts in years. A day later, the chief content officer made a sudden exit and was immediately replaced. Just a week after that, the market responded unfavorably to Netflix’s Q3 results, causing the stock to drop sharply. There are many reasons for Netflix’s woes, not the least of which are increasingly heavy competition for viewers and its failure to land marquee shows—the kind of shows that convince people to maintain their subscription instead of canceling it in favor of Disney+, Prime Video, or one of the many other options. While there’s little doubt that Netflix will make it through this challenge, it may never regain the market dominance it once held. I have a daring suggestion for Netflix that I’d like to think could help it: make more shows that are clean and suitable for family viewing. To frame it another way, stop putting sex, nudity, and harsh profanity in nearly every show. There are many potential subscribers who are eager to be entertained, but not by shows they deem unsuitable or inappropriate. I’ll grant that Netflix has viewing data that probably shows its TV-MA content is especially popular, but data can only count the people who watched a show, not the ones who never pressed play in the first place. It’s also can’t tell whether the sex and swearing are essential to those who watch it, or whether they’d watch it even if it was much cleaner. Perhaps you could think about it this way: a single explicit sex scene in a series is unlikely to gain more viewers than it will lose. What I mean is that a content warning on IMDb or Common Sense Media stating that a show contains an explicit sex scene is enough for me and many others to skip that entire show. But I very much doubt the opposite is true—that a person will learn that there is no sex scene and decide to skip it on that basis. Some of us simply have no interest in viewing such things and will guard both ourselves and our families from seeing them. For those who don’t believe me, I’m sure I can put them in touch with a thousand people who will affirm what I’m saying. I am convinced there is a deep desire for shows and movies we can watch without cringing, without feeling violated, and without knowing we are watching what we consider not only unsuitable but immoral. It’s not that we’re prudes or opposed to sex—we’re all for it. It’s that we think sex and nudity are for private contexts , not public ones, and that some matters are to be kept between a husband and wife rather than displayed for all the world to see. Sex is so good and powerful that making it public diminishes it rather than elevates it, which means we deliberately avoid shows and movies that feature it. I would say something similar about language . Does a show need to drop hundreds of F-bombs across just a few hours of runtime? Does it need to constantly use the name of God as a swear word? It doesn’t need any of this. Once again, is it more likely that people will not watch shows unless they are profane, or that they will avoid them if they are? I think the answer is obvious: many more people will be driven away by swearing than drawn by it. If I had to offer one more piece of advice, it would be to stop tampering with beloved intellectual properties to make them consistent with modern sensibilities. Why not just make adaptations that are faithful to the vision of the original creators and let us deal with the differences between their context and today’s? Have the courage to let the stories stand on their own without inserting modern messaging. I strongly believe this would do more to provoke good thinking and spur important conversations. There’s no need to be so heavy-handed. To summarize, I think Netflix has been going about this all wrong and has been creating content that alienates an eager audience rather than drawing it in. So Netfl
articles.content_zh:
Netflix似乎陷入了困难时期. 公司联合首席执行官最近宣布将解雇约1000名员工,这是多年来最大幅度的削减。 一天后,首席内容官突然退出,立即被替换. 仅仅一周后,市场对Netflix的Q3结果反应不佳,导致股票急剧下降.

Netflix的悲哀有许多原因, 更是观众竞争日益激烈, 以及它未能登陆马奎节目,

Netflix虽然毫无疑问会渡过这个挑战,但可能永远无法恢复它曾经占据的市场支配地位。 我对Netflix有一个大胆的建议, 我想可以帮助它: 做更多干净、适合家庭观看的节目。 以另一种方式设定它,停止把性,裸体,以及苛刻的淫秽在几乎所有的节目中.

有许多潜在的订阅者渴望娱乐,但并不是通过他们认为不合适或不适当的展示。 我同意Netflix的收看数据可能显示其TV-MA内容特别受欢迎,

也无法分辨性与誓词对于观看者是否至关重要, 也许你可以这样想: 系列中一个单一的显性场景不太可能获得比它失去的更多的观众.

我的意思是,一个内容警告 互联网电影数据库(IMDb)上或Common Sense Media上 声明,一个节目包含一个明确的性场景,足够我和许多其他人跳过整个节目. 但我非常怀疑相反的情况是真实的——一个人会得知没有性场景,并据此决定跳过.

我们中有些人根本不关心看这些东西,并将保护我们自己和我们的家人不看到它们。 我敢肯定, 我可以和一千人联系,

我深信,人们非常渴望看一些节目和电影,而无需相信,无需感到被侵犯,也无需知道我们正在看我们认为不合适和不道德的东西。 我们不是故意或反对性爱,

我们觉得性与裸体是私人事务, 性是如此的美好和强大, 使它公开 减少它而不是提升它, 这意味着我们故意避免 节目和电影 我会说类似的东西的语言。

演出需要投下数百枚F炸弹吗? 难道它需要不断使用上帝之名作为誓词吗? 它不需要这些。 复次,是人不看秀,非有妄言,或避之不见,更何况?

我认为答案是显而易见的:更多的人会因为宣誓而被驱逐,而不是被它吸引。 如果我不得不再提一个建议,那就是停止篡改所爱的知识产权,使之符合现代的敏感性.

为何不只做忠实于原始创造者愿景的改编,让我们处理他们的背景与今天的不同? 要有勇气让这些故事独立存在,而不插入现代信息。 我坚信,这将更有助于激发良好的思维,刺激重要的对话。 也不必如此粗暴。

总结一下,我认为Netflix一直把事情搞错了,并创造出让热心的观众疏远的内容,而不是把它引进来. 所以说网友

articles.content: Good morning. The God of peace be with you today. Sales & Deals Some of today’s noteworthy Kindle deals include Al Mohler’s reader-friendly commentary on Hebrews, Julie Lowe’s guide to safeguarding our homes, and Marty Machowski’s family Christian devotional. Recommended Reading Discerning Between Godly and Worldly Grief. I think we all sometimes have to try to determine whether a person is displaying godly grief or worldly grief. Sam Crites offers three marks to help us make that determination. Harvest in Fearful Times. Here’s Melissa Edgington on trusting the Lord with an uncertain future. “I’ve seen various types of hand-wringing over the past week about governments and militaries and potential power grid disruptions. I watched one video, and then social media began showing me a different side of the internet, where cowboy hat-wearing men hand out ‘top secret insider knowledge’ from the front seat of their pickup trucks. In fact, I saw individuals from all sides of the political spectrum worrying out loud about how much water they should have on hand, how many weeks’ worth of prescriptions, how many canned goods and what types of communication devices would be best.” Can I Love My Enemies While Addressing Wrongs and Protecting Myself? “Practically speaking, how then should we demonstrate godly love for our enemies—the kind of love that redeems and restores instead of perpetuating sin and injustice? Let’s consider three implications of godly love that help answer this question…” Jeremy Oliver offers counsel on a sensitive matter. Is Missions Too Costly for Kids? I think a lot of people wonder whether life on the mission field could cost their children too much. Jessica B. writes from experience. “Are my children also called to this? As a mama missionary, I wonder about our fitness for the task when our family of eight clogs airport security and labors in language study and ministry like a well-meaning circus. Will my kids catch a deadly virus from the airport carpet? Will beans be lunch every day? How can we possibly replace years spent with grandparents and a vibrant children’s church? Will they become healthy adults when this calling cuts not only us but them?” How AI Brought a Mathematician to Ecclesiastes. This is an especially interesting article from Alan Noble. “Nobody—not even the most informed futurist—knows the effect AI will have on careers in the future. Some predict we’ll mostly adapt and find new vocations. Some predict we’ll all be living lives of leisure in a hyper-abundant economy while robots do all the labor. But if I had to guess, I’d predict that some people are going to have at least some of their valuable labor replaced by AI in the near future. And when that happens, people will have a crisis of meaning.” Don’t Stock the Pantry With Temptation. Darryl Dash warns against stocking the pantry with temptation. “We are used to preparing for almost everything. We prepare our clothes, our food, our vacations, and more. Paul is saying that whatever you do, do not prepare to sin. Instead, actively take steps to cut temptation out of your life. Deliberately arrange your life so that sinful desires are harder to satisfy. Avoid certain environments. Put a filter on your phone. Cancel that streaming service. Throw away those books. Cut out influences that tempt you toward sin.” Headlines Here are just a couple of interesting headlines from Christian news outlets. Christianity Today reports that Churches Face a Shortage of Worship Leaders . “A growing shortage of worship leaders has researchers, educators, and pastors wondering if it’s time to rethink music ministry recruitment and preparation.” Maybe some churches will ask whether they actually need a worship leader, since I have often wondered whether it’s a necessity for many of them. articles.title: To Sustain Inner-City Church Plants, Adopt a Missionary Model
articles.summary: To plant churches in these spaces, we need to think like missionaries.
articles.summary_zh: 要在这些地方建造教堂，我们需要像传教士一样思考。
articles.title_zh: 为了维持内城教会植物，采用传教士模式
articles.content: In a conversation at church one Sunday, a pastor told a friend of mine, “Your friend should quit trying to plant churches in the inner city. It doesn’t happen because it can’t happen.” I was visiting this friend just before COVID-19 hit, speaking at a separate church about our ministry, New England Urban Church Planting. Our organization was new, and my sinful inclination was to think, Oh, you just wait and see! My friend was equally defensive. Yet this pastor was onto something: It rarely happens, and it is indeed hard. Why is church planting in our nation’s neglected inner cities so rare? Why are underserved urban communities overlooked by gospel-preaching churches? Stakeholders in our ministry have discussed these questions since 2009, leading to the organization’s founding in 2020. We’ve learned a lot in these years of full-time work as we’re growing this network of inner-city planters. The work is hard for two key reasons. Yet it’s possible. And it’s crucial. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations (Matt. 28:19)—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. To plant churches in these spaces, we need to think like missionaries. Problem Unless you grew up in the inner city, serving there is a cross-cultural experience. This is the first reason church planting hard. Ruby Payne asks her readers if they can survive in poverty: Do you know how to keep your clothes from being stolen from a laundromat? Do you know how to move in half a day? Do you know how to keep your car from getting repossessed if you fall behind on payments? Discipling men and women in the inner city can be exasperating when they have a new burner phone frequently. Inner-city pastors need to know how to preach and how to administer Narcan. And behind all that is the sound of gunshots, fights, loud TVs, and the quiet exit of well-meaning suburban Christians who came to help but didn’t last long. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. Evangelicalism often feels like it’s married to only one culture: suburbia. Postwar Americans migrated from our cities to set up homes and churches in the suburbs. In 1940, 15 percent of Americans lived in the suburbs. By 2000, that number was 50 percent. Evangelicals were a disproportionately high percentage of those who made the move. As this happened, Brian Miller argues , the values of suburbia melded with and shaped the values of evangelicalism. Churches in impoverished neighborhoods are rarely financially self-sustaining—the second challenge. Even if a pastor disciples his church toward generosity, being generous with a poverty-level income won’t pay the bills. So pastors who serve in these places get beaten down by serving a needy congregation while holding two other jobs “on the side.” It’s unsustainable. We don’t believe the answer for inner-city pastors should be a bi- or trivocational life. Solution The solution to these two challenges is within reach: the model of a supported foreign missionary. Since the late 18th century, the church has been training and sustaining men and women for gospel work in unfamiliar places, where they cannot expect the financial support of locals. This training-and-supporting model should be applied to inner-city church planting. The change we need has four aspects. The first is a change of heart. We need gospel-saturated hearts that understand that all people are impoverished by sin. Those living in a homeless encampment share the same fundamental condition as the wealthy suburbanite. Filled with gospel grace, we can move toward the poor because we’re more alike at heart than we are different. Our hearts must be shaped by the reality of Christ’s initiative to leave the riches of heaven for us, to become poor for us, that we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). Second, we need to believe that God’s heart is particularly inclined toward the overlooked (Ps. 72:12–14) and toward those generous toward them (Prov. 14:

articles.title: Report Cards on Your Actions Won’t Fix Your Heart
articles.summary: From GLP-1s to political reposts to mindfulness streaks, we’re all keeping score. Jesus says you can’t know who you are until you look at your heart.

articles.title_zh: 关于您行动的报告卡片无法修复您的心脏
articles.content: Who am I? All cultures, human philosophies, and religious systems try to answer this question in a way that leads to a meaningful life. We want to find in them a path that allows us to say, “Who am I? I’m a good person. I’m someone who is living a good and right life.” What paths toward goodness and righteousness are being offered today? They’re as vast and varied as ever. One popular path is to optimize your life via medical improvements, ranging from plastic surgery to GLP-1s. The more you can “ humanmaxx ” your body to look healthier and be stronger, the more likely you’ll be considered an ideal human being—a good person to hire, to be friends with, to date or marry. Political engagement is another common path. Your goodness is determined by how connected you are to particular political movements. You can feel like you’re a good person when you make sure you quickly like and repost all Zohran Mamdani’s videos. Or alternatively, you’ll be affirmed as a good person by how aggressively you go after or insult people who like Mamdani. Paths our culture offers to the good life are often combined. Your sense of how good a person you are is measured by a mixture of how long you’ve engaged in therapy, how many hours you volunteer at your children’s school, and how long your streak is on your mindfulness app. Tara Isabella Burton, in her book Strange Rites: New Religions for a Godless World , argues that people have formed their own religious systems by drawing from various religions and philosophies. People have become “creators of their own bespoke religions, mixing and matching spiritual and aesthetic and experiential and philosophical traditions.” We’re doing a DIY project, grabbing and piecing together whatever’s around us, hoping we can come up with something to help us in our journey. So, what path does Christianity offer to assure us we’re living a good and righteous life? Keeping Score The Christian approach is to address what the Bible calls the heart. The heart is the Bible’s shorthand term for describing the part of you that drives and motivates you, what dictates your thoughts and emotions. Christianity starts with the heart because this is the only real way by which you can determine who you are and what needs to change. We see the contrast between the religious and cultural approach and the Christian approach in Jesus’s interaction with the Pharisees in Matthew 15:1–20. The Pharisees confront Jesus to ask him why his disciples don’t wash their hands before eating. Handwashing before meals was one of the many religious rules the Pharisees had developed, practiced, and called others to practice. For the Pharisees, the best answer to the question “Who am I?” was based on how well they followed their set standards. If a person kept the standard and had a life that could be observed to follow all the rules, then that person could definitively say to themselves and those around them, “I’m a good person who is living a good and right life.” Jesus’s story about the Pharisee in Luke 18:9–14 is another example. The Pharisee intently notes in his prayer how he, unlike the tax collector praying next to him, fasts twice a week and always gives the full tithe. Jesus describes the Pharisees in Matthew 6 as people who make sure their regular prayers can be seen and affirmed by all. The Pharisees weren’t alone in this approach. Greco-Roman religion had its own rules and standards to follow. Its gods demanded rituals, sacrifices, and festivals to appease and honor them. Performed rightly, they’d result in people securing the blessing they needed from the gods, thus assuring them their lives were good and righteous. Jesus, however, reframes the Pharisees’ questioning by showing that their approach doesn’t go far enough. Right living and human flourishing demands more than one’s outward actions. It requires harder interior examination. And that means looking at the heart. Jesus says, “What comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart” (

你对一个人有多好的感觉,是通过你从事治疗的时间、你在学校志愿工作多少小时、以及你的心智应用上多久来衡量的。

记分 基督教的方法是解决"圣经"所说的"心". 心灵是圣经的简称,用来描述你推动和激励你,决定你思想和情绪的部分。 基督教以心为起点,因为这是你决定自己是谁和需要改变的惟一真正方法.

它的神要求举行仪式,祭祀,并举行节日来安抚和尊崇他们. 让他们得到神赐予的祝福, 但耶稣重新定义了法利赛人的质疑,

articles.content: The following is the substance of a pamphlet published by Archibald G. Brown, a student and then great ally of C. H. Spurgeon in the cause of the gospel in London. Brown here draws attention to a practice that was gaining ground in the churches of his day: that of holding ‘amusements’ of various kinds, which obscured, diverted from, and in some cases replaced the proper ministry of local churches. Brown was savagely attacked in the wake of the publication of the pamphlet, derided as ‘a kill-joy,’ ‘a morbid pietist,’ and ‘a sour bigot.’ His meaning, however, had been deliberately misrepresented. 1 Brown nowhere objects to all amusement per se , but amusement which masquerades as ministry, distracting the church and deceiving needy sinners. While the context in which Brown wrote may be different from ours, we need to hear his burden for a Church—and for Christians—to make a decisive break with the world and its practices. An Evil in the Camp of the Lord DIFFERENT days demand their own special testimony. The watchman who would be faithful to his Lord and the City of his God has need to carefully note the signs of the times and emphasize his witness accordingly. Con­cerning the testimony needed now, there can the little, if any, doubt. An evil is in the professed camp of the Lord—so gross, so brazen in its impudence—that the most short-sighted of spiritual men can hardly fail to notice it. During the past few years it has developed at an ab­normal rate, ever for evil. It has worked like leaven until now the whole lump ferments. Look which way you may, its presence makes itself manifest. There is little if any­thing, to choose between Church, Chapel, or Mission Hall. However they may differ in some respects, they bear a striking likeness in the posters that figure upon and dis­figure their notice boards. Amusement for the people i s the leading article advertised by each. If any of my readers doubt my statement, or think my utterance too sweeping, let them take a tour of inspection and study “the announce­ments for the week” at the doors of the sanctuaries of the neighbourhood; or let them read the religious advertise­ments in their local papers. I have done this again and again, until the hideous fact has been proved up to the hilt, that “amusement” is ousting the preaching of the gospel as the great attraction: “Concerts,” “Entertain­ments,” “Fancy Fairs,” “Smoking Conferences,” “Dramatic Performances,” are the words honoured with biggest type and most startling colours. The burden of the Lord is upon me in this matter The Concert is fast becoming as much a recognised part of church life as the Prayer Meeting, and is already, in most places, far better attended. “Providing recreation for the people” will soon be looked upon as a necessary part of Christian work and as binding upon the Church of God, as though it were a Divine command, unless some strong voices be raised which will make themselves heard. I do not presume to possess such a voice, but I do entertain the hope that I may awaken some louder echoes. Anyway, the burden of the Lord is upon me in this matter, and I leave it with Him to give my testimony ringing tone, or to let it die away in silence. I shall have delivered my soul in either case. Yet the conviction fills my mind that in all parts of the country there are faithful men and women who see the danger and deplore it and will endorse my witness and my warning. Gratifying the Flesh and Retaining a Comfortable Conscience It is only during the past few years that “amusement” has become a recognized weapon of our warfare and de­veloped into a mission. There has been a steady “down grade” in this respect. From “speaking out,” as the Puri­tans did, the Church has gradually toned down her testi­mony; then winked at and excused the frivolities of the day. Then she has tolerated them in her borders, and now she has adopted them and provided a home for them under the plea of “reaching the masses and getting the ear of the

在过去几年里,它以异常的速度发展,永远是邪恶的。 直到现在,它一直工作着,就像离开一样。 看看你们可以走哪条路,它的存在就变得明显了。 教会、礼拜堂或传教堂之间几乎没有任何选择。

然而,它们在某些方面可能有所不同,它们在海报上带有惊人的相似性,这些海报上显示它们的通知板并毁容。 为人民提供娱乐 我是每篇广告的主要文章

如果我的读者怀疑我的发言,或者认为我的言论过于笼统,让他们巡视视察,在附近圣所门口研究“一周的公告”;或者让他们在当地报纸上阅读宗教广告。

在令人发指的事实被证实之前,我一再这样做,即“辱骂”正在驱使福音的传道成为伟大的取景:“关注”、“参与”、“盛会”、“吸烟会”、“戏剧表演”是用最出名和最令人惊叹的颜色表达的言论。

主的重担在我这里 音乐会正迅速成为教会生活中 公认的部分 与祈祷会一样 并且已经,在大多数地方,

“为人民提供娱乐”将很快被视为基督教工作的必要部分,对上帝的教会具有约束力,似乎这是神的命令,除非有人发出强烈的声音,让自己听到。 我并不认为拥有这种声音,但我确实希望能够唤起一些更响亮的回声。

无论如何,上帝的重任 由我负责这件事, 我留给他 让我的证词响亮的语气, 或者让它静静地死去。 无论哪种情况,我都会送出我的灵魂 然而,这一信念使我满怀信心,即全国各地都有忠实的男女看到这种危险并对此感到痛惜,并将赞同我的证人和我的警告。

修行并保持舒适的良知 直到过去几年,“暴行”才成为我们战争的公认武器并发展成一个特派团。 这方面的“级别”稳步下降。 正如普里坦人所做的那样,教会从“大声疾呼”开始,逐渐淡出她的遗言;然后轻视并原谅了今天的纷争。

然后,她在边境上容忍他们,现在她收养了他们,在“影响群众,让人民听到他们的声音”的恳求下,为他们提供了家园。

articles.title_zh: 邪恶如何运作
articles.content: Audio Transcript What does evil look like? And sound like? And feel like? Is evil like a horror film set in a haunted forest in a remote cabin at night with floorboards creaking under uninvited footsteps? Or is evil the most scandalous murder trial in the headlines? Is evil more quiet, like in white-collar crimes and embezzlement? Or is it a bloody civil war? There are many forms evil can take. But at its core, how evil works is more essential than all those things I just described. Today on Ask Pastor John: how evil works. This week in our Bible reading, we come upon a trio of texts that collectively reveal to us Satan’s multifront assault — how he works in this world. He is a spiritual deceiver of minds, he is a prosecuting accuser in the heavenly courtroom, and he is a behind-the-scenes influence in human rebellion. He seems to work in a lot of different ways. In John 8 we see him as a liar and murderer. In 2 Peter 2–3 we see him as the deceiver and destroyer. And in Job 4–6 we see him as the provocateur and accuser. Those roles help reveal his work to us in the world. And as we rehearse these roles in our Bible reading this week, we have this email from an anonymous young man. “Pastor John, when I think about spiritual warfare, I often first think about physical things like illness and addiction and even demonic possession. But I wonder if I am missing a larger picture. How much influence does Satan have in this world, and how does he use it? How much of his power is physical? How much of it is unseen? And where do you see him most at work in our modern culture? Is it in obvious sins? Or in subtler ways to keep people from the gospel? How can I see his work without getting preoccupied with him?” A great question with clear purpose. Here’s how Pastor John answered this very question from a young man named Josh in 2018. How Satan Works The word Satan is a transliteration of the Hebrew Satan (śāṭān) and basically means “opponent” or “adversary.” The Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament always translates Satan with diabolos in Greek, which means “devil”; we always translate diabolos in English, in the New Testament, “devil.” And diabolos puts a more specific focus on the meaning of the opponent or adversary because diabolos basically means “slander” or “accuse.” It’s used not only to refer to the devil; several times in the Pastoral Epistles of Paul, it’s used to refer to people who are slandering others, speaking evil of them, being false about them. So, even though this supernatural being, this fallen angel and archenemy of God, has a remarkable power in the material or physical realm — he can make people sick, he can throw them in prison, he can even kill them — nevertheless, his main way of opposing God and destroying God’s people is not in the physical or material realm but in the mental or intellectual or moral realm. In other words, the best way to think about his power is not in terms of physical strength but moral deception. Let me try to illustrate this from the Bible. Here’s the passage that piles up more designations of Satan than any other passage in the Bible. If you need one or two verses to put the identity and work of Satan before you, it would be Revelation 12:9–10. Here it says, “And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent.” And remember what the Bible said in Genesis 3:1 about him. He’s subtler than every beast. So, it’s his subtlety that’s being focused on in his serpent-like reality. “[He] is called the devil [diabolos: slanderer, liar, cheat] and Satan [adversary], the deceiver of the whole world” (Revelation 12:9). I don’t think you can say anything more sweeping or more basic than Revelation 12:9–10. “The accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God” (Revelation 12:10). So, at the center of Satan’s purpose is to deceive on earth and to accuse in heaven. If he can deceive you about God and Christ, you will perish. If he can successfu

音频记录 邪恶是什么样子? 听起来像? 感觉如何? 邪恶像恐怖片一样 被设定在幽灵森林里 在一个遥远的小屋里 在夜里 地板在不受邀请的脚步下出动? 或者邪恶是头条新闻上 最可耻的谋杀审判? 邪恶是不是更安静, 就像白领犯罪和贪污? 还是一场血腥内战? 邪恶可以采取多种形式。

但从核心上讲,邪恶是如何起作用的 比我刚才描述的那些事情更重要。 今天在"问约翰牧师:邪恶是如何起作用的"上. 这个星期,我们阅读圣经时,看到一连串的文本,这些文本集体向我们揭示了撒旦的多面攻击——他是如何在这个世界上工作的。

他是精神上对思想的欺骗者,是天庭上的起诉者,也是人类叛乱的幕后影响者. 他似乎以很多不同的方式工作. 在约翰8号 我们把他看成一个骗子和杀人犯 2,彼得2,3,我们把他视为欺骗和驱逐舰. 在工作4 -6,我们把他视为挑衅者和控告者。

这些角色有助于向我们揭示他的作品。 当我们在本周的圣经阅读中排练这些角色时, 我们收到一封匿名青年的电子邮件。 “约翰神父,当我想到精神战争时,我常常首先想到身体上的东西,如疾病和成瘾,甚至恶魔般的拥有。 但我想知道我是否错过了更大的画面。

撒旦在这个世界上有多少影响,他如何使用? 他的体能有多强? 有多少是看不见的? 在我们的现代文化中,你在哪里见到他? 是在明显的罪? 还是用更微妙的方式阻止人们接受福音? 我怎么能看他的作品, 一个有明确目的的大问题.

约翰牧师在2018年回答一个名叫乔什的年轻人的问题, 撒旦如何运作 撒旦一词是希伯来撒旦(śāṭān)的转写,基本上是指"反对"或"反派". 希伯来"旧约"的希腊语译名总是用希腊语diabolos来翻译撒旦,意思是"恶魔";

在新约中, 而diabolos则更具体地关注对手或对手的含义,因为diabolos基本上意味着“slander”或“acuse ” 。 它不仅用来指向魔鬼;

因此,尽管这个超自然的存在,这个倒下的天使和上帝的敌人,在物质或物理领域拥有出众的力量——他可以使人们生病,可以把他们扔入监狱,甚至可以杀死他们——尽管如此,他反对上帝和毁灭上帝人民的主要方式并不是在物质或物质领域,而是在精神或智力或道德领域.

换句话说,思考他的力量的最佳方式不是从体力的角度,而是从道德上欺骗. 让我从圣经中说明这一点。 与圣经其他任何段落相比, 如果你需要一两首诗来将撒旦的身份和作品放在你面前,那将是启示录12:9-10.

articles.title: Help for Beginners and Seasoned Preachers: A Review of David Jackman’s From Text to Teaching
articles.summary: Seeing preaching as a science helps us understand that there are tools we can apply to do the work better. Seeing it as an art reminds us that the work requires us to pay attention to the beauty of Bible proclamation.   The post  Help for Beginners and Seasoned Preachers: A Review of David Jackman’s From Text to Teaching  appeared first on  9Marks .
articles.summary_zh: 将讲道视为一门科学有助于我们理解，我们可以运用一些工具来更好地完成工作。把它看作一门艺术提醒我们，这件作品需要我们关注圣经宣讲的美丽。帮助初学者和经验丰富的传教士：大卫·杰克曼（ David Jackman ）的《从文本到教学》（ From Text to Teaching ）一文首先出现在9Marks上。
articles.title_zh: 初学者和经验丰富的传教士的帮助：大卫·杰克曼从文本到教学的回顾
articles.content: Abstract: Jeremy Meeks reviews David Jackman’s From Text to Teaching: A Guide to Preparing Bible Talks and commends it as a helpful resource for anyone who preaches or teaches the Bible in any context. This brief book offers discussions of the art and science of preaching and the process of preparation, and it provides an inside look at Jackman’s own preparation to preach 1 Corinthians 1–4. The final chapters offer checklists that will be practically useful for preachers, and the appendix contains the author’s own template for preparing a Bible talk. Both beginners and seasoned preachers and teachers will benefit from this book. David Jackman, From Text to Teaching: A Guide to Preparing Bible Talks . Matthias Media, 2021. 92 pp. Even seasoned preacher needs to go back to basics sometimes and be refreshed. Similarly, guys starting out need instruction—someone to teach them how to go about the craft. Often the most helpful teachers are those who have lots of experience. What is even better is if such a preacher has also spent substantial time training others to preach. Ideally, that preacher/trainer has such command of the material that he is able to distill his insights and counsel into a tight, readable book. We have been given such a gift in David Jackman’s little volume From Text to Teaching . In just 92 pages, Jackman provides a lifetime of wisdom for the beginner and the seasoned preacher alike. As he explains in the introduction, he is addressing (as evidenced in the title) the skill of Bible teaching more generally and not solely preaching. This might turn away preachers who don’t consider themselves to be giving “Bible talks,” but that would be the preacher’s loss. The weight of what we get to do every time we open the Bible and teach from it in any context is rightly esteemed by Jackman. The Art and Science of Preaching The book begins by discussing the “Art and Science of Preaching.” Both aspects of preaching—art and science—must be held onto if we are to do it well. Seeing preaching as a science helps us understand that there are tools we can apply to do the work better. Seeing it as an art reminds us that the work requires us to pay attention to the beauty of Bible proclamation. Preaching is more than using the Bible to communicate. Rather, our task is to preach what the text says, that is, giving the meaning of what it says, in context, for the people sitting in front of us. Jackman’s convictions will be new to some, common to others, but beneficial to all. The Process of Preparation A substantial chapter is dedicated to the “Process of Preparation”. Here Jackman helps the Bible preacher/teacher think through how to put a message together. As a preacher who trains other preachers, I’m constantly asked how I do this on a weekly basis, and I enjoy hearing how others do it as well. Jackman has sage advice. He reminds us that we should always be praying (an obvious but seriously neglected aspect of preparation). He is also clear that we should use the time we have strategically. We never have as much time as we would like, and we often think we need more time than we do. The fact is that preachers often waste a lot of time because they are not strategic. Jackman recommends setting aside a few blocks of time in the week (four sessions that are each two to three hours). What is vital is that the preacher figures out what works well for him and plans his schedule accordingly. Jackman then gives helpful advice on how to go about studying and writing out the sermon inside those blocks of time, and this advice is helpful for those at all levels of proficiency. Invited into the Author’s Study The next three chapters (3–5) of the book are pure gold. In essence, Jackman invites us into his study to listen in as he walks through his process of preparing messages on 1 Corinthians 1–4. Here we get insights into how his suggested process works in actual texts. This is something many books on preaching neglect to do, leaving the rea
articles.content_zh:
摘要:杰里米·米克(Jeremy Meeks)评论了大卫·杰克曼的"从文字到教学:准备圣经谈话的指南",并称赞它是任何背景中宣扬或教授圣经的人的有用资源. 这本简短的书提供了对布道的艺术和科学以及准备过程的讨论,它提供了杰克曼自己为布道1科林斯1–4的准备的内观.

最后的章节提供了对传道者实际上有用的核对表,附录中包含了作者自己准备圣经演讲的模板. 初学者和老练的传道人和教师都将受益于这本书。 David Jackman,《从文字到教学:准备圣经会谈指南》,Matthias Media,2021年。

甚至老练的传教士有时也需要回到基础,被刷新. 类似地,开始的人需要教书,有人教他们如何操作这款工艺。 最有帮助的教师往往是经验丰富的教师。 更好的是,如果这种传道者也花大量时间训练其他人传道。

理想的情况是,传教士/教官对材料有如此高的指挥力,他能够将自己的见解和咨询意见提炼成一本紧凑可读的书。 在大卫·杰克曼的"从文字到教学"一书中,我们得到了这样的礼物。 在92页里,杰克曼为初学者和老练的传道者提供了一生的智慧.

正如他在导言中所解释的,他正在讨论(如标题所证明的)《圣经》教学的技巧更普遍,而不仅仅是传道。 这可能会让那些不认为自己在进行“圣经会谈”的传道者退后,

每当我们打开圣经并在任何背景中从中教导时,我们所能做的事情的分量都得到了杰克曼的正确尊重. 该书首先讨论了“影响艺术与科学”。 如果我们要做得好,就必须坚持艺术和科学两个方面的传道。

将传道视为一种科学,有助于我们理解,我们可以应用一些工具来更好地开展工作。 把它看作是一门艺术,提醒我们,这部作品需要我们关注"圣经"宣言的美. 意义不仅仅是用"圣经"来沟通.

相反,我们的任务是宣扬案文所说的话,即在背景上赋予案文所述的含义,供坐在我们前面的人民使用。 杰克曼的信念对一些人来说是新的,对另一些人来说是共同的,但对所有人都有好处。 1. 编写过程

在这里,杰克曼帮助"圣经"的传道人/老师思考如何将一个信息集中起来. 作为一名培养其他传教士的传教士, 我经常问每周我怎么做, 杰克曼有圣人的建议 他提醒我们,我们应当永远祈祷(准备工作中一个明显但被严重忽略的方面)。

他还明确指出,我们应该从战略角度利用我们的时间。 我们从来没有像我们想要的那样多的时间,我们常常认为我们需要比我们多的时间。 事实是道教经常会因为不具有战略意义而浪费大量时间. 杰克曼建议在一周内留出几块时间(每两到三小时四会).

重要的是,传道者要知道什么对他很有效,并据此规划他的时间安排。 杰克曼随后就如何研究并写出这些时间段内的布道给出了有益的建议,而这个建议对于所有水平的熟练程度的人都是有帮助的. 书中接下来的三章(3–5)是纯金.

基本上,杰克曼邀请我们进入他的书房 在他行走的过程中聆听 他准备了科林斯1 -4的信息。 在这里,我们深入了解他建议的进程如何在实际文本中发挥作用。 这是很多书 关于布道 忽略做,留下的灵性

articles.title: Claire Rosinkranz Heard God at 11. Now She’s Learning to Hear Him Differently
articles.summary: Six years after a ukulele song made her a TikTok phenomenon, the pop songwriter is learning to hear God differently — and to be okay living in the middle.
articles.summary_zh: 在一首尤克里里歌曲使她成为TikTok现象的六年后，这位流行歌曲作者正在学习以不同的方式聆听上帝—并且可以在中间生活。
articles.title_zh: 克莱尔·罗辛克兰兹（ Claire Rosinkranz ）在11岁时现在，她正在学会以不同的方式倾听他的声音
articles.content: Claire Rosinkranz is trying to describe what the last few years have felt like, and she keeps landing on the same word: momentum. Not the kind she chased. The kind that showed up on its own, at 16, and never fully let her catch up to it. “It feels really good, honestly it’s kind of hard to understand how it feels at all,” she says backstage at a music festival. “When I was 16 I had a lot of crazy momentum, and I’ve been telling my team, I just didn’t realize anything that was happening. And so I still feel like I don’t know what’s happening. But I get to sing and dance.” “Backyard Boy” turned a California teenager with a ukulele and a home studio into one of pop’s more unlikely breakouts, a song that racked up millions of TikTok recreations before she’d finished high school. Rosinkranz was already a lifer by then. She’d been writing songs since she was 8 and training as a ballerina before deciding, at 11, that music was the thing. Now 22, with two albums behind her, she is still working out what it means to have built a career on momentum she never planned for. “I gotta learn a lot of patience,” she says. The success of that first song, she says, set her expectations in a way she’s been unwinding ever since. “I ended up getting a lot of success from that song, and so all I knew was success when it came to music,” she says. “So feeling that kind of ebb and flow has been a challenge.” The deeper lesson has been separating who she is from what she makes. Someone in her life has been trying to drill it into her that her worth doesn’t live in her output. “My identity is not in what I do, but in who I am,” she says. “That can be really hard when you get compliments and value from everything that you do in this world. I’m still learning that there’s a lot of ebbs and flows in this industry, and learning how to be in the middle of that.” Being in the middle of things is a phrase she comes back to more than once, and it stretches past her career into how she talks about God. She grew up with a faith that felt less like a decision than a default setting. “God was kind of in my nature,” she says. “Religion was a little bit more like taught to me.” The distinction matters to her more now than it used to. She describes a recent conversation with her therapist in which she admitted she doesn’t hear God the way she once did, half expecting to be told something was wrong. “I was like, I feel like I don’t hear God that much or in the way that I used to, and she was like, I actually don’t completely agree,” Rosinkranz says. “I think that you maybe just hear God differently. I really resonated with that.” Lately, she’s been wondering whether the change is less about losing God’s voice than learning its new frequency. “I’m really learning how to be in the middle of a lot of things, and being okay with being a little bit more fluid instead of having this really crazy concept of right and wrong,” she says. “I feel like I’m a little bit more black and white than I would like to acknowledge, and you can’t really have a lot of growth or change if you don’t.” Her spiritual life shows up in practical, almost mundane ways. Yoga, horseback riding, long afternoons at the beach. She talks to God the way other people talk to a friend, and she asks for dreams, treating them as ground she can meditate from. But the clearest version of the story lives in a memory she comes back to whenever she needs to remember why she’s doing any of this. She was 11, in the back of her cousin’s car, weighing a choice between two loves: ballet and music. “I was sitting there and I was like, God, am I gonna do dance or music, because I was also very passionate about ballet,” she says. “I swear that I heard this other voice that wasn’t myself. 克莱尔·罗辛克兰兹(Claire Rosinkranz)试图描述过去几年的感受,她不断以同一个词来登陆:"动力". 不是她追求的那种 那种在16岁的时候独自出现 却从未完全让她赶上 在音乐节的后台,

“当我16岁时, 我有很多疯狂的动力, 所以我仍然觉得自己不知道发生了什么。

但我可以唱歌跳舞。 “Backyard Boy ” ( Backyard Boy ) , 将一个带着一首乌克勒和一家家庭工作室的加州青少年变成了一个更不可能突围的流行作曲家,这首歌在她读完高中之前就挤出数百万个TikTok娱乐。 罗辛克兰兹那时已经是个活人了 她从八岁起就开始写歌,

现在22号,她身后有两张专辑,她仍然在想着在她从未计划过的动力上建立事业的意义. 她说,“我必须学会很多耐心。” 她说,第一首歌的成功使她的期望定下来,从那时起,她一直没有变。 “我最后从这首歌中获得了很多成功,

“因此,感到这种喘息和流动是一个挑战。” 更深刻的教训是 将她是谁 与她所做的。 她一生中有人一直试图钻入她身上, “我的身份不在于我的工作,而在于我是谁。” “当你从你在这个世界上所做的一切中获得赞美和价值时,那会很难。

我仍然在学习这个行业中有很多东西, 身处中间是她不止一次的复出语句,从她的职业生涯延伸到她如何谈论上帝. 她长大时的信仰 感觉不像是决定 她说,“上帝是我的天性。”

“宗教更像是教我的。” 区别对她来说比以前更重要 她描述最近与治疗师的谈话, 她承认自己听不到上帝的旨意,

”罗辛克兰兹说, “我认为你也许只是听到上帝不同的声音。 我确实对此有共鸣。” 最近,她一直在想,改变是否与其说是失去上帝的声音,不如说是学习新的频率。

“我真的在学习如何在很多事情中间,

“我觉得我比我想承认的要黑白一点, 她的精神生活以实用,几乎平庸的方式出现. 瑜伽,骑马出行,长午入海. 她跟上帝说话 就像别人跟朋友说话一样 她要求做梦 把他们当作可以冥想的地面

但最清晰的剧本仍停留在记忆中, 她当时11岁,在她表哥的车后座上,权衡了两种爱的选择:芭蕾和音乐. “我坐在那,我就像,上帝,我要跳舞还是音乐,因为我对芭蕾也非常热情。”

「我发誓, 我听到另一个声音, 这就是真正把我带到今天这个地步的事物和声音。” 之后她直接去找了母亲. 她记得曾告诉她, “看到一切真的很酷。

articles.title_zh: N.T.赖特：基督徒需要一个比我们大多数人所描绘的更大的神
articles.content: N.T. Wright was a boy in a choir singing Handel’s Messiah when Isaiah first got into his head. “Comfort, comfort my people” and “He was wounded for our transgressions” became part of his mental furniture, he says, and the furniture stayed. By his teens he loved the book enough to consider an Old Testament PhD. He chose Romans instead, partly because Paul quotes Isaiah constantly and gave him a lifelong excuse to keep going back. His new book Into the Heart of Isaiah: The Meaning and Message of Isaiah 40-55 is what came of it, a walk through sixteen chapters he calls one of the most extraordinary poems ever written. If they had been dug out of a scroll in the sands of Libya or Jordan, he told RELEVANT, the whole world would put them on the front page. “This is an amazing piece of writing.” Because they sit in the middle of the Old Testament, he says, many readers just think “bit of the Bible, not sure what that’s about.” He reads them three ways: as the ancient Israelites heard them, as Jesus and the apostles used them, and as they speak to the Church now. Starting with the first, Wright says, “gives us a kind of stability to any other interpretations we then come to.” Some of the best-known lines in American Christianity come from these chapters, including “Mount up with wings as eagles” and “No weapon formed against thee shall prosper.” Wright says anyone reaching for that second verse should remember that an enemy may be claiming the same verse for themselves. After all, in the First World War, British and German forces sang some of the same hymns and claimed the same God’s protection. Context helps, he says, even if we never get all of it. These chapters are addressed to a people exiled for their sin and told that God has dealt with it. Read them as a promise about my success, my salvation, a happy marriage or a thriving business, and “that’s not the story that those verses belong to.” God can give those things, he says, usually inside a larger story about belonging to a people sent to the world, which “may involve pain, suffering, renunciation, et cetera, as well as fulfillment. But let’s never imagine that they’re the whole thing.” He starts the exile story with Adam and Eve, the first people sent out of the garden, and says Israel was the people called to rescue the whole human race, which is why exile brought despair. A people in that position needs forgiveness as well as a way home. The center of the passage, as he reads it, is that God, who had left Jerusalem and the temple to their fate, “is coming back himself in person to sort it all out.” The New Testament applies the same words to John the Baptist getting ready for Jesus. War, Money and Sex Asked whether exile describes the Church now, Wright says he is careful. Five centuries ago Martin Luther wrote about the Babylonian captivity of the Church and cast himself as the one leading it home, a story Wright calls a gross oversimplification, one Luther may have come to see as “over-egging the pudding.” Exile follows idolatry, though, so he names the idols he sees: Mars, Mammon and Aphrodite, or war, money and sex. Each one makes demands and shuts down objections. The military needs it, the markets need it, everybody does it. Part of the problem, he says, is that the Western Church “has joined in the worship of war, has joined in the worship of money, has joined in the worship or at least the collusion with erotic love.” He adds that people need money and defense, and that God gave us our erotic selves. “But when you make them idols and when you give them power over you, then as individuals and as a culture and alas as a church, you’re heading for the rocks.” The rebuke he returns to most is about heaven. The idea that Christianity is about a soul going to heaven when it dies, he says, comes from Plato and from writers like Plutarch, a pagan priest, and not from the Bible. “The name of the game in Christianity is that heaven is going to come to earth.” He points to the
articles.content_zh:
N. T. Wright是唱着汉德尔的弥赛亚的合唱团中的一个男孩,当时以赛亚刚入脑. 他说,“安慰我的人,安慰我的人”和“他因我们的过错而受了伤”,成为他精神家具的一部分,家具也留下了。 在他十几岁的时候,他喜欢这本书 足以考虑一个旧约博士。

他选择了罗马人取而代之,部分原因是保罗不断引用以赛亚的话,并给了他终生的借口来继续后行. 他的新书"入以赛亚之心:以赛亚40-55的意义与信息"正是由此而来,他通过16个章节的走来,称这为有史以来最出众的一首诗.

如果从利比亚或约旦的沙子上挖出卷轴,他告诉相关人士,全世界都会把它们放在头版。

“这是一部惊人的著作。” 因为他们坐在《旧约》的中间,他说,许多读者只是认为“圣经的比特词,不知道是什么。 ” 他读了他们三种方式:古代以色列人听到他们,耶稣和使徒使用他们,现在他们向教会说话.

或他们自己。 毕竟,在第一次世界大战中,英国和德军演唱了部分同名颂歌并声称得到同名神的保护. 他说,即使我们永远得不到一切,背景还是有帮助的。 这些章节是针对一个因罪行被放逐的民族的,并告诉上帝已经处理了.

读这些诗句是为了保证我的成功、我的救赎、幸福的婚姻或兴旺的生意,并且“这些诗句不属于这个故事。” 他说,上帝可以给这些东西,通常是在一个关于属于被送到世界的民族的大故事中,“这可能涉及痛苦、痛苦、放弃等等,以及实现。

但让我们永远不要想象, 他以亚当和夏娃为开头的放逐故事,第一批被派出花园的人,并说以色列是被叫来拯救整个人类的人,这就是放逐带来绝望的原因. 处于这种地位的人既需要宽恕,也需要回家。

正如他所读到的,通道的中心是让耶路撒冷和圣殿走向命运的上帝,“正在亲自回来整理一切。” "新约"对浸信会的约翰(John) 准备接受耶稣也适用了同样的话. 战争、金钱和性问题问流亡者是否描述教会,

5个世纪前,马丁·路德(Martin Luther)写了一篇关于巴比伦人对教会的囚禁并把自己当做回家的领头羊,莱特(Wright)称这故事过于简单化,一位路德(Luther)可能已经看成是“过度的布丁了 ” 。 出走虽然跟随偶像,所以取出他所见到的偶像的名字:火星,马蒙和阿佛洛狄忒,或者战争,金钱和性.

每一个都提出要求并关闭反对。 军方需要它,市场需要它,每个人都这样做。 他说,问题的一部分是西方教会“加入了对战争的崇拜,加入了对金钱的崇拜,加入了对金钱的崇拜,或者至少与色情爱相勾结”。 他补充说,人们需要金钱和防卫,上帝给了我们自己的性。

“当你们以偶像为偶像,当你们以个人、文化、教堂为主宰时,你们就走向石头去。” 他回到多数人的责难 是关于天堂的 他说,基督教是关于灵魂去天堂的观念,来自柏拉图和普鲁塔克等作家,是异教牧师,而不是圣经.

“在基督教中,游戏的名称是天堂将降临到地上。” 他说
