featured.content: I regret to inform you, dear reader, that heaven tourism is back. The genre possibly never went away entirely, but it did at least disappear from the bestseller lists for several years. Sadly, it has returned in Gabe Poirot’s 18 Days in Heaven , which was one of the bestselling Christian books last month and even made its way to the New York Times list of bestsellers—a feat most authors can only dream of. Out of sheer magnanimity (and perhaps a morbid sense of curiosity), I read it so you don’t have to. 18 Days in Heaven Gabe Poirot Before I tell you what it’s all about, here’s a brief history of heaven tourism. Don Piper kicked off the genre in 2004 with 90 Minutes in Heaven , and it proved a surprise hit that quickly dominated the sales charts, eventually tallying upwards of 8 million copies sold. Todd Burpo’s Heaven Is for Real followed in 2010 with over 10 million copies sold. That same year brought Kevin and Alex Malarkey’s The Boy Who Came Back from Heaven , which sold more than a million copies before Alex recanted his story and the publisher pulled it. The genre went on to deliver many more heaven books and a handful of less-popular hell books like Bill Wiese’s 23 Minutes in Hell , though none ever reached the same heights as the first few—no pun intended. My contribution to the genre was little more than reviewing several of the books and coining the snarky phrase “heaven tourism,” which, much to my delight, soon caught on . The genre inevitably ran its course, but has now returned in Gabe Poirot’s 18 Days in Heaven: I Left My Body. I Met Jesus. What He Told Me Will Alter Your Eternity . Sadly, but not surprisingly, it is just as bad as its predecessors, mixing truth with errors and documented facts with spurious speculations until it is as confusing and unreliable as any of them. 18 Days in Heaven follows the standard pattern by beginning with an account of a terrible accident—in this case, a head injury that resulted from a skateboarding mishap. Poirot, a young evangelist with a sizable YouTube following, was rendered comatose and remained hovering between life and death for 18 days. But while his body was inert, his soul was transported to heaven, where it experienced heavenly wonders, not the least of which was spending time with Jesus. What did he see and experience there? Many things, of course, some of which he is able to describe and many of which he insists he cannot, either because God told him not to or because they defy description. What can he describe? Jesus’s eyes, in which “I saw all the colors that had ever existed or could exist, all in one. He was the deepest ocean of liquid love that had no end. A spectrum of intensity that only increased the longer I stared. His eyebrows, hair, jawline, arms, chest, heart, stature, ears, forehead, eyelashes, teeth, mouth, skin, and complexion all said the same thing: I love you, I love you, I love you.” He describes Jesus’s scars which “were like an ocean that had no floor,” and had the name “Gabriel” written immediately above them. He learned from them that Jesus has completely and eternally forgotten his sins so that he could no longer remember them even if he wanted to. He smelled Jesus and observed that his “fragrance wasn’t like the humidity of the Florida Everglades. No, this was something eternal—an everlasting fountain of fire, not just surrounding me but burning into me. Wrapping around me like a robe, like a living garment of pure, unending presence. It felt burning hot and freezing cold at the same time.” He heard Jesus say many words and noted that his “words were not just a separate entity that He ‘released.’ They were like the sharpest spears that went right into the core of my very being. But these spears were not separate from Him—they were Him.” Poirot even saw his own conception: “The light from Father God united with the earthly seed from my father and the egg of my mother in that moment, and I began my existence on earth. featured.content_zh:
我很遗憾地告诉你,亲爱的读者 天堂旅游又回来了 流派可能从未完全消失,但至少从畅销书榜上消失了几年.

不幸的是,它回到了Gabe Poirot的"天堂18天"中,这是上个月最畅销的基督教书籍之一,甚至走进了纽约时报畅销书榜,这是大多数作者只能梦想的功绩。 我读了这篇文章,

同年,凯文和亚历克丝·马拉克的"从天堂回来的男孩"(The Boy Who Came from Heaven)也带来了,后者在亚历克丝收回他的故事并被出版商拉出之前就售出超过一百万份. 虽然没有人能达到与前几本书相同的高度,

我对这个流派的贡献不过是回顾几本书, 但现在又回到了Gabe Poirot在天堂的18天:我离开了我的身体。 我遇见了耶稣。 他告诉我 Will 改变你的永恒

可悲但并不令人惊讶的是,它同其前身一样糟糕,把事实与错误相混淆,把有记录的事实同虚假的猜测相混淆,直到它同其中任何一个都一样令人困惑和不可靠。 18天的"天堂"遵循了标准模式,首先讲述了一起可怕的事故——在此情况下,由于滑板出事而造成头部受伤.

Poirot是一位年轻的福音传播者,他带着一个庞大的YouTube跟随,因此被昏迷并徘徊在生与死之间长达18天. 但虽然他的身体是惰性的,他的灵魂被运到了天堂,在那里它经历了天堂的奇事,其中最起碼是和耶稣一起度过. 他在那里看到了什么? 体验什么?

当然,许多事情,有些是他能够描述的,有些是他坚持不能描述的,要么是因为上帝告诉他不要描述,要么是因为他们藐视描述。 他能描述什么? 耶稣的眼睛,其中,“我看到了曾经存在或可能存在的所有颜色,都是一种颜色。 他是无尽的液体爱最深的海洋

Over the weekend you’ll find Saturday’s Weekend A La Carte plus Sunday’s Works & Wonders, which shares content that is just right for a Sunday morning. I hope you enjoy reading it all as much as I have enjoyed putting it together. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals are headlined by Joel Beeke’s A Radical, Comprehensive Call to Holiness . You may also be interested in a book about women who overcame a difficult past or a biography written for a younger audience. Recommended Reading Selfies Are Not the Self: Forming Embodied Youth in a Disembodied Age. This article from Harvest USA has some helpful insights about young people and their mobile devices. “Increasingly, research shows that teenagers know their technology is making them miserable. They don’t love their phones, but they hate missing out. They know the noise is making them sick, but they’re terrified of the silence. When teenagers are so thirsty for connection and validation that they’ll go to a well they know is poisoned just to get a drink, what an amazing opportunity we have as the church to offer something better, something truly beautiful. We don’t want our youth ministries to be known for what they lack. We want them to be known for their abundance.” Can’t You Just Love Everyone? Jeremy Walker addresses churches that think their calling is to “just love everyone.” “Why not just love one another? Why build walls, make distinctions, establish boundaries, and draw lines? Why confront sins? Why not welcome all equally? Can’t you just love everyone?” 4 Applications for the Order of Love—From the Home to the Ends of the Earth. Speaking of love, Alex Kocman addresses the necessity of rightly ordering our love. “Augustine’s idea of ordo amoris —the ‘order of love’—reflects the Scriptural pattern of directing our affections to first love God, then to love our families, and then to extend that love outward to others. This theme of ordered love has wide-ranging implications—from the home to the ends of the earth. But just as preaching without application is lifeless, so too is a study of love without practical exhortation. Here are four admonitions…” Effective Altruists and the Spreadsheet Gospel. Writing for TGC, Nathan Leamer addresses the effective altruism ideology that is so influential in Silicon Valley. “Over the past decade, an emergent secular philosophy has taken root in Silicon Valley. It now drives many conversations around politics and technology, particularly as its ideas shape how our society approaches artificial intelligence. Known as ‘effective altruism,’ this worldview is having a moment. The Economist recently called the philosophy ‘this century’s biggest idea’ and labeled the movement as ‘admirable, but dangerous.'” Your Thoughts Are Shaping Your Life. “Your thoughts are shaping your life.” That might sound like the kind of thing Joel Osteen or a New Age practitioner would say, but there is truth to it. “Our thought life matters more than we often realize. The conversations we replay in our minds, the offenses we revisit, and the fears we entertain can shape how we see our circumstances and respond to the people around us. I know how easily my thoughts can become consumed by something that has happened or something I fear might happen. Before long, I find myself responding to the present through the lens of thoughts I have been rehearsing.” Don’t Despise the Red Flags. featured.title_zh: 周末单点菜肴（ 11月7日）
featured.content: Welcome to Weekend A La Carte. I hope you find something here, whether a longform article, a reader recommendation, or something else entirely, that makes your weekend just a little bit better. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include several newer and older books that are all worth at least thinking about. If you’re interested in doing some theological reading, Westminster Books is offering up to 57% off the three-volume set of Warfield’s works. Also, I haven’t reviewed it yet, but did want to briefly recommend the new graphic novel adaptation of Pilgrim’s Progress . It seems to be priced just about equally at Westminster Books and Amazon (for me, at least). Recommended Reading Canada’s Maclean’s magazine has an interesting article about the Hutterites and their caution when it comes to modern technologies. The author, like so many of us, is alarmed by the ways technology overtakes our lives, and sees that the Hutterites may have a healthier relationship to it. Most of us—including me—are worried that we’ve all become desensitized to the manifold and multiplying ways technology is negatively affecting our lives. Social media has been blamed for rising rates of political polarization and radicalization, damaging young people’s ability to form relationships and eroding mental health. And we’re all trying to figure out what to do about it. Slick startups sell devices you tap with your phone to “brick” it (that is, blocking distracting social media, apps and internet access). There are apps to remove short-form videos from social media feeds. There are now social media bans in place for youth in Australia, in parts of Europe and Asia and, this June, proposed in Canada. Sales of dumbphones and flip phones have grown in the past few years. Even landlines are trendy again. But this is like pushing back the tide with a broom. For most of us, technology feels like a force of nature that will wash over us whether we want it to or not. The Hutterites are more optimistic. They think if they can keep their distance from the wider world, and adopt the right set of rules around technology, they can hold onto its positive features and simply seal out what they don’t like. Read: The Hutterites’ Guide to Technology. The New York Times was in touch with many Gen Zers and explains how their entry into the job market is much different from previous generations. I think it’s easy for those of us who are older to act as if Gen Z is lazy or otherwise not putting in much effort, but this article ought to give us some compassion. They described a process that is lonely, opaque and impersonal, in which it is hard to tell whether one is being rejected by a hiring manager or an A.I. screener. The problem is not just that hiring has slowed across the labor market, or that the specter of A.I. is threatening entry-level positions, they said. It was that they could not get a real, live human being to speak to them. Ever. About anything. The same language came up over and over in their responses: They felt as if they were throwing their applications into “the void.” Some of them opted for slightly different terminology — a “black hole” or an “abyss” — but they painted a similar picture of the application process as a swirling vortex where aspirations and cover letters vanish, unlikely to be retrieved. One part that jumped out to me was the person who insists on they/them pronouns. I would imagine that is a huge red flag for people in charge of hiring! Read: Searching for Jobs, Gen Z Feels Like It’s Staring Into ‘The Void’. The Verge has a lengthy article that describes the bizarre and heterodox gospel according to Peter Thiel. It’s a time of apocalyptic worldviews in Silicon Valley. The latest AI doom cycle is driven by effective altruism (EA), a philosophy that has lurked around the fringes for years but recently burst into the mainstream because its adherents are embedded across the AI industry, from Anthropic to newly appointed AI safety watchdog METR. featured.content: October was a strong month for new Christian books. I tried to keep you in the loop week by week, but I also wanted to provide a roundup for the end of the month. Of all the books that came our way in October, here are the ones that most stood out to me, arranged in what I think is a nice new format. As always, I’ve included the publisher’s editorial description for each. Book of the Month Crossway · Hardcover · 736 pages The Westminster Confession of Faith: A Comprehensive Commentary on Its History, Theology, and Application Edited by J. V. Fesko, John R. Muether, and D. Blair Smith If I had to put one book on the top of the stack this month, it would probably be this commentary on the Westminster Confession of Faith—and I say that as a Baptist who respects, but does not hold to, the WCF. The contributors include Sinclair Ferguson, Chad Van Dixhoorn, and Kevin DeYoung. This is a reference work that pastors and serious readers will want to add to their libraries. “This essential collection of essays presents an accessible guide to the Westminster Confession of Faith for 21st-century readers. Each chapter is devoted to a section of the historic document, carefully studying its context, its significance to the faith, and its application, as well as any controversies.” Buy it at Amazon · Westminster Books For Your Own Soul Books for any thoughtful Christian reader. Crossway · Hardcover · 264 pages Finally Home: The Christian Hope of Heaven Dane Ortlund In this book, Dane Ortlund ( Gentle and Lowly ) turns his attention to heaven. He draws on Scripture, of course, and also on writers like Thomas Goodwin, Jonathan Edwards, and C. S. Lewis. “If we are not in Christ, this life is the best we will ever experience. If we are in Christ, this life is the worst we will ever experience. … In Finally Home , Dane Ortlund plunges into the word of God and the wisdom of the saints to help us rightly think about heaven, and to draw strength from our coming future more deeply than we ever have before.” Buy it at Amazon · Westminster Books IVP · Paperback · 192 pages Everyday Discipleship: How Faith Shapes the Most Practical Areas of Life Jeremy Treat This is a practical book that teaches how following Jesus extends into every part of life, including those that are very ordinary, like meals, work, rest, and technology. It includes a discussion guide for groups. “Pastor Jeremy Treat understands this disconnect. In Everyday Discipleship , he dismantles the harmful sacred-secular divide that leaves many Christians feeling spiritually compartmentalized, uncertain about how faith applies to ordinary life, and unable to fully enjoy Christ in the entirety of our lives.” Buy it at Amazon Banner of Truth · Clothbound · 248 pages God Is Our Refuge and Strength: 150 Devotionals Through the Psalms William Boekestein & Rob Ventura Every Banner of Truth release is noteworthy, isn’t it? featured.content: Good morning. My gratitude goes to Ligonier Ministries for sponsoring the blog this week to ensure you know about the new Grow app . It’s a free download and offers a lot of great content. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include a variety of deals spanning a bunch of different eras and genres. Recommended Reading Jessica Lee writes about the growing no contact movement in which people sever their relationships with people they find toxic or problematic. I think of the young women I mentor who are flooded with reels, encouraging them that the best way to deal with the strained relationship with their mom is to put up higher boundaries that limit contact, or to cut off contact altogether. Even if they don’t take these drastic measures, they cannot help being influenced by the ideas, and neither can we. We are steeped in a therapy culture that talks a lot more about self-care than self-sacrifice, and we would be naive if we didn’t acknowledge the formative influence it has on us. And so, when relationships (whether with a parent, sibling, or friend) get hard, as they inevitably will, our first impulse is often toward self-preservation (putting up higher boundaries) and not self-sacrificial presence and faithfulness. Read: Going No Contact?: Ruth and Faithful Presence. Madeline Livingston has been going through a time of deep sorrow, and from that perspective writes a meditation about grief and glory. In my grief, I can turn to a Savior who has known human frailty and deep suffering, a Savior who in his most desperate moment prayed, “Let this cup pass from me. Yet not as I will, but as you will” ( Matthew 26:39 ). I can trust in the goodness and provision of a Father who did spare his own Son, but gave him up to rescue us and make us his own ( Romans 8:32 ). I can rest in the compassion of a Maker who collects all my tears in his bottle ( Psalm 56:8 ), a Good Shepherd who carries me safely through the lowest valley and restores my soul ( Psalm 23 ). As Sorrow and Suffering take me by the hand, they invite me to run to the solid ground of God’s promises made yes and amen through Christ. They urge me on to seek solace in the only place it can truly be found, in a arms of a Father who is my “refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” ( Psalm 46:1 ). Read: When Sorrow & Suffering Take You by the Hand. Sarah Eekhoff Zylstra did a lot of interviews to try to arrive at some best practices for churches that are evangelistically effective. Her article offers a lot of food for thought. Thirty years ago, evangelical churches leaned on programs like Evangelism Explosion or Continuous Witness Training to deliver evangelistic focus and training, church leader Thom Rainer said. Those structured initiatives fit well in a culture that was more Christian and more institutionalized—it took an average of 20 church members to reach one person for Christ per year. Today, it takes 50, Rainer said. “Evangelism efficacy, evangelism effectiveness, has definitely diminished.” That trend is likely to continue. As social media and AI fill our time and increase our social anxiety, even relational evangelism is growing more difficult. Read: Best Practices from Evangelistically Effective Churches. Like Darryl Dash, I’ve been hearing and reading a lot of doom and gloom lately, much of it related to the rise of AI. But also like Darryl, I don’t feel particularly alarmed. I read quite a few predictions of doom over the weekend, including some from self-professed tech optimists. Supposedly, some infrastructure in the United States is under attack. The idea is that AI is becoming too powerful and will overwhelm whatever safeguards we have in place to protect things like our water systems and electricity. The proposed solution is to prepare for the disaster by buying generators, solar panels for generators, and stockpiling water and other basic supplies. However, the authors acknowledge that there is little we can do to truly protect ourselves from the da
featured.content_zh: 早上好,你好吗? 感谢利戈尼耶各部赞助本周的博客, 这是免费的下载, 今天的销售和交易包括一系列跨越不同时代和流派的交易。 建议阅读 Jessica Lee写道,人们与他们发现有毒或有问题的人们断绝关系,但这种接触运动却在不断增加。 我想到那些我辅导的年轻女性,她们被卷轴淹没,鼓励她们,处理与母亲的紧张关系的最佳方式是设置更高的界限限制接触,或者完全切断接触. 即使他们不采取这些激烈的措施,他们也受不了这些想法的影响,我们也不能这样做。 我们身处一种治疗文化中,谈论自我护理比自我牺牲要多得多,如果我们不承认它对我们的形成影响,我们就会天真。 因此,当关系(无论是与父母、兄弟还是朋友的关系)变得困难时,我们的第一个冲动是往往朝向自我保护(提出更高的界限),而不是自我神圣的存在和忠诚。 读:去去不接触? 鲁斯和忠实的存在。 马德琳·利文斯通经历了一段深深的悲痛时期,从这个角度看,他写了一篇关于悲痛和荣耀的冥想. 在我悲痛中,我可以求助于一个知道人类脆弱和深重苦难的救世主,一个在他最绝望的时刻祈祷的救世主,“让这个杯子从我身边流过。 然而,不是我愿意,而是你愿意”(Matthew 26:39.). 我可以相信一个父亲的善良和供养,他确实饶了自己的儿子,但为了拯救我们而放弃了他,使我们成为自己的父亲(罗马8:32. 我可以安心地忍受一个造物主的怜悯,他把所有的眼泪都收在他的瓶中(诗篇56:8),一个好牧人,他把我安全地带入最底层的山谷并恢复我的灵魂(诗篇23. 当悲伤和受苦将我牵上手时,他们邀请我跑到上帝通过基督许下的承诺的坚实地步。 他们敦促我在一个真正能找到的地方寻求安慰,在一个父亲的怀抱中,他是我的“抵抗和力量,在困难中非常现成的帮助”(第46:1段)。 读取:"悲伤"和"受苦受难"由"手取""你"时. Sarah Eekhoff Zylstra做了很多访谈,试图为福音派有效的教堂达成一些最佳做法. 她的文章为思考提供了很多食物. 教会领袖汤姆·赖纳(Thom Rainer)说, 这些结构化的倡议非常适合一种更加基督教化和更加制度化的文化——平均每年需要20名教会成员为基督而接触一个人。 今天,它需要50,雷纳说。 “福音会的功效,福音会的功效,肯定已经下降。” 这一趋势很可能继续下去。 由于社交媒体和AI填补了我们的时间并增加了我们的社会焦虑,甚至连关系福音派也越来越困难. 读取:Evangelistic 有效教会的最佳做法。 与达里尔·达什(Darryl Dash)一样, 我最近也听到并阅读了许多末日与忧郁, 但与达里尔一样, 我读到很多关于周末末日的预言, 包括一些自以为是的技术乐观主义者的预言。 假设美国的一些基础设施受到攻击。 这个想法是AI正在变得太强大,并且会压倒我们现有的保护诸如我们的供水系统和电力之类的东西的保障措施. 拟议的解决办法是通过购买发电机、发电机太阳能电池板以及储存水和其他基本用品来为灾难做好准备。 然而,作者们承认,我们无法真正保护自己,使其免受歧视。

featured.summary: It’s difficult to discern whether someone has been converted if you’re hazy on what conversion is.   The post  Why the Doctrine of Conversion Matters for Membership Interviews  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.summary_zh: 如果你不知道什么是皈依，就很难辨别某人是否已经皈依。帖子Why the Doctrine of Conversion Matters for Membership Interviews首次出现在9Marks上。
featured.title_zh: 为什么转换原则对会员面试很重要
featured.content: Abstract: David Burnette explains why the doctrine of conversion is so crucial for pastors and churches as they carry out their responsibilities in affirming new members as believers. We must not only understand what conversion is but also be able to apply it to the lives of real people. After giving some basic reminders about membership interviews and identifying things that we are not looking for as evidence of conversion, Burnette provides four questions to help us evaluate whether a prospective member has been converted. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . “I wasn’t living right. I was getting drunk, partying, just doing whatever I wanted. And then it was like God just stopped me in my tracks. I knew something had to change. That’s when I started coming to church, and one Sunday, I felt like the preacher was talking directly to me. Right then I knew I needed to become a Christian, and I got baptized a few weeks later. That was about a year ago, and ever since then I’ve pretty much been coming to church and trying to do what’s right.” That’s how Ben responded when you asked him how he became a Christian. Ben recently moved to your city, and he just completed your church’s four-week New Members Class. Now, as the final step in the process—often called a “membership interview”—you as a pastor must decide whether you will recommend Ben for membership at the next members’ meeting. For the purposes of this article, I’m concerned primarily with the question of whether Ben is converted. I’m assuming he meets your church’s other membership requirements. No doubt you’ve heard similar testimonies, even if the details differ. There’s been some kind of change in the person’s life, and they seem sincere, but it’s not yet clear that this change was rooted in the gospel. So you’ll need to do some more probing. Putting Our Doctrine of Conversion to Work Testimonies like Ben’s remind us why having a biblical doctrine of conversion is so crucial when it comes to the church’s responsibility to affirm new members as believers. After all, it’s difficult to discern whether someone has been converted if you’re hazy on what conversion is . For an explanation of the doctrine of conversion, see Michael Lawrence, Conversion (Crossway, 2017); see also the article by Gregg Allison titled “You Can’t Make I t Happen: The Spirit and the Doctrine of Conversion” in this issue of Church Matters . Testimonies like Ben’s also remind us that we must be able to apply our doctrine of conversion to real-life people in real-life situations. Some prospective members will be new Christians, while others will be less mature in their faith; some will have been converted for years but still have significant blind spots; still others will think they’re Christians when they haven’t truly been converted. And those aren’t the only complicating factors. Some will have a hard time articulating the very truths they profess; others will fail to mention basic aspects of the gospel in their interview; more than a few will be unsure as to how and when they recognized their need for a Savior. All these factors (and more) mean that wisdom and discernment are needed when we are interviewing prospective members. Reminders for Our Approach Before thinking through some practical ways to probe further with testimonies like Ben’s, a few basic reminders may be helpful. Your Knowledge Is Limited Unlike Jesus, we can’t look into a person’s heart, which means our decisions about someone’s spiritual state are never infallible. The very fact that Jesus gave instructions about excommunication indicates that he knew the church would sometimes welcome in those who weren’t truly converted (see Matt. 18:15–18). Even the apostle Paul was wrong about his one-time co-worker Demas. Prior to Demas’s departure, Paul mentions him twice when he refers to his fellow workers in the gospel ministry (Col. 4:14; Ph lm. 24). Ou

featured.title: Unclear Evangelism Leads to Unclear (and False) Conversions
featured.summary: When we appeal to people’s carnal desires, we should not be surprised when our “converts” are more in love with the world than with our Savior.   The post  Unclear Evangelism Leads to Unclear (and False) Conversions  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.summary_zh: 当我们呼吁人们的肉体渴望时，当我们的「皈依者」更爱世界而不是我们的救主时，我们不应该感到惊讶。“不明确的传福音导致不明确（和虚假）的转换”一文首先出现在9Marks上。
featured.title_zh: 不明确的传福音会导致不明确（和虚假）的皈依
featured.content: Abstract: John Lee explains how bad evangelistic methods and approaches can lead to false conversions. When we are unclear about the urgency of conversion, the cost of conversion, or the accountability that should accompany conversion, we risk leaving people deceived about their eternal state. Ultimately, our job is simply to proclaim the gospel clearly, trust God to open people’s hearts to the truth, and provide ongoing discipleship to those who respond in repentance and faith. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . Maybe you’re like me and you grew up in a church that did altar calls. My church’s zeal for evangelism was real, and I can still tell you the names of individuals who came to know the Lord through those gospel presentations. But like me, you may also have walked down the aisle to accept Jesus as your Lord and Savior at least five times. The thing is, I believe I was sincere every time I walked the aisle. So why do it over and over again? There was clearly a misunderstanding, despite my church’s good intentions—and my own. The methodology of our ministry affects the fruit of our ministry. Or as Mark Dever has put it, “What you win them with is what you win them to .” Unclear invitations often lead to confused converts. Below I want to consider three different ways this lack of clarity in our evangelism manifests itself and how this can lead to conversions that, in time, prove themselves false. Unclear Urgency I was a disobedient kid. When my mother was particularly exasperated, she’d count down from ten. I had a choice: either obey or dig my heels in and rebel. But as I grew older, I became immune to her shot clock and more accustomed to her threats. My mom’s words fell on deaf ears. Bad evangelism capitalizes on this kind of “countdown” strategy. It puts eternity in the balance based on a singular moment and a one-time decision to follow God—or abandon him forever. And while unbelievers may initially respond positively, their “faith” often doesn’t last. As a result, they may become immune to the gospel because they assume they’ve already tried it. “But,” you might say, “isn’t conversion an urgent matter? Do we not care about people’s eternal destiny?” Absolutely! But we want to place appropriate pressure on their conscience, not just on their choice. Unbelievers need to make a thoughtful decision rather than simply meeting our demands in a singular moment in time. Panic urges them to turn off their critical thinking for the sake of survival. The focus is on an immediate decision rather than the weight of God’s eternal judgment. Unclear Cost At the same time, panicked evangelism is sometimes replaced with what we might call chill evangelism. Chill evangelism attempts to downplay urgency in order to make the decision to follow Jesus more palatable. To take one example, some recent invitations have defined following Jesus as “doing as he did.” The call is to adopt his behavior, particularly his compassion toward the brokenhearted. But following Jesus is about more than adopting a certain kind of spirituality and lifestyle; it’s also about salvation from the judgment of a holy God. Nor is it something you can dabble in; it requires real sacrifice. Jesus says in Matthew 10:38, “Whoever doesn’t take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” As Bonhoeffer famously said, “When Christ calls a man, he bids him come and die.” Dietrich Bonhoeffer, The Cost of Discipleship (Simon Schuster, 1959), 89. Conversion costs something. Saying yes to Jesus means saying no to sin, to our own passions, and to our former life. The question is: Does our evangelism draw attention to what people must give up? Conversion doesn’t propel us further toward our goals. Rather, it fundamentally reframes our goals in light of God’s kingdom. When we appeal to people’s carnal desires, we should not be surprised when our “converts” are more in love with the world

The post  What Conversion Looks Like in Messy People (Like Me)  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.summary_zh: 所有罪人，无论过去的创伤、生活的混乱、社会经济背景或教育程度如何，都必须通过悔改和对基督的信心以同样的方式皈依。帖子What Conversion Looks Like in Messy People (Like Me)首次出现在9Marks上。
featured.title_zh: 乱七八糟的人（像我一样）的转化是什么样子
featured.content: Abstract: Mez McConnell points out that the fruit of conversion looks different in everyone’s life, particularly for those who come out of difficult, or “messy,” backgrounds. McConnell illustrates this point by giving two contrasting conversion stories. Then, based on his own background and his ministry among others with difficult backgrounds, he offers five reminders to help pastors minister to such individuals and discern whether they have, in fact, been converted. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . If you’ve been a pastor for a while, it’s likely that you’ve seen some people convert from difficult backgrounds. The Lord saved me from a very difficult past and has given me a ministry to many who come from a similar place. In this piece, I am going to share two conversion stories: one “clean” story and one messy. In God’s kindness to me, I have seen people like John and Jane (who you’re soon to meet) come to saving faith through the witness of my local church. In considering the similarities and differences in John and Jane’s conversions, I pray you grow in boldness, discernment, and patience as you faithfully proclaim the gospel and help people live it out in their own lives. John, a college student who has been attending your Sunday services for some time, asks to speak with you. You meet up and he tells you about his growing conviction over his sin and of his need to repent and place his faith in Christ (those aren’t the terms he uses, but that’s what he means). You feel sure that he is being genuine and so you pray with him and urge him to trust in Christ. Soon after, John tells you that he is now a Christian and so you put him in touch with a mature believer in the church to begin the discipleship process. As the weeks and months progress, you begin to observe a real spiritual hunger in John as he devours the Bible, attends a small group, and comes regularly to a class on Christian doctrine. John begins to pray earnestly in the public meetings, and he volunteers to serve the church body in a number of different ways. So far, so good. John appears to be “soundly converted.” Conversion Doesn’t Always Look the Same Now, let’s change the story to Jane, a single mom of three with an addiction to cannabis and prescription painkillers. What does conversion look like for her? Should we think about “lowering the bar” for people like Jane from so-called “messy” backgrounds? In other words, should we expect less spiritual fruit from Jane than we do from John? And should we expect the spiritual maturation process to be slower, too? Back to Jane and her cannabis and pill addiction. She is in your office talking about feeling convicted of sin and of her desire to put her faith in Jesus for salvation (again, those aren’t the terms she uses, but that’s what she means). As with John, you feel that she is being genuine, and when she tells you a short time later that she’s now trusting in Jesus, you put her in touch with a mature lady in the church to disciple her. However, unlike John, Jane is irregular when it comes to attending Sunday services. Often she turns up late, if she bothers turning up at all. When she does appear, the children are normally loud and fidgety and cause all manner of distractions to those around them. featured.content_zh: 摘要:Mez McConnell指出,皈依的果实在每个人的生活中都不同,对那些从困难或 " 迷思 " 背景中出来的人来说尤其如此。 McConnell通过给出两个对比的转换故事来说明这一点. 然后,他根据自己的背景以及他的部会和其他有困难背景的人,提出5个提醒,帮助牧师部长向这些人提供帮助,并查明他们是否实际上已经皈依。 编辑说明:这篇文章取自9Marks牧师杂志《教会事务》, 如果你做了一段时间的牧师, 你可能已经看到一些人从困难的背景皈依。 上帝把我从一个非常艰难的过去中拯救出来,并且给了我一个部属给来自类似地方的许多人. 在这部作品中,我将分享两个转换故事:一个是“干净的”故事,一个是混乱的。 我看见约翰和珍(你们很快会见到他们)这样的人, 在考虑约翰和简的皈依过程中的相似之处和差异时,我祈祷你在忠实地宣示福音并帮助人们在自己的生活中生活的同时,以大胆、分辨和耐心地成长。 约翰,一个大学生 他一直在参加你的星期天服务 一段时间,要求与你说话。 他告诉大家,他越来越相信自己的罪过,需要忏悔和信仰基督(这些不是他所用的条件,而是他的意思)。 你确信他是真的 所以你和他一起祈祷 并且敦促他相信基督 不久,约翰告诉你,他现在是基督徒,所以你让他与教会中成熟的信徒联系,开始门徒礼仪过程. 随着数周和数月的进步,你开始在约翰吞噬"圣经"时,观察到一个真正的精神饥饿,参加了一个小团体,并定期来到一个有关基督教教义的班级. 约翰开始在公开会议上真诚祈祷,他自愿以多种不同的方式为教会机构服务. 目前还不错 约翰看来是“貌似被转化了 ” 。 我们改编成Jane的故事, 她的皈依是什么样子? 我们是否应该考虑让Jane这种来自所谓“迷信”背景的人“降低律师资格”? 换句话说,我们是否应该期望简的精神果实比约翰少? 我们是否应期望精神成熟的过程也放慢? 回到简和她大麻和药瘾。 她正在你办公室里谈论被判定有罪的感觉, 以及她希望相信耶稣以救赎的愿望(这又不是她使用的术语, 与约翰一样,你觉得她很真实,当她稍后告诉你她现在信任耶稣时,你让她在教堂里与一位成熟的女士联系,让她成为门徒。 然而,与约翰不同的是,简在参加星期天礼拜时是不规则的. 她经常迟到,如果她烦恼的话。 当她出现时,孩子们通常声音大而虚无,给周围的人带来各种分心。 少数成员评论说,当她坐在他们(后来被确定为大麻)附近时,经常有强烈的气味从她身上冒出. 当被问到她的精神状况时,她变得非常动画化她的信仰,并对她大幅度削减了大麻消费感到骄傲. 这位纪律严明的女士报告说,她偶尔参加《圣经》的学习,自从她表示相信基督以来,她只参加了一次小组会议。 你开始对简的皈依的真实性产生怀疑。 某天晚上,当一个教会成员打电话通知你时,事情就变得头疼了

featured.summary_zh: 把我们从自己手中解救出来？不，耶稣死是为了把我们从神的愤怒中拯救出来。帖子The Reason for Church: A Review首先出现在9Marks上。
featured.title_zh: 建立教会的原因：回顾
featured.content: Abstract: Paul Alexander reviews Brad Edwards’s book The Reason for Church , highlighting strengths of the book’s cultural diagnosis while also identifying weaknesses in its prescription for how our current problems should be addressed by the church and the gospel. Edwards emphasizes how sin has affected the way we relate to one another, but he does not adequately address the way our sin affects our relationship with God. Readers will benefit from many of Edwards’s insights, but those who believe that the church’s primary mission is to make disciples through the proclamation of the gospel will find substantive areas of disagreement with his view of the church and its mission. Brad Edwards, The Reason for Church: Why the Body of Christ Still Matters in an Age of Anxiety, Division, and Radical Individualism . Zondervan, 2025. 240 pp. When many of us first read David Wells’s No Place for Truth back in the day, we felt like we did when we saw our first Trans Am. You know who you are—don’t deny it. I know, Christian cultural analysis is more than just “cool” or “awesome.” It’s public theology for evangelism. But shouldn’t it be at least a little thrilling to apply Christian logic to public trends? The world never tires of rephrasing the Serpent’s question, “Did God really say . . .?” Our age now rallies around a therapeutic spirituality, justified by victimhood as a new virtue, expressed through social media, aflame with anti-institutionalism. That leaves the local church looking so . . . 1900s, which implies we need not just a reason for God but a reason for church. The title of Brad Edwards’s book, The Reason for Church , tips us off that Edwards hews more to the apologetics of Tim Keller than to the systematics of David Wells. Edwards is an intellectually sophisticated critic of the meta-modern malaise. Thankfully, he loves Christ and the church more than anything in this world. He pastors The Table, a PCA congregation in Colorado that subscribes to the Westminster Confession of Faith. This book earned Christianity Today’s 2025 Book of the Year for its well-informed cultural analysis, penetrating insights, shrewd applications, and flecks of gospel gold. After reading it, I was not surprised to learn The Reason for Church also earned Edwards The Gospel Coalition First-Time Author Award. Edwards turns phrases like pancakes, but he’s not a show-off. He’s heartfelt, and he’s got personal stories from ministry in his own local church that verify and illustrate his analysis and applications. He writes like he’s done this before. Approach Edwards articulates his social critique of late modernity as Burkean conservatism, focused through the political lens of Yuval Levin and Jonah Goldberg, filtered through the sociological insight of Charles Murray, and lit by the psychological findings of Jonathan Haidt. The “little platoons” of local mediating institutions that put us shoulder to shoulder with people across the political aisle are disappearing (79, 93; think Putnam’s Bowling Alone ). We are fracturing the republic into politically homogeneous ghettos by ZIP code. With no buffer between the individual and the political, everything becomes political, impersonal, ultimate . . . and contentious. Diagnosis Today, individualism hijacks individuality such that self becomes sacrosanct. Boomers built churches on Peter Drucker’s pragmatism, which ended up offering Sunday consumers “a Coldplay concert with a TED talk” (14, 16). The church’s customer-is-king technique only manipulates our Main Character Syndrome, making church a provider of goods and services, and excusing us for treating each other as non-player participants in a reality where self is still the star of the show (47–48). Therapy teaches us to prize intuitional over institutional spiritualities (28–35, channeling Philip Rieff and Carl Trueman), so people retreat from churches that call them to repent, choosing instead safe spaces that affirm them in sin. Social media disintegrates
featured.content_zh: 摘要:保罗·亚历山大评论了布拉德·爱德华兹所著"教会的理由"一书,强调了该书文化诊断的优点,同时也指出了该书如何由教会和福音书解决我们当前问题处方的弱点. Edwards强调罪恶如何影响我们彼此的关系,但他没有充分处理我们的罪恶如何影响我们与上帝的关系。 读者将会从爱德华兹的许多见解中获益,但那些认为教会的首要使命是通过宣示福音来培养门徒的人会发现他对于教会及其使命的看法存在实质性的分歧. 布拉德·爱德华兹 《教会的理由:为什么基督的身体在焦虑、分裂和激进个人主义的时代仍然重要》,Zondervan,2025年。 当我们许多人第一次读到大卫·威尔斯的《真理无所归宿》时, 你知道自己是谁, 我知道,基督教文化分析不仅仅是“酷”或“优美”的。 这是福音派的公共神学。 将基督教逻辑运用到公众潮流中, 世界从未厌倦重写蛇人的问题,“上帝真的说过吗?” 我们这个时代现在围绕着一种治疗性精神, 以受害者为理由, 这让当地教会看起来如此 1900年代,这意味着我们不仅需要上帝的理由,还需要教会的理由. Brad Edwards的书标题是《教会的理由》, 爱德华兹是一位在知识上精密的批评者,对"元-现代"的弊病进行了批判. 谢天谢地,他更爱基督和教会,比世界上任何事物都要多. 他在科罗拉多州的一个常设仲裁法院会众中担任牧师,赞同威斯敏斯特信仰忏悔书。 这本书赢得了基督教今日2025年的"年度之书",因为它有丰富的文化分析、深入的见解、精通的应用以及福音黄金的花纹。 在读完之后,我并不惊讶地得知"教会的理由"也获得了爱德华兹福音联盟的"第一次作者奖". Edwards的口味就像煎饼, 他的内心深处, 他写得像以前一样。 接近爱德华兹阐述他对后期现代主义的社会批评为伯克南保守主义,通过尤瓦尔·莱文和约拿·高德伯格的政治透镜来聚焦,通过查尔斯·默里的社会学见解来过滤,并被乔纳森·海德的心理发现所点燃. 当地调解机构的“小排”让我们与政治道上的人并肩并肩(79,93;认为普特南的保龄球是孤独的 ) 。 根据ZIP代码,我们把共和国分裂成政治上单一的犹太区。 在个人和政治之间没有缓冲,一切都变成政治的,非人性的,终极的.和有争议. 今天的诊断,个性主义劫持了个性,以至于自我变得神圣. Boomers根据彼得·德鲁克的实用主义建造了教堂,最终提供星期天的消费者们“与TED谈话的冷戏音乐会”(14,16)。 教会的顾客-王牌技术只操控了我们的主要性格综合症,使教会成为商品和服务的提供者,并责怪我们在现实中将对方视为非玩家参与者,而现实中自我仍然是节目的主角(47–48). 治疗教导我们把直觉的奖赏给制度性精神(28–35,引导菲利普·里夫和卡尔·特鲁曼),因此人们从号召他们悔改的教堂中退缩,选择了安全的地方来证实他们的罪恶。 社交媒体解体

featured.title: Aiming for Conversion in Our Preaching
featured.summary: Worse than offending unbelievers is treating them like they are believers. Instead, we must aim to help sinners see their sin and confess their need for Christ. This spiritual clarity is not cruel, but kind.   The post  Aiming for Conversion in Our Preaching  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.summary_zh: 比冒犯非信徒更糟糕的是，像对待信徒一样对待他们。相反，我们必须致力于帮助罪人看到他们的罪，并承认他们需要基督。这种精神上的清晰不是残酷的，而是善良的。在我们的讲道中， “瞄准皈依”一文首次出现在9Marks上。
featured.title_zh: 在我们的讲道中瞄准皈依
featured.content: Abstract: Sam Romine argues that although the preaching that takes place in the weekly gathering should primarily be aimed at believers, pastors should also aim at the conversion of unbelievers in their preaching. He points as evidence to to the prophets of the Old Testament as well as the apostle Paul’s comments about the presence of unbelievers in the gathering in 1 Corinthians 14:23–25. Romine closes with three practical exhortations to help pastors put this into practice. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . Some things are just meant to go together. A warm slice of apple pie with vanilla ice cream. Cozying up with a book on a rainy day. Watching fireworks light up the night sky with a grilled hot dog in hand. Preaching exegetically through a passage and calling for the conversion of sinners—well, that may be taking things a bit too far! As I’ve reflected on preaching with other pastors, it seems there’s a common temptation to underplay preaching for conversion while aiming to preach expositionally as though these two are incompatible or only awkwardly related. Why is this? Some are simply trying to guard against sloppy exposition that ignores the point of the text. Others have been scarred by past experiences of manipulative altar calls and forced invitations, so they seek to distance themselves from these methods. On the other hand, the failure to preach for conversion sometimes arises from biblical convictions. Since the church is for the gathering of believers, why should we take time away from them to tell unbelievers how to have their sins forgiven? Biblical Patterns and Grounds for Preaching for Conversion While I wholeheartedly agree that the Sunday sermon should primarily have God’s people in view, there is biblical precedent to aim for conversion in our preaching. Consider two examples: the Old Testament prophets and the apostle Paul. 1. An Observation from the Old Testament Prophets I love the prophets. They consistently leave me in awe of God’s majesty and glory, as God is shown to be holy and sovereign and, at the same time, kind and gracious. In this they provide a masterful example of how to weave in calls for sinners to repent while still speaking words of correction, comfort, and hope to believers. For instance, nearly all the prophets speak of impending judgment for Israel’s sin and promises of God’s future grace. Hosea pleads with Israel “to return to the LORD your God” (Hos. 14:1). In Joel, God urges the people to “return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning” (Joel 2:12). Amos calls for the people to “seek the LORD and live,” (Amos 5:4) and Zechariah similarly adds, “Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you” (Zech. 1:3). Of course, Israel is not like the church in that God’s Old Covenant people comprised both believers and unbelievers. Yet we can learn from the way the prophets addressed not only the faithful among God’s people but also those with uncircumcised hearts. God’s concern for the salvation of sinners is demonstrated by repeated calls for repentance. 2. Paul’s Sunday Gathering Observation In 1 Corinthians, Paul addresses several topics pertaining to when believers “come together as a church” (1 Cor. 11:18). Here he makes an important yet often overlooked observation about these gatherings: we are to expect unbelievers to be present. Paul knows the church is made up of those who are “in Christ” (for example, see 1 Cor. 1:2, 4), yet he makes room for the attendance of non-Christians in the weekly gathering. We see this in at least two ways. First, he speaks of “outsiders or unbelievers” entering the gathering when the “whole church comes together” (1 Cor. 14:23). These unbelievers are clearly distinguished from the church. Second, Paul desires the conversion of such people, and he speaks of how powerful it is when unbelievers see God’s people worshipping
featured.content_zh: 摘要:萨姆·罗明(Sam Romine)认为,虽然每周集会中进行的传道活动应主要针对信徒,牧师在传道中也应以皈依不信者为目标. 他向"旧约"的先知以及使徒保罗(Paul)指出,他们认为,在1 Corinthian 14:23–25的集会中,有不信者。 罗明最后提出了三个实际的劝告来帮助牧师将这一点付诸实践. 编辑说明:这篇文章取自9Marks牧师杂志《教会事务》, 有些东西只是要一起走 有香草冰淇淋的苹果派 与一书相会于一雨天. 看着烟花用烤热狗放出夜空中来. 透过一段路, 要求改造罪人, 我考虑过与其他牧师一起传道, 似乎有一种常见的诱惑, 为什么? 有些人只是想防止无视案文要点的草率言论。 另一些人则被过去操纵祭坛和强迫邀请的经历所伤痕累累,因此他们试图与这些方法保持距离. 另一方面,不宣扬皈依有时源于圣经信仰. 既然教堂是供信士们聚会的,我们为什么要花时间告诉不信道的人们,他们的罪过怎么得到宽恕呢? 传承转换的圣经模式和基础 虽然我衷心同意星期天的布道应该让上帝的子民来观望,但我们的布道却有以皈依为目的的圣经先例。 考虑两个例子:旧约先知和使徒保罗. 1. 《旧约》先知的观察,我爱先知。 他们总是让我敬畏上帝的光荣和荣耀,因为上帝被证明是神圣和主权的,同时也是仁慈和仁慈的。 他们以此为表率,说明怎样在劝告罪人悔罪的同时,仍对信士说出改正、安慰和希望的话。 例如,几乎所有的先知都谈到即将对以色列的罪过做出判决,并许诺真主今后给予恩惠。 霍西恳求以色列“回到耶和华你的神身边”(霍斯14:1)。 在乔尔,真主敦促众人“全心全意地归依我,斋戒、哭泣、哀悼”(约尔2:12)。 阿莫斯呼吁人民“向耶和华求生”(Amos 5:4),撒迦利亚同样补充道,“归顺我,万能的耶和华说,我将归顺你”(Zech 1:3)。 当然,以色列与教会不同,因为上帝的旧约中的人既包括信徒也包括不信者。 然而,我们可以从先知们对待上帝人民中的忠实者以及那些有未受洗心的人的方式中吸取教训。 上帝对拯救罪人的关注,表现在一再呼吁忏悔. 2. 保罗的 " 星期日聚会观察 " 在一科林斯,保罗谈到与信徒 " 作为教堂一起来 " (第11:18节)有关的几个专题。 在这里,他对这些聚会作了重要但常常被忽视的观察:我们期望那些不信的人在场。 保罗知道教堂是由那些"在基督中"的人所组成的(例如,见1 Cor. 1:2,4),然而他却为非基督徒出席周会提供了空间. 我们至少从两个方面看到这一点。 首先,他在“整个教堂合在一起”时(第1章第14:23节)谈到“外来者或不信者”进入集会。 这些不信者与教会明显不同. 第二,保罗希望这种人的皈依,他说,当不信道的人们看见真主的百姓崇拜的时候,这种皈依是多么强大。

featured.title: Eight Enemies of Pastoral Friendship
featured.summary: Biblical friendship is not a luxury for pastors. It is one of God's ordinary means of sustaining us for long-term ministry.   The post  Eight Enemies of Pastoral Friendship  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.summary_zh: 圣经友谊不是牧师的奢侈品。这是神支持我们长期事奉的常用方法之一。帖子“田园友谊的八个敌人”首先出现在9Marks上。
featured.title_zh: 田园友谊的八个敌人
featured.content: Abstract: Dave Kiehn argues for the importance of friendship for pastors while noting eight different “enemies” that can easily get in the way. These enemies, or obstacles, to pastoral friendships include things like pride, busyness, insecurity, and other issues related to the pastor’s heart and habits. Far from being luxuries, friendships are one of the means God uses to sustain pastors in their work. Pastoral ministry is often described as lonely, but, for most, it doesn’t need to be. From the opening pages of Scripture, God declares that it is not good for man to be alone. Throughout redemptive history, the Lord strengthened his servants through faithful companions. Moses had Joshua. David had Jonathan. Paul had Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, Titus, Luke, and many other fellow laborers. Even our Lord surrounded himself with the Twelve and enjoyed a uniquely close friendship with Peter, James, and John. The church has long recognized the necessity of Christian friendship. Few, though, have captured the beauty of it better than J. C. Ryle: A friend is one of the greatest blessings on earth. Tell me not of money—affection is better than gold; sympathy is better than lands. He is the poor man who has no friends. This world is full of sorrow because it is full of sin. It is a dark place. It is a lonely place. It is a disappointing place. The brightest sunbeam in it is a friend. Friendship halves our troubles and doubles our joys. J. C. Ryle, Practical Religion: Being Plain Papers on the Daily Duties, Experience, Dangers, and Privileges of Professing Christians ( Baker Book House , n.d. ) , 336. Many others have echoed Ryle’s celebration of the blessing of friendship. C. S. Lewis famously observed, “Friendship is born at that moment when one person says to another, ‘What! You too? I thought I was the only one.’” C. S. Lewis, The Four Loves (Geoffrey Bles, 1960), 65. Charles Spurgeon added, “Friendship is one of the sweetest joys of life. Many might have failed beneath the bitterness of their trial had they not found a friend.” Charles H. Spurgeon, “ The Friend of God, ” in The Metropolitan Tabernacle Pulpit , vol. 33 (Passmore & Alabaster, 1887), sermon no. 1938. John Owen reminded us that Christ himself calls us his friends, John Owen, Of Communion with God the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost (1657). and Tim Keller observed that the entire history of redemption can be viewed as one great act of divine friendship. Timothy Keller, “Friendship” (sermon, Redeemer Presbyterian Church, May 29, 2005), Gospel in Life, https://gospelinlife.com/sermon/friendship-2/ . Yet if friendship is such a gift, why do so many pastors struggle to cultivate deep, lasting relationships? Sometimes it’s because of a lack of opportunity, though this seems rarer. More often, friendship is lost to enemies in our own hearts and habits. There are definitely more, but here are eight such enemies of friendship to be on the lookout for. 1. Pride: “I Don’t Need Anyone” One of the greatest threats to pastoral friendship, as with any kind of friendship, is pride. Pride whispers to us that mature pastors should be self-sufficient. It convinces us that asking for help is weakness and that admitting struggles will diminish our leadership. Scripture tells a different story. “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (Prov. 16:18). James reminds us that “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. 4:6). Peter illustrates this danger vividly. Jesus had told him and the other disciples that they would fall away, yet Peter confidently declared, “Even though they all fall away, I will not” (Mark 14:29). Within hours he denied Christ three times. Pride convinces us we are strong enough to stand alone. Humility invites other brothers to speak into our lives before we stumble and fall. featured.content: Abstract: Kyle Hoffsmith commends David Odom’s Youth Ministry Deconstructed , a book that helps churches evaluate and “deconstruct” their current youth ministry aims and practices in order to reconstruct their youth ministry in a way that is biblical, sustainable, and contextual. Hoffsmith highlights four main strengths of the book: it integrates youth ministry into the church as a whole; it encourages youth ministries to partner with parents; it encourages churches to evaluate their current practices; and it encourages churches to focus on spiritual growth rather than numbers. David Odom, Youth Ministry Deconstructed: Rethinking Your Ministry to Build Lasting Faith in Students . B&H Academic, 2026. 288 pages. There is much discussion today about what youth ministry should look like in the church. Some argue that teenagers should be fully integrated into the life of the church and treated as adults, which means that youth ministry (as it is typically understood) largely disappears as children get older. On the other hand, some churches believe that students should have their own age-segmented ministry throughout their high school years, where most of what is taught and planned is specifically for them. And there are plenty of positions in between. This isn’t merely a disagreement over church polity, as all churches must decide how best to minister to the teenagers among them. These young people need to be evangelized, taught, and shepherded in a way that helps them grow into mature followers of Christ “in the midst of a crooked and twisted generation” (Phil. 2:15). I would agree with professor, author, and youth ministry veteran David Odom that youth ministry needs a “deconstruction.” Odom uses this term as a play on words, as many today speak of “deconstructing” their faith. He uses it to exhort churches to tear down, or deconstruct, the structures and strategies they have used for decades to minister to teenagers. This deconstruction phase comprises the book’s first six chapters, as Odom offers metrics for evaluating your youth ministry in various areas, including spiritual growth, discipleship, and discipleship environments. Then chapters 7–10 focus on building back up, or reconstructing, your youth ministry in a way that is biblical, sustainable, and contextual. Church leaders will undoubtedly find places where they differ with Odom’s approach or his specific applications in certain areas, yet the issues and questions he raises are worthy of reflection. Rather than summarize each chapter, I want to commend Youth Ministry Deconstructed to church leaders by highlighting four main strengths of the book. 1. Youth Ministry Fits Within the Church as a Whole There has been concern for a while now about how youth ministry has created silos in the church. The most encouraging thing about this book is that Odom wants to integrate youth ministry within the church as a whole. So, for instance, when it comes to a question like, Should teenagers skip the corporate gathering to go to a youth worship service? Odom says, “Don’t allow a youth-only worship gathering to become a substitute for intergenerational corporate worship. Teenagers in the church benefit both young people and the congregation” (126). And when it comes to the question, Why does youth ministry exist? he points to an example of a student ministry that uses the following discipleship strategy: “The process for the student ministry is the same as the church as a whole” (112). featured.summary: ‘Scroll Less, Live More’ helps teens and parents develop the tech skills they need to live a life rooted in reality and steeped in wisdom.

featured.title_zh: 与青少年一起养成健康的科技习惯
featured.content: Each Sunday night at youth group, our time of worship through singing is followed by a short sermon then small-group discussion. The high school kids in the group I lead know the routine. Before we open the Scriptures, we pull our chairs into a circle. Then we take out our phones and stack them in a pile on the floor in the middle of the ring. We won’t touch those screens again until the Bible-study hour is done. The phone stack is a simple habit. But it’s helped the students in our group pay closer attention to both one another and the Bible text. In his practical new book, Scroll Less, Live More: 10 Healthy Tech Habits for Teens , Samuel James commends a number of similar practices. His goal is to give teenagers “a vivid picture of what it looks like to apply [biblical] wisdom to technology usage in today’s digital age” (155). James recognizes that simple, repeatable practices can help young people resist the foolishness today’s tech promotes so they can instead grow in the fear of the Lord. Great Power, Great Responsibility Scroll Less, Live More builds on the foundation James laid in his previous book for adults, Digital Liturgies: Rediscovering Christian Wisdom in an Online Age . One of his main premises is that technology isn’t neutral. Rather, it’s a powerful force that “shapes and influences us in ways we aren’t always aware of” (30). One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. To illustrate this truth, James points to tech invented in the 19th century: Before the telephone . . . people just accepted that if they weren’t in the same room as somebody, they couldn’t communicate with that person in the moment. After the telephone was introduced, being able to communicate with someone in a different place at any time became not only possible but also important. (125) Similarly, 21st-century tech such as generative AI brings with it both new possibilities and greater expectations: “AI’s capability to produce an amazing variety of work and art with very little direct human involvement creates an expectation that using it regularly for these purposes is normal” (127). The more we off-load our creativity and effort to it, the more we believe we should do so. One way tech changes us is by changing our expectations. Digital technology changes us in other ways too. James draws on the work of tech realists such as Neil Postman , Nicholas Carr , and Marshall McLuhan , but he makes their perspective accessible for adolescents. James repeatedly shows young people how poor digital habits affect their cognition, emotions, and relationships. Living on a phone will slow down thinking, leaving teens feeling anxious, or even angry, amid daily interactions that then become more awkward and strained. Way of Wisdom: Guard Your Heart How do we help young people avoid this path? James gives teens some practical encouragements, telling them to charge their phones somewhere other than in their bedrooms overnight. He also provides a list self-examination questions to help them grow in self-awareness and he appeals to family rules such as only using devices in open areas of the home. But ultimately, James is convinced that using technology well involves more than simply following a list of dos and don’ts. He writes, We don’t need a huge list of rules that will have to be updated every time Apple releases a new phone or a new social media app; we need something that will help us determine how to use technology well in any circumstance. We need wisdom. (16–17) Proverbs says, “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and the knowledge of the Holy One is insight” (9:10). James is clear that growing in wisdom and the knowledge of the Lord requires more than adjusting one’s screen-time settings; it takes guarding one’s heart. 每个星期天晚上,在青年团体,我们通过唱歌进行礼拜的时间,接着是简短的布道,然后是小组讨论。 我带领的高中生们都懂规矩 在打开"圣经"前,把椅子拉入一圈. 然后我们拿出我们的电话 把它们堆在地上 戒指中间。

featured.content: Abstract: Sam Crites offers three ways to help pastors distinguish between worldly grief and godly grief based on Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians 7:10. Only godly grief produces true repentance, and such grief can be discerned by mourning over sin, not merely its consequences; a genuine desire for reconciliation, no matter the cost; and an earnest desire to please God, not the world. The fruit of godly grief usually becomes evident over time through ongoing repentance and faith in Christ. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . I was discipled by a man named Steve Tucker. He was a simple man full of simple lessons, and one of those simple lessons has stuck with me: a true mark of genuine conversion and its effects is how willing someone is to repent of their sin. However, genuine repentance is a tricky thing. When I catch my children doing something wrong, they are more than willing to “repent,” especially when punishment is imminent. They go from enjoying their wrongdoing to shedding tears. But it’s not always easy to tell if they are grieved over upsetting me or because they know there will be consequences for their actions. Pastors have to make a similar determination when a member is confronted for their sin. Is this person shedding tears only because they were caught in sin, or are they truly repenting? Both kinds of grief can look the same, at least on the surface, but only one leads to life. Those who refuse to repent give evidence that they haven’t been converted. So how can we tell the difference? Three Marks of Godly Grief Since we cannot see the heart of a man, we must look at the fruit of his life—the marks of repentance that accompany genuine conversion. Heart change, not behavior modification, is always the aim. Therefore, we must discern the external evidences of the Spirit’s internal work. This is where Paul’s words to the Corinthians can help us out. He says, “For godly grief produces a repentance that leads to salvation without regret, whereas worldly grief produces death” (2 Cor. 7:10). Notice that genuine repentance is produced by “godly grief.” Allow me, then, to put forward three marks of repentance from 2 Corinthians 7 that are evidence of godly grief. This list is not meant to be exhaustive but merely a helpful tool for discerning true repentance and, therefore, genuine conversion. 1. Godly Grief Leads to Mourning over Sin, Not Simply Its Consequences In 2 Corinthians 7, Paul describes how restless and anxious he was as he awaited the Corinthians’ response to his previous letter. But when Titus came, Paul was comforted because his report brought news of the grief of the Corinthians—not grief over the harshness of Paul’s letter but grief over their own sin. We’re reminded that godly grief is first and foremost a response to sin and not merely its consequences. David says to God in Psalm 51:4, “Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight.” How could David be so insensitive? What about Uriah and Bathsheba? Or the child who died? David was aware of how the consequences of his sin affected others, but he felt greater anguish in his heart over how he had offended the Lord. And this should be true for all who repent: they should care most about how their sin has offended their Lord. This is the fruit of understanding the gospel, as the sufferings of Christ on the cross were the payment due for our sin. On the other hand, a preoccupation with the sin of others, a tendency to shift the blame to someone else, or grief that is only short-lived—all these are indications that an individual is not mourning because they have offended the Lord, but instead because of the consequences of their sin. 2. featured.title: Your Church May Know Less Bible Than You Think (And What to Do About It)
featured.summary: A new survey indicates Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it.

featured.content: In November 1900, Mark Twain delivered a speech titled “The Disappearance of Literature” to the students at Connecticut Wesleyan University. With signature slyness, he told them , “I don’t believe any of you have ever read Paradise Lost , and you don’t want to. That’s something that you just want to take on trust. It’s . . . the definition of a classic—something that everybody wants to have read and nobody wants to read.” Twain was noting the beginning of the illiteracy rockslide that we now witness as an avalanche. The statistics we see in the age of smartphones and social media bear out our eroded literacy: In 2003, average Americans older than age 15 read 21.9 minutes on a given day. By 2010, the number had dropped to 18.3 minutes, and in 2025, it had sunk to 16.2 minutes a day. Imagine how ChatGPT will gut that number even further in the next few years. America is moving rapidly into a postliterate reality, a sort of new Dark Ages, one in which we consume information in images and sound bites, all predigested for us by others. Consider the implications for a system of belief whose transmission from one generation to the next is staked on a book. Christian Literacy Crisis A new survey from Lifeway Research throws into stark relief the chasm between Christian commitment to and knowledge of the Bible. More than 2,000 Christians who attend church in a typical month were surveyed across eight categories of Bible knowledge: major people, passages, events, divisions of Scripture, and more. The researchers designed questions around what would be typically well known rather than obscure. Two out of three respondents scored less than 60, a failing grade. Fifty-five percent could not correctly name the first king of Israel. Only 11 percent could correctly order four major Old Testament events, and only 27 percent could correctly order four major New Testament events. Forty-four percent failed to identify the book of Mark as belonging to the Gospels. Two out of three respondents wrongly believed Hezekiah was a book of the Bible, and 44 percent believed the Gospel of Thomas was as well. Christians have succumbed to the general literacy crisis of the culture. The “people of the Book” don’t read it. The Bible itself, the classic of all classics, has apparently become a book that every Christian wants to have read, and few Christians want to read. If we do read to sustain our faith, we’re more likely to read books about the Bible than the Bible itself. We may consume sermons or podcasts or use devotional resources that cherry-pick verses to give us a positive emotion in 10 minutes or less, but largely, we’ve become curators of other people’s opinions about a book we don’t read ourselves. Failure of Discipleship I believe these results show a failure of discipleship strategies, one with massive implications: We cannot pass along to someone else what we ourselves don’t know. How can the church fulfill the Great Commission if it’s incapable of teaching others to observe everything Jesus commanded? The numbers show we haven’t taught even the basics. If the church were a local public school responsible for teaching basic math and reading, we would receive a failing grade and face funding sanctions. The ‘people of the Book’ don’t read it. Yet, according to a 2024 Lifeway Research survey of 2,620 Protestant pastors, 52 percent are satisfied with the state of discipleship and spiritual formation in their churches. Twenty-nine percent report that they regularly evaluate discipleship progress among their congregations. featured.content: Not long ago, my son asked me about all the people King David killed in 2 Samuel 8. We’ve been reading through that book during family devotions before bed. He’s right to be disturbed. So we had a conversation about why he’s unnerved, how we develop moral instincts, and how we’d respond to someone who rejects God because of these and similar accounts in the Old Testament. We did apologetics together. As he gets a little older, I’ll point him toward the YouTube channel of my friend Gavin Ortlund, who does an excellent job of answering many hard questions about Christianity and the Bible. Then, a few years later, I’ll point him to Gavin’s books, including his latest, Why Christianity Makes Sense: A Book About Jesus, the Mysteries of the World, and the Longings in Your Heart (Zondervan Reflective). He’s back on Gospelbound to discuss all things apologetics, from the multiverse, to slavery, to morality as merely a taste for sugar, to winning the lottery 10 billion times in a row. featured.title: I Was a Justice Warrior. I Needed the Whole Gospel. You Do Too.
featured.summary: Most Christians today see these two gospel aspects as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined.
featured.summary_zh: 今天，大多数基督徒将这两个福音方面视为同一个圣经馅饼的一部分。但我们往往看不到它们必然交织在一起。
featured.title_zh: 我是一名正义战士。我需要完整的福音。你也是。
featured.content: From 2016 to 2018, I was a social media justice warrior. I spent my time on Facebook and Twitter confronting the powerful and comfortable, championing justice issues, and fighting for racial and political reconciliation. If you read my posts, you might not have guessed that I grew up in a conservative Christian home nestled in suburbia, or that I spent every day of my education, starting at age 4, in Christian schools. In my upbringing, I learned the rich depths of the Christian faith. I surrendered my life to Jesus, and I learned that Jesus came to seek to save the lost. Yet that evangelistically oriented world of my youth was intentionally sanitized and separated from the painful realities of poverty and injustice just 10 minutes down the road. When I discovered this disparity, I became a justice warrior online. And while that posture was certainly a reaction to my upbringing, I wasn’t being a hypocrite. My social media advocacy reflected my actual life. I’ve lived and worked in an underresourced neighborhood since 2001. During my first 15 years in the neighborhood, I grew burdened over the disconnect I saw between the conditions my neighbors faced daily and how many in the American church live. The political, racial, and socioeconomic divide between my church life and neighborhood gutted me. So when I went online, I was convinced I was sharing the true gospel. Yet that “gospel” I shared was merely centered on producing tangible results in the here and now, not on affecting eternity. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. Two Gospel Aspects I began to see two aspects in the biblical gospel. Let’s call them the gospel of the cross and the gospel of the kingdom . The gospel of the cross is the good news that Jesus Christ saves and adopts believers as his children through his substitutionary death and glorious resurrection. We’re all born alienated from God. In sin, we’re his enemies. In Christ, as we believe the good news, we’re reconciled to God (Rom. 5:6–10) and assured of eternal life with him (John 3:16). As Peter writes, “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Pet. 3:18). Moreover, the cross aspect of the gospel emphasizes that those entrusted with this message must share it with a lost and dying world (Matt. 28:18–20). The gospel of the cross must be heralded; it must be proclaimed. It is the priority. From this gospel flows every good gift. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. The gospel of the kingdom is the good news that God’s will for justice, goodness, and peace is already being unleashed. As God’s children, believers are invited to play a part in seeing that kingdom mission come to fruition. Jesus begins his ministry by preaching a message that proclaims “good news to the poor” and “liberty to the . . . oppressed” (Luke 4:18). He calls his hearers to repent, including from ways they’ve oppressed and neglected the poor (Matt. 3:2; 4:17). He specifically rebukes the Pharisees for neglecting “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (23:23). Paul, too, teaches that the gospel not only reunites us to God but also works justice by reconciling divided peoples to one another in the church. He writes, “For [Christ] himself is our peace, who has made us both [ethnic groups] one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Eph. 2:14). We fulfill the law and live out the gospel’s kingdom implications through our identity as shalom -makers (Matt. 5:9). The kingdom aspect of the gospel equips us with a vision for pursuing God’s will “on earth as it is in heaven” (6:10), that is, for seeing all things made new (Rev. 21:5). 如果你读过我的文章, 你可能没有猜到 我成长在一个保守的基督教家庭 在郊区, 或者我每天的教育, 从4岁开始在基督教学校。 在我成长的过程中,我学会了基督教信仰的丰富深度. 我把自己的生命交给耶稣,我得知耶稣是来寻求拯救失落者.

然而,这个以福音为本的我青年世界被故意洗涤,并在仅仅10分钟之内就脱离了贫困和不公正的痛苦现实。 当我发现这种差距时,我成了在线上的正义战士。 虽然这种姿态无疑是对我的成长的反应, 我的社交媒体宣传反映了我的真实生活.

自2001年起, 在附近15年里, 我对邻居每天面临的状况 和美国教堂里有多少人的生活脱节感到负担沉重。 我的教会生活和邻居之间的政治、种族和社会经济鸿沟使我心碎。

所以当我上网时,我确信我分享了真正的福音。 然而,我所分享的“神灵”仅仅集中于在这里和现在产生实际结果,而不是影响永恒。 我所需要的是一个全方位的福音,它既围绕上帝的王国使命,也围绕着他为十字架上的罪人而牺牲的死亡。

我开始看到圣经福音中的两个方面。 让我们称之为十字架的福音和王国的福音。 十字架的福音是好消息,耶稣基督通过他的替代死亡和光荣的复活来拯救和接纳信徒作为自己的孩子. 我们天生都与上帝隔绝。 在罪恶中,我们是他的敌人。

在基督中,我们相信好消息,我们与上帝和解(5:6-10室),并保证与上帝永生(John 3:16). 正如彼得所写的那样,“基督也曾因罪恶而受苦,善人因不义者而受苦,以便他把我们带到上帝面前”(第3:18页)。

此外,福音的交叉方面强调,受委托传达这一信息的人必须与一个迷失和垂死的世界分享(Matt. 28:18-20)。 十字架的福音必须预告;必须宣布。 这是优先事项。 从这个福音中流传着每一个好礼物.

我所需要的是一个全方位的福音,它既围绕上帝的王国使命,也围绕着他为十字架上的罪人而牺牲的死亡。 王国的福音是好消息,上帝对正义、善良与和平的意志已经释放。 作为上帝的子孙,信徒们被邀请在确保王国使命取得成果方面发挥作用。

耶稣在部里首先发出一个信息,宣称“向穷人提供好消息”和“向......受压迫的人提供自由”(公爵4:18)。 他呼吁他的听众悔改,包括他们压迫和忽视穷人的方式(Matt. 3:2;4:17)。 他特别斥责法利赛人忽视“较重要的法律事项:正义、慈悲和忠诚”(23:23)。

保罗也教导道,福音不仅使我们与上帝团聚,而且通过在教会中调和分裂的人民来伸张正义。 他写道,“[基督]自己是我们的和平,他使我们两个[种族群 都成了和平,并用他的肉体打破了敌对的分隔墙”(Eph 2:14)。

我们履行法律,通过我们作为立法者的身份,活出福音的王国影响(马特:9)。 福音的王国方面为我们提供了追求上帝的旨意的愿景,即 " 在地上像在天上一样 " (6:10),即看到一切事物都变新(Rev.21:5)。 王国的福音 必须通过神圣的 行动而存在

featured.title: Lessons from Lloyd-Jones on Preaching and Politics
featured.summary: Here are three lessons we can learn from Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis.
featured.summary_zh: 在政治危机时期，我们可以从马丁·劳埃德-琼斯（ Martyn Lloyd-Jones ）的事工中学到三个教训。
featured.title_zh: 劳埃德-琼斯关于讲道和政治的教训
featured.content: “I was never worried for a second about a man like Hitler.” This isn’t the statement of a madman or of someone privileged enough to be removed from the horrors of the war. These are the words of a pastor who was under immediate threat from the Nazi leader and who’d put on the full armor of God and prepared for battle. Adolf Hitler invaded Poland on September 1, 1939; the very next day, Martyn Lloyd-Jones was installed as an associate pastor at Westminster Chapel in London, where he would faithfully preach for the next 30 years. One year after the preacher took the pulpit, Hitler began his bombing campaign over London. Of the roughly 700 churches in the area, 624 were damaged by the bombings and 91 were totally destroyed. To the surprise of many, Westminster Chapel, one of London’s largest churches at the time, wasn’t destroyed in the bombing blitz. Iain Murray, in his classic biography on Lloyd-Jones , writes about one Sunday morning when a bomb hit close to the Chapel right in the middle of Lloyd-Jones’s Lord’s Day prayer. The bomb shook the entire building, and plaster and dust fell down on the congregation, including on “the Doctor,” as Lloyd-Jones was known. After a pause, Lloyd-Jones simply continued his prayer and the service went forward unimpeded. Lloyd-Jones offers a needed corrective to our politically anxious times. Some Christians resort to despair, while others attempt revolution. What we need is a political theology that still preaches Christ when the bombs go off. Here are three lessons we can learn from Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis. Refuse Saul’s Armour When it became apparent that England was entering the war, Lloyd-Jones sent his wife and their two children back to Wales and away from the city, not knowing what would become of it. In a brief and urgent correspondence to his wife, he writes , “Leave yourself and me too, and everything in God’s hand and you will find peace and rest.” With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. Because of fear and panic, many began to abandon the weapons of the church and replace them with the weapons of the state. But Lloyd-Jones refused to blur the lines. When the war was at its worst and his congregation had been reduced to few because of death and displacement, he remained resolute in affirming 2 Corinthians 10:4: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (KJV). Lloyd-Jones refused to allow revolutionary alliances and tactics to infiltrate the church: Alas, far too often the church has tried to meet the world and its persecuting power with like weapons to those employed by the enemy. She has made alliances with the state and she has tried to strengthen herself in a material sense. She has been slow to discover what David discovered long ago in his fight with Goliath, that she cannot fight in the armour of Saul, but must ever use her own weapons with which she is familiar and with which she is meant to use. Lloyd-Jones saw a parallel between those in Saul’s armory who were looking to outfit David for battle with new calls from within the church to align herself with the state. Like David’s pitiful sling, prayer may appear in the world’s eyes woefully insufficient weaponry against fascism. But God’s weapons are greater than the weapons of men. Reject the Partisan Gospel Lloyd-Jones saw that the church was particularly vulnerable to political idolatry when fear had gripped the people. Like the Israelites shaking at the sight of Goliath, we often feel the only reasonable response is to find our own “strong man” to fight our battles. 第二天,马丁·劳埃德-琼斯 被安置在伦敦的威斯敏斯特礼拜堂做副牧师 他将在接下来的30年里忠实地传教 传教士攻下弹坑一年后,希特勒开始对伦敦的轰炸战役. 在该地区约700座教堂中,有624座被炸毁,91座被完全摧毁。

我们需要的是政治神学 当炸弹爆炸时它仍然宣扬基督 以下是在政治危机时期我们可以从劳埃德-琼斯部学到的三个教训。 拒绝索尔的盔甲,当英格兰显然正在进入战争时,劳埃德-琼斯将他的妻子和他们的两个孩子送回威尔士,并离开这座城市,不知结果如何.

在与他妻子的简短和紧急的通信中,他写道:"离开你和我,以及上帝手中的一切,你会得到安宁和安息。 随着炸弹在高空飞翔,教堂里许多人呼吁革命,但劳埃德-琼斯呼吁祈祷. 随着炸弹在高空飞翔,教堂里许多人呼吁革命,但劳埃德-琼斯呼吁祈祷.

由于恐惧和恐慌,许多人开始放弃教会的武器,代之以国家的武器. 但劳埃德-琼斯拒绝模糊界限.

当战争处于最糟糕的状态,他的集会由于死亡和流离失所而减少到极少数时,他仍然坚决申明2科林斯人10:4:“我们战争的武器不是肉体的,而是通过上帝而强大的力量来拉倒坚固的控制力”(KJV)。

劳埃德-琼斯拒绝让革命联盟和战术渗透到教会中:唉,教会经常试图用类似武器来对付世界及其迫害敌人者的力量. 她与国家结盟,并试图在物质上加强自己。

她一直缓慢地发现大卫很久以前在与高丽的战斗中发现的东西,即她不能在索尔的盔甲中作战,但必须永远使用自己熟悉的,本意使用的武器.

劳埃德-琼斯在索尔的军械库里看到了一个相似之处, 与大卫的悲哀一样,祈祷可能出现在世界的眼中,令人悲哀的是,反对法西斯主义的武器不足。 但上帝的武器比人的武器还要大

拒绝Lloyd-Jones党福音书, 认为当恐惧笼罩人民时, 与在戈利亚斯面前摇晃的以色列人一样,我们常常感到唯一合理的反应是找到我们自己的“强人”来战斗。 在教会历史上,我们经常转向国家政治。

featured.title: Building a Workplace Where People Flourish (with Landon Hobson)
featured.summary: What happens when a seminary-trained economist takes over a pet-products plant? Landon Hobson, CEO of Cosmos Corporation, shares how paid mission days, a book club, and a ‘make the coffee’ ethic help ordinary workers flourish.
featured.summary_zh: 当受过神学院培训的经济学家接管宠物产品工厂时会发生什么？ Cosmos Corporation首席执行官兰登·霍布森（ Landon Hobson ）分享了带薪传教日、读书俱乐部和“制作咖啡”伦理如何帮助普通工人蓬勃发展。
featured.title_zh: 打造让人们茁壮成长的工作场所（与Landon Hobson一起）
featured.content: Landon Hobson is the CEO of Cosmos Corporation, a family business outside St. Louis that makes pet care and household cleaning products sold in 70 countries. With degrees in theology and economics, Landon never expected to run a 250,000-square-foot manufacturing plant—until his father-in-law asked him to take over the company, and he sensed that God had been preparing him for exactly that. Landon describes how his faith shapes Cosmos’s culture: tuition support for any degree an employee wants to pursue, a “Better Book Club” that pays people to read, five paid mission days a year, and a core value of being “willing to make the coffee” for the person behind you. He answers hard questions about whether making dog shampoo really matters to God, and he speaks candidly about the hard years—supply chain disruptions, a drop in sales, and layoffs of people he cared about. He also explains why CEOs need pastors who aren’t passive, and what he has gained from a group of believing business leaders who share the same struggles. Resources Mentioned: To Change the World by James Davison Hunter Every Good Endeavor by Timothy Keller A Public Faith by Miroslav Volf Work in the Spirit by Miroslav Volf
