featured.title: The Missing Piece in John Mark Comer’s Quiet Time
featured.summary: ‘Into the Quiet’ effectively critiques the ills of our hectic cultural moment, but it also promotes a spirituality that could quickly become disconnected from Scripture.
featured.summary_zh: “进入宁静”有效地批评了我们忙碌的文化时刻的弊端，但它也促进了一种可能很快与圣经脱节的灵性。
featured.title_zh: 约翰·马克·科默安静时光中缺失的部分
featured.content: According to a recent Pew Research study, more than half of U.S. adults report spending too much time on their smartphones. Even those who acknowledge the negative effects of smartphone addiction find it incredibly difficult to cut back. Excessive screen time isn’t just harming our productivity and connection with other people; it also makes practicing spiritual disciplines more challenging. In his latest book, Into the Quiet: Following Jesus in a World of Noise , John Mark Comer argues that “nurturing a practice of solitude, silence, and stillness is utterly indispensable to a flourishing spiritual life” (26). This timely book addresses important issues in a lively, engaging, and accessible manner. And though the staccato prose style sometimes borders on gimmicky, it’s never dull. Comer dons three hats, appearing as technoskeptic, therapist, and mystic. I responded differently to each: cheering the first, querying the second, and rejecting the third. Into the Quiet effectively critiques the ills of our hectic cultural moment, but it also makes questionable claims about the spiritual value of silence and promotes a spirituality that could quickly become disconnected from Scripture. Comer as Technoskeptic Comer’s consistent message is that readers need to intentionally disconnect from an increasingly noisy world. By “noise,” he means both literal sounds and the ever-present flood of distraction enabled by digital devices. The result is that “it is now possible to go through our entire lives and never be alone ” (18, emphasis original). Channeling secular authors like Jonathan Haidt and Johann Hari, Comer argues that constant noise threatens our well-being, whether we’re religious or not. But this dynamic is especially harmful for Christians. “Are we really surprised that . . . when we sit down to pray, we can barely even pay attention?” he asks (20). Our always-on lives differ greatly from the example of Jesus, who models a strategy of “retreat and return” (30). He ministers to the crowds and then withdraws to solitary places to pray (e.g., Matt. 14:23). This is the book’s strongest material, a timely warning with which I wholeheartedly agree. Comer as Therapist But then Comer moves in another direction. He advances therapeutic claims that may be helpful to some people but that aren’t clearly grounded in Scripture. According to Comer, solitude forces a confrontation with pain that serves an essential psychological purpose: All of this stuff is in you . . . leaking out like toxic pollution into the water supply of your relational world . . . it’s asking to be dealt with. To be given a moment to speak, say its piece. To be healed. Released. (85) While the imprecatory psalms and the psalms of lament certainly model honest prayer before the Lord, and self-examination is clearly a biblical imperative, Comer’s specific claims seem more informed by extrabiblical therapeutic practices than by Scripture itself. Is it actually true that “naming our feelings out loud allows our bodies to process and discharge pain without it getting lodged in our cores” (100)? That doesn’t sound like Scripture. According to Comer, solitude forces a confrontation with pain that serves an essential psychological purpose. The primary biblical support he gives for the practice of naming feelings to discharge pain is Jesus’s prayer in the garden of Gethsemane, an incident that provides the “template” for “the moments of our own Golgothas” (101). The problem is that Jesus in the garden isn’t surfacing old “toxic pollution” from “the water supply of [his] relational world” with an eye toward therapeutic healing (85). He’s facing an imminent crisis and asking the Father for either deliverance from or strength to face the trial set before him. Whatever the value of surfacing past trauma, Gethsemane doesn’t establish Comer’s claims on that point. 据Comer说,孤独迫使与痛苦的对峙为基本的心理目的服务: 所有这些东西都在你体内, 渗出像有毒污染一样, 渗入你关系世界的水供应中, 得到时间说话,说说它的片段。 以被疗之. 释之.

(85) 虽然圣诗和哀叹的圣诗无疑是上帝面前的模范诚实祷告,而且自我检查显然是圣经的必经之义,但比起《圣经》本身,考美尔的具体主张似乎更能从圣经外的治疗做法中得到启发。

事实上,“大声点出我们的感情,使我们的身体能够处理和释放痛苦,而不将痛苦放在我们的核心中”(100)。 这听起来不像圣经。 据Comer说,孤独迫使一种与痛苦的对抗,这为基本的心理目的服务.

耶稣在Gethsemane的花园里祈祷,这是他为“我们自己的Golgothas(101)时刻”提供“时代”的主要圣经支持。 问题在于花园里的耶稣并没有从“关系世界的供水”中冒出老“有毒污染”,

他正面临迫在眉睫的危机, Gethsemane并没有证明Comer对此的主张。 来者如神秘 对于跟随Comer的作品的人来说,这不会令人惊讶,但他也强调一种神秘的形式.

featured.title_zh: 做人意味着什么？ ： 12篇论文回答了一个紧迫的问题
featured.content: No question today is more pertinent than this: What does it mean to be human? With declining belief in God and rising secularization come renewed debates concerning human nature. Culture now seems to hold to two contradictory beliefs: Either that we’re entirely material beings, meaningless clumps of matter in an endless void; or that we’re sovereign masters who determine our own meaning, with an internal sense of who we are that we dare not defy. It’s no surprise that rejections of God lead to confusion concerning the image of God and the biblical teaching that we’re humbly related to this material cosmos and yet dignified as the crown of creation. With the advent of artificial intelligence and ongoing debates about race, gender, and sexuality, it’s all the more important to be clear about what we are and who we’re made to be. Learning about a Christian theological anthropology is no mere academic exercise. It gets to the heart of who we are, explains our daily experience, and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. A Christian theological anthropology gets to the heart of who we are and pushes us toward the love of neighbor and the common good. In my book, For Us and for Our Salvation , I seek to address these issues by providing a biblical, theological, and practical introduction to the doctrines of humanity and sin. In this article, I present 12 theses that summarize a biblical and Reformed-catholic theological anthropology that I explain throughout the book. These 12 theses, I hope, can ground us as we stand in culture’s ever-changing landscape. 1. All human beings are made in the image of the triune God and are thus called to represent, enjoy, and glorify God forever. God creates each individual according to his image. The first-person plural in Genesis 1:26 indicates that the whole triune God is the archetype for the human being, for each person of the Trinity shares a singular divine substance (see also Col. 1:15–17). Humans are created as representatives of God and are thus religious creatures made to have communion with their Origin. Therefore, each human being as such is created good, with dignity and agency. Our religiosity, corrupted by the fall, doesn’t lead us to cease being religious but rather causes us to elevate and idolize one aspect of creation over others, as we prefer the creature over the Creator (Rom. 1:18–23). We refuse to acknowledge God as the end for which we were made, and we seek enjoyment in other things—we idolize good, created reality and render it ultimate. 2. The doctrine of the image of God entails both ontological and ethical affirmations. God creates humans as embodied souls with intellectual and volitional capacities, and he calls humans to represent him by a proper exercise of those faculties in righteousness, holiness, and true knowledge. Human beings are endowed with capacities for wisdom and righteousness. A twofold metaphysical concept is important here: act and potency. Potency refers to the natural power that distinguishes a particular kind of thing from other kinds, and act refers to the exercise of that power. Humans, for instance, are the kinds of beings endowed with the potency to think rationally, but the actualization of those potencies is a distinct matter. Edward Feser clarifies , In arguing for the existence of active potencies or causal powers, Scholastic writers emphasize the point that a cause is not always bringing about its characteristic effect. . . . My power to write must therefore be distinguished from this or that actual, particular action of writing, as a standing precondition of the latter. Infants or those in a comatose state due to some serious injury, therefore, continue to be image-bearers, even while the potency for wisdom or will isn’t actualized in any way. featured.content_zh:
今天的问题莫过于: 何谓为人. 随着对上帝信仰的下降和世俗化的不断加深,关于人性的辩论又再度出现。 文化现在似乎持有两种相互矛盾的信念: 要么我们完全是物质生物,

或者我们是决定自己意义的主权主人, 对上帝的拒绝导致对上帝形象和圣经教义的困惑, 即我们与这个物质宇宙有着神圣的关系,

随着人工智能的出现和关于种族、性别和性问题的持续辩论的到来,更需要弄清楚我们是什么人,我们是谁。 学习基督教神学人类学不仅仅是学术实践. 它触及我们是谁的心脏, 解释我们的日常经历, 并把我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。

一个基督教神学人类学 得到了我们的心脏 我们推向邻居的爱和共同利益。 在我《为了我们和我们的救世主》一书中,我试图通过提供一本圣经、神学和关于人类和罪恶理论的实际介绍来解决这些问题。

在这篇文章中,我提出了12篇论文,总结了一本圣经和改革天主教神学人类学,我在整个书中都对此作了解释. 我希望这12篇论文能让我们在文化不断变化的地貌中落脚。 1. 所有的人都是以三月神的形象塑造的,因此被召唤来代表、享受和永远颂扬上帝。

上帝根据他的形象创造每个人。 创世纪1:26中的第一人称复数表示,整个三角神是人类的原型,对于三位一体的每个人来说,都有一个独特的神性物质(另见1:15-17). 人类是作为上帝的代表而创造的,因此是宗教的生物,被赋予与他们的起源有共性.

因此,每个人都是善良、有尊严和有作用的。 我们的信仰被堕落所腐蚀, 并不导致我们不再信奉宗教,

我们拒绝承认真主是我们的末日,我们寻求享受,我们崇拜善神,创造现实,使它达到极点。 2. 关于上帝形象的理论包括本体论和伦理论。

上帝以智慧和意志能力创造人性,他号召人通过正确行使正义、圣洁和真正知识的才能来代表他。 人类拥有智慧和正义的能力。 这里有两个元概念很重要:行为和效力。

强力(potency)是指将某种特定事物与其他类型区分开来的自然力量,行为是指行使这种力量. 例如,人类是具有理性思考能力的生物,但是,这些能力的实现是一个独特的问题。

Edward Feser澄清说,在主张存在主动的力量或因果力量时,学术作家强调一个原因并不总是能产生其特征效应。  . 因此,我的写作能力必须与这种或那种实际的、特别的写作行动区分开来,作为后者的长期先决条件。

因此,婴儿或因严重伤害而处于昏迷状态的人继续是形象的持有者,即使智慧或意志的力量根本没有实现。 同样,那些在认知上受损的人仍然具有理智和意志的能力或基本能力,尽管这种能力的表现与其他人不同,而且即使存在这种能力。

featured.title_zh: 你就不能爱所有人吗？
featured.content: “Love one another.” This is one of the undeniable imperatives of Christianity. God is love (1 John 4:8, 16). We must love one another (1 John 4:11). By this love all men know that we are Christ’s disciples (John 13:35). Love fulfills the law (Romans 13:10). So why not just love one another? Why build walls, make distinctions, establish boundaries, and draw lines? Why confront sins? Why not welcome all equally? Can ’ t you just love everyone? The impulse and the argument “just to love everyone” is superficially attractive, even apparently compelling. However, the argument uses Bible language the way Satan does — selectively and deceptively. When tempting Christ, the devil selectively quoted Scripture but twisted the whole sense (cf. Matthew 4:5–7; Psalm 91:11–12). It is possible to use Bible language while ignoring the context, imposing a different meaning on the words and drawing false conclusions based on faulty assumptions. This regularly happens with the meaning of love . Does it really matter? Yes . Churches are disrupted and even destroyed by the confusion created by such shallow reading and reasoning. The language of love is thoroughly scriptural, but we need to handle our Bibles carefully. We need to understand the true definition and the proper direction and order of love. Love Defined and Established Think of love’s definition and foundation. Love does not appear in a vacuum, a sort of glowing, amorphous cloud of feeling which we can press into any mold. Rather, God defines it carefully. God’s love sets the standard for our love: In this the love of God was made manifest among us, that God sent his only Son into the world, so that we might live through him. In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. (1 John 4:9–11) God’s love, which we reflect and replicate by the Spirit’s power, is not a generic niceness but a determined act of the divine will, directed toward the utterly unlovely. It does not at all diminish or dilute the reality of sin. It faces sin’s pollution, punishment, and power head-on, fully honoring divine justice as well as divine mercy. It is love manifested in sacrifice, love determined to do heavenly good to its object, to make the unlovely lovely through whatever righteous means necessary. Christian people show a similar Godlike and Christlike love toward one another. Anticipating his sacrifice, our Lord says, A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another. By this all people will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another. (John 13:34) Christlike love for other believers is a mark of a true disciple. Because God in Christ sets the standard for what love looks like, we cannot collapse Christian love into mere sentimentality, a kind of anodyne sweetness that overlooks or dismisses sin and downplays righteousness. Love Directed and Ordered Think also of love’s direction and order. Our love for our brothers demonstrates our love for God himself (1 John 4:20–21). Our Lord goes to the cross for his beloved people out of love to his Father. The structure of the greatest commandment reveals both direction and order: First , love the Lord your God entirely, and second , love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:37–40; Mark 12:29–31). While not denying a proper love of affinity, Christ calls us to a crowning love of supremacy: We are to love Christ more than father or mother, son or daughter (Matthew 10:37). Love for our nearest and dearest might even be considered hatred in comparison to the love that we have for him (Luke 14:26)! We must not, then, think of love first in its horizontal dimension toward men. featured.content_zh:
“彼此相爱。” 这是基督教不可否认的当务之急之一。 上帝是爱(1约翰4:8,16). 我们必须彼此相爱(1约翰4:11). 我们都是基督的门徒(John 13:35), 爱满足法(罗马语:13:10). 那为什么不只相爱呢? 为什么建造围墙、区分、划定界限和划定界限? 为什么面对罪恶?

为什么不平等地欢迎大家? 你就不能只爱每个人吗? 冲动和“仅仅爱每个人”的论点表面上具有吸引力,甚至显然具有说服力。 然而,这一论点使用与撒旦一样的圣经语言——有选择和欺骗. 当诱惑基督时,恶魔有选择地引用了圣经,但扭曲了整个意义(参见马太福音4:5–7;诗篇91:11–12).

可以同时使用圣经语言而忽略上下文,将不同的含义强加于词上,并根据错误的假设得出错误的结论. 这经常发生在爱的意义。 这真的重要吗? 对 教会被这种浅浅的阅读和推理造成的混乱所扰乱甚至摧毁。

爱的语言是彻头彻尾的文字,但我们需要仔细处理我们的圣经. 我们需要了解真正的定义,以及爱的正确方向和秩序. 爱的定义和基础。 爱情不会出现在真空中, 一种发光的,无形态的感受云, 我们可以压进任何模具。 相反的,上帝是精心定义的。

上帝的爱为我们的爱设定了标准: 在这件事情中,上帝的爱在我们中间被显现出来,上帝把他唯一的儿子送入了世界,以便我们通过他而生存. 爱不是我们爱上帝 而是他爱我们 派他儿子来为我们的罪孽辩护 被爱,如果上帝如此爱我们, 我们也应该相爱。

(1 John 4:9-11)上帝的爱,我们用精神的力量来反映和复制,不是一种一般的善意,而是神意志的坚定行为,直接对准完全不爱的人。 它丝毫没有削弱或淡化罪恶的现实。 它面临着罪恶的污染、惩罚和权力,完全尊重神圣的正义和神圣的慈悲。

爱表现在牺牲中,爱决心为它的目标做天上的好事,通过任何必要的正义手段使不爱的人变得可爱. 基督教徒对彼此的爱 表现出类似上帝和基督的爱

我们的主说,在期待他的牺牲时,我给你新的戒律,即你们彼此相爱:正如我一直爱你们一样,你们也要彼此相爱。 由此一切众生悉知汝等为我弟子,若有相爱. (约翰13:34) 基督爱其他信徒是真正的门徒的标志.

因为上帝在基督中为爱的外表设定了标准, 我们不能把基督教的爱 变成单纯的多愁善感, 一种忽视或否定罪孽和贬低正义的厌倦的甜言蜜语。 Love Directed and Ordered 想想爱的方向和秩序。 我们对我们兄弟的爱显示了我们对上帝本人的爱(1 John 4:20–21).

我们的主为了他敬爱的百姓去十字架 为了他父亲 最伟大的戒律结构揭示了方向和秩序:第一,完全爱主你的神,第二,像爱自己一样爱邻居(Matthew 22:37–40;Mark 12:29–31).

基督在不否认亲情的同时, 要求我们拥有至高无上的爱: 我们比父亲或母亲、儿子或女儿更爱基督(Matthew 10:37)。 相较于我们对他的爱,对亲近和最亲近的爱甚至可能被视为仇恨(公爵14:26)! 那么,我们决不能在对男人的横向层面首先想到爱情。

爱必须首先垂直地向上帝倾斜,以应对他对我们的爱,然后横向地向他人倾斜。 "爱"对男人 牺牲爱T

featured.title_zh: 任务对儿童来说是否太昂贵？
featured.content: Are my children also called to this ? As a mama missionary, I wonder about our fitness for the task when our family of eight clogs airport security and labors in language study and ministry like a well-meaning circus. Will my kids catch a deadly virus from the airport carpet? Will beans be lunch every day ? How can we possibly replace years spent with grandparents and a vibrant children’s church? Will they become healthy adults when this calling cuts not only us but them? Are the unreached regions of the Joshua Project map reserved for singles? Our family’s plane-ticket prices alone might argue that case. Does the church only send the strong? In the world’s economy, our crew is inefficient and slow to get the job done. Risk Worth Reward The missionary call may cost our precious children extra bouts of food poisoning, power outages, awkward cultural moments, and loneliness. It may even, like Perpetua Broten and Ezra, Violet, and Calvin Pals , require their lives. When Jesus called his followers, he asked for painful, costly sacrifice. He reminded them that though foxes and birds return each day to their burrows and nests, he had no place to lay his head (Matthew 8:20). He called his disciples to take no change of clothes or spare coin for their ministry (Matthew 10:9–10). And yet he said, “There is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold” both now and in eternity (Mark 10:29–30). God’s economy is not man’s. Jesus calls kids to go with moms and dads to serve the nations because God’s kingdom advancement is for families too, and the risk is worth its reward. The forward momentum of God’s kingdom does not exclude our children. The garden mandate to be fruitful and multiply now expands spiritually, and we take our kids along. We aren’t disqualified from overseas ministry if we’re changing diapers on the hour. God is the author of life and the genius behind the family design. Our dominion over the earth as image-bearers includes those in our care, even if they look too small to slay dragons. The risks of going with kids in tow are many; only the rewards of trust and obedience eclipse their reality. If we pursued mere adventure or greater cultural appreciation, we would be the “most to be pitied” (1 Corinthians 15:19). But if God calls us to glory in Christ in dungeon-like places, teaching our children to cup their hands around their mouths and cry to prisoners, “Come out!” then we offer them diamond-quality joy (Isaiah 49:9, 61:1). We weep with our kids over the cost they see and feel in their own lives, helping them gather the broken pieces of their hearts to hand to Jesus, teaching them firsthand that Christ’s flesh and blood satisfy. Shepherding Your Flock Before my two oldest children were dunked in the cold mountain water of our village in baptism, they testified to God’s grace in their lives. God had shown them his best at their worst. I flinched inwardly as I heard them recall dangerous accidents and desperate emotions in our time overseas. But when it turned darkest, God shone brightest. If it were up to me, I would have taken an eraser to God’s plan of pain for them. If I had, I would also have unknowingly rubbed out his intimate deliverances. The pleasure of following God to the farthest reaches of the planet with your kids is finding that God is there too. All that said, our family just moved ministry locations overseas due to prolonged isolation and our kids’ growing need for friends and community. Missions is a family affair and worth the risk, while at the same time, God does not depend on our presence in a place to accomplish his purposes, and he cares specifically for our kids. Our kids’ particular needs are not at odds with our calling but can direct our feet and make us wise shepherds of our flock. God is not biting his nails on the sidelines of our missionary service, hoping we’ll perform well enou

值得回报的风险 传教士的召唤可能使我们珍贵的孩子们额外损失食物中毒、断电、尴尬的文化时刻和孤独。 它甚至可能像Perpetua Broten和Ezra、Violet和Calvin Pals一样需要他们的生命。 当耶稣召唤他的追随者时,他要求痛苦,昂贵的牺牲.

他提醒他们,虽然狐狸和鸟儿每天返回他们的洞穴和巢穴,但他没有地方安顿头颅(Matthew 8:20). 他叫门徒们不要为他们的部会换衣服或多余的硬币(Matthew 10:9-10).

然而,他却说,“没有人离开过家,也没有人离开过兄弟姐妹,也没有人离开过母亲、孩子或土地,为了我和福音,现在和永远都得不到一百倍”(Mark 10:29-30)。 上帝的经济不是人类的经济。

因为上帝的王国进步也是为了家庭, 上帝王国的前进势头并不排除我们的孩子。 花园的任务富有成果,倍增,现在精神上有所扩展,我们带着我们的孩子一起走.

如果我们换尿布, 上帝是生命的作者,也是家庭设计背后的天才. 我们作为形象持有者对地球的统治权包括那些受我们照顾的人,即使他们看起来太小,不能杀死龙。 和孩子一起被拖走的风险是很多的;只有信任和服从的回报掩盖了他们的现实。

如果我们仅仅追求冒险或更大的文化欣赏,我们将“最可怜”(科林斯15:19)。 但是,如果上帝在类似地牢的地方召唤我们在基督中荣耀,教我们的孩子用手握住嘴,向囚犯喊叫,“出来吧!”那么我们给他们提供钻石质量的快乐(以赛亚49:9,61:1)。

我们和孩子们一起为他们自己生活中所看到和感受到的代价而哭泣,帮助他们收集心碎的碎片交给耶稣,并亲身教他们基督的血肉满足。 在我两个年长的孩子 被浸在村里的寒冷山水里之前 他们证明了上帝的恩惠

上帝在他们最坏的时候 给他们展示了他最好的一面 当我听到他们回想起我们海外时代的危险事故和绝望情绪时,我内向退缩。 但当它变得最黑暗时,上帝会闪耀 如果由我决定的话,我本来会用一个抹除器去完成上帝给他们的痛苦计划。 如果我有的话,我也会不知不觉地 抹去他的亲切奉献。

和你们的孩子一起跟随上帝到达地球最远的地方的乐趣 就是发现上帝也在那里 我们的家人因为长期孤立和孩子对朋友和社区的日益需求,刚刚将部属迁往海外。

使命是一种家庭事务,值得冒风险,与此同时,上帝并不依赖我们的存在来实现他的目的,他特别关心我们的孩子. 我们的孩子的特殊需求与我们的召唤并不矛盾,

featured.title: To Sustain Inner-City Church Plants, Adopt a Missionary Model
featured.summary: To plant churches in these spaces, we need to think like missionaries.

featured.title_zh: 为了维持内城教会植物，采用传教士模式
featured.content: In a conversation at church one Sunday, a pastor told a friend of mine, “Your friend should quit trying to plant churches in the inner city. It doesn’t happen because it can’t happen.” I was visiting this friend just before COVID-19 hit, speaking at a separate church about our ministry, New England Urban Church Planting. Our organization was new, and my sinful inclination was to think, Oh, you just wait and see! My friend was equally defensive. Yet this pastor was onto something: It rarely happens, and it is indeed hard. Why is church planting in our nation’s neglected inner cities so rare? Why are underserved urban communities overlooked by gospel-preaching churches? Stakeholders in our ministry have discussed these questions since 2009, leading to the organization’s founding in 2020. We’ve learned a lot in these years of full-time work as we’re growing this network of inner-city planters. The work is hard for two key reasons. Yet it’s possible. And it’s crucial. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations (Matt. 28:19)—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. To plant churches in these spaces, we need to think like missionaries. Problem Unless you grew up in the inner city, serving there is a cross-cultural experience. This is the first reason church planting hard. Ruby Payne asks her readers if they can survive in poverty: Do you know how to keep your clothes from being stolen from a laundromat? Do you know how to move in half a day? Do you know how to keep your car from getting repossessed if you fall behind on payments? Discipling men and women in the inner city can be exasperating when they have a new burner phone frequently. Inner-city pastors need to know how to preach and how to administer Narcan. And behind all that is the sound of gunshots, fights, loud TVs, and the quiet exit of well-meaning suburban Christians who came to help but didn’t last long. Christ has commanded us to make disciples of all nations—this includes in our own nation’s inner cities. Evangelicalism often feels like it’s married to only one culture: suburbia. Postwar Americans migrated from our cities to set up homes and churches in the suburbs. In 1940, 15 percent of Americans lived in the suburbs. By 2000, that number was 50 percent. Evangelicals were a disproportionately high percentage of those who made the move. As this happened, Brian Miller argues , the values of suburbia melded with and shaped the values of evangelicalism. Churches in impoverished neighborhoods are rarely financially self-sustaining—the second challenge. Even if a pastor disciples his church toward generosity, being generous with a poverty-level income won’t pay the bills. So pastors who serve in these places get beaten down by serving a needy congregation while holding two other jobs “on the side.” It’s unsustainable. We don’t believe the answer for inner-city pastors should be a bi- or trivocational life. Solution The solution to these two challenges is within reach: the model of a supported foreign missionary. Since the late 18th century, the church has been training and sustaining men and women for gospel work in unfamiliar places, where they cannot expect the financial support of locals. This training-and-supporting model should be applied to inner-city church planting. The change we need has four aspects. The first is a change of heart. We need gospel-saturated hearts that understand that all people are impoverished by sin. Those living in a homeless encampment share the same fundamental condition as the wealthy suburbanite. Filled with gospel grace, we can move toward the poor because we’re more alike at heart than we are different. Our hearts must be shaped by the reality of Christ’s initiative to leave the riches of heaven for us, to become poor for us, that we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9). featured.title_zh: 关于您行动的报告卡片无法修复您的心脏
featured.content: Who am I? All cultures, human philosophies, and religious systems try to answer this question in a way that leads to a meaningful life. We want to find in them a path that allows us to say, “Who am I? I’m a good person. I’m someone who is living a good and right life.” What paths toward goodness and righteousness are being offered today? They’re as vast and varied as ever. One popular path is to optimize your life via medical improvements, ranging from plastic surgery to GLP-1s. The more you can “ humanmaxx ” your body to look healthier and be stronger, the more likely you’ll be considered an ideal human being—a good person to hire, to be friends with, to date or marry. Political engagement is another common path. Your goodness is determined by how connected you are to particular political movements. You can feel like you’re a good person when you make sure you quickly like and repost all Zohran Mamdani’s videos. Or alternatively, you’ll be affirmed as a good person by how aggressively you go after or insult people who like Mamdani. Paths our culture offers to the good life are often combined. Your sense of how good a person you are is measured by a mixture of how long you’ve engaged in therapy, how many hours you volunteer at your children’s school, and how long your streak is on your mindfulness app. Tara Isabella Burton, in her book Strange Rites: New Religions for a Godless World , argues that people have formed their own religious systems by drawing from various religions and philosophies. People have become “creators of their own bespoke religions, mixing and matching spiritual and aesthetic and experiential and philosophical traditions.” We’re doing a DIY project, grabbing and piecing together whatever’s around us, hoping we can come up with something to help us in our journey. So, what path does Christianity offer to assure us we’re living a good and righteous life? Keeping Score The Christian approach is to address what the Bible calls the heart. The heart is the Bible’s shorthand term for describing the part of you that drives and motivates you, what dictates your thoughts and emotions. Christianity starts with the heart because this is the only real way by which you can determine who you are and what needs to change. We see the contrast between the religious and cultural approach and the Christian approach in Jesus’s interaction with the Pharisees in Matthew 15:1–20. The Pharisees confront Jesus to ask him why his disciples don’t wash their hands before eating. Handwashing before meals was one of the many religious rules the Pharisees had developed, practiced, and called others to practice. For the Pharisees, the best answer to the question “Who am I?” was based on how well they followed their set standards. If a person kept the standard and had a life that could be observed to follow all the rules, then that person could definitively say to themselves and those around them, “I’m a good person who is living a good and right life.” Jesus’s story about the Pharisee in Luke 18:9–14 is another example. The Pharisee intently notes in his prayer how he, unlike the tax collector praying next to him, fasts twice a week and always gives the full tithe. Jesus describes the Pharisees in Matthew 6 as people who make sure their regular prayers can be seen and affirmed by all. The Pharisees weren’t alone in this approach. Greco-Roman religion had its own rules and standards to follow. Its gods demanded rituals, sacrifices, and festivals to appease and honor them. Performed rightly, they’d result in people securing the blessing they needed from the gods, thus assuring them their lives were good and righteous. Jesus, however, reframes the Pharisees’ questioning by showing that their approach doesn’t go far enough. Right living and human flourishing demands more than one’s outward actions. It requires harder interior examination. And that means looking at the heart. Jesus says, “What comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart” (

你的善良取决于你和特定政治运动的关系 也觉得自己是个好人, 或以你对马姆达尼的追求或侮辱来证明你是一个好人。 我们的文化为美好生活提供的道路常常是结合在一起的。

你对一个人有多好的感觉,是通过你从事治疗的时间、你在学校志愿工作多少小时、以及你的心智应用上多久来衡量的。

Tara Isabella Burton在她所著"陌生的Rites:新宗教为无神的世界"一书中认为,人们通过从各种宗教和哲学中汲取来形成自己的宗教体系.

人们已经成为“他们自己所讲的宗教的创造者,混合和配合精神和美学以及体验和哲学传统。” 我们正在进行一个DIY计划, 抓取和整理我们周围的东西, 希望我们能想出一些东西来帮助我们的旅程。 基督教给我们提供了什么途径来保证我们过着美好和正义的生活?

记分 基督教的方法是解决"圣经"所说的"心". 心灵是圣经的简称,用来描述你推动和激励你,决定你思想和情绪的部分。 基督教以心为起点,因为这是你决定自己是谁和需要改变的惟一真正方法.

法利赛人在祷告中故意记下他如何与旁边的收税者不同的是,他每周斋戒两次并总是给满分之一. 耶稣在"马太福音"6中将法利赛人描述为确保他们的定期祷告能被所有人都看到和肯定的人. 法利赛人并不孤单。 格雷科-罗马宗教有自己的规则和标准可以遵循。

它的神要求举行仪式,祭祀,并举行节日来安抚和尊崇他们. 让他们得到神赐予的祝福, 但耶稣重新定义了法利赛人的质疑,

正确的生活和人类的繁荣需要不止一种外向行动。 这需要更严格的内部检查。 并谓观心相. 耶稣说,“从口中出出的东西从心脏中得来。”

featured.content: Audio Transcript What does evil look like? And sound like? And feel like? Is evil like a horror film set in a haunted forest in a remote cabin at night with floorboards creaking under uninvited footsteps? Or is evil the most scandalous murder trial in the headlines? Is evil more quiet, like in white-collar crimes and embezzlement? Or is it a bloody civil war? There are many forms evil can take. But at its core, how evil works is more essential than all those things I just described. Today on Ask Pastor John: how evil works. This week in our Bible reading, we come upon a trio of texts that collectively reveal to us Satan’s multifront assault — how he works in this world. He is a spiritual deceiver of minds, he is a prosecuting accuser in the heavenly courtroom, and he is a behind-the-scenes influence in human rebellion. He seems to work in a lot of different ways. In John 8 we see him as a liar and murderer. In 2 Peter 2–3 we see him as the deceiver and destroyer. And in Job 4–6 we see him as the provocateur and accuser. Those roles help reveal his work to us in the world. And as we rehearse these roles in our Bible reading this week, we have this email from an anonymous young man. “Pastor John, when I think about spiritual warfare, I often first think about physical things like illness and addiction and even demonic possession. But I wonder if I am missing a larger picture. How much influence does Satan have in this world, and how does he use it? How much of his power is physical? How much of it is unseen? And where do you see him most at work in our modern culture? Is it in obvious sins? Or in subtler ways to keep people from the gospel? How can I see his work without getting preoccupied with him?” A great question with clear purpose. Here’s how Pastor John answered this very question from a young man named Josh in 2018. How Satan Works The word Satan is a transliteration of the Hebrew Satan (śāṭān) and basically means “opponent” or “adversary.” The Greek translation of the Hebrew Old Testament always translates Satan with diabolos in Greek, which means “devil”; we always translate diabolos in English, in the New Testament, “devil.” And diabolos puts a more specific focus on the meaning of the opponent or adversary because diabolos basically means “slander” or “accuse.” It’s used not only to refer to the devil; several times in the Pastoral Epistles of Paul, it’s used to refer to people who are slandering others, speaking evil of them, being false about them. So, even though this supernatural being, this fallen angel and archenemy of God, has a remarkable power in the material or physical realm — he can make people sick, he can throw them in prison, he can even kill them — nevertheless, his main way of opposing God and destroying God’s people is not in the physical or material realm but in the mental or intellectual or moral realm. In other words, the best way to think about his power is not in terms of physical strength but moral deception. Let me try to illustrate this from the Bible. Here’s the passage that piles up more designations of Satan than any other passage in the Bible. If you need one or two verses to put the identity and work of Satan before you, it would be Revelation 12:9–10. Here it says, “And the great dragon was thrown down, that ancient serpent.” And remember what the Bible said in Genesis 3:1 about him. He’s subtler than every beast. So, it’s his subtlety that’s being focused on in his serpent-like reality. “[He] is called the devil [diabolos: slanderer, liar, cheat] and Satan [adversary], the deceiver of the whole world” (Revelation 12:9). I don’t think you can say anything more sweeping or more basic than Revelation 12:9–10. “The accuser of our brothers has been thrown down, who accuses them day and night before our God” (Revelation 12:10). featured.title_zh: 初学者和经验丰富的传教士的帮助：大卫·杰克曼从文本到教学的回顾
featured.content: Abstract: Jeremy Meeks reviews David Jackman’s From Text to Teaching: A Guide to Preparing Bible Talks and commends it as a helpful resource for anyone who preaches or teaches the Bible in any context. This brief book offers discussions of the art and science of preaching and the process of preparation, and it provides an inside look at Jackman’s own preparation to preach 1 Corinthians 1–4. The final chapters offer checklists that will be practically useful for preachers, and the appendix contains the author’s own template for preparing a Bible talk. Both beginners and seasoned preachers and teachers will benefit from this book. David Jackman, From Text to Teaching: A Guide to Preparing Bible Talks . Matthias Media, 2021. 92 pp. Even seasoned preacher needs to go back to basics sometimes and be refreshed. Similarly, guys starting out need instruction—someone to teach them how to go about the craft. Often the most helpful teachers are those who have lots of experience. What is even better is if such a preacher has also spent substantial time training others to preach. Ideally, that preacher/trainer has such command of the material that he is able to distill his insights and counsel into a tight, readable book. We have been given such a gift in David Jackman’s little volume From Text to Teaching . In just 92 pages, Jackman provides a lifetime of wisdom for the beginner and the seasoned preacher alike. As he explains in the introduction, he is addressing (as evidenced in the title) the skill of Bible teaching more generally and not solely preaching. This might turn away preachers who don’t consider themselves to be giving “Bible talks,” but that would be the preacher’s loss. The weight of what we get to do every time we open the Bible and teach from it in any context is rightly esteemed by Jackman. The Art and Science of Preaching The book begins by discussing the “Art and Science of Preaching.” Both aspects of preaching—art and science—must be held onto if we are to do it well. Seeing preaching as a science helps us understand that there are tools we can apply to do the work better. Seeing it as an art reminds us that the work requires us to pay attention to the beauty of Bible proclamation. Preaching is more than using the Bible to communicate. Rather, our task is to preach what the text says, that is, giving the meaning of what it says, in context, for the people sitting in front of us. Jackman’s convictions will be new to some, common to others, but beneficial to all. The Process of Preparation A substantial chapter is dedicated to the “Process of Preparation”. Here Jackman helps the Bible preacher/teacher think through how to put a message together. As a preacher who trains other preachers, I’m constantly asked how I do this on a weekly basis, and I enjoy hearing how others do it as well. Jackman has sage advice. He reminds us that we should always be praying (an obvious but seriously neglected aspect of preparation). He is also clear that we should use the time we have strategically. We never have as much time as we would like, and we often think we need more time than we do. The fact is that preachers often waste a lot of time because they are not strategic. Jackman recommends setting aside a few blocks of time in the week (four sessions that are each two to three hours). What is vital is that the preacher figures out what works well for him and plans his schedule accordingly. Jackman then gives helpful advice on how to go about studying and writing out the sermon inside those blocks of time, and this advice is helpful for those at all levels of proficiency. Invited into the Author’s Study The next three chapters (3–5) of the book are pure gold. In essence, Jackman invites us into his study to listen in as he walks through his process of preparing messages on 1 Corinthians 1–4. Here we get insights into how his suggested process works in actual texts. This is something many books on preaching neglect to do, leaving the rea
featured.content_zh:
摘要:杰里米·米克(Jeremy Meeks)评论了大卫·杰克曼的"从文字到教学:准备圣经谈话的指南",并称赞它是任何背景中宣扬或教授圣经的人的有用资源. 这本简短的书提供了对布道的艺术和科学以及准备过程的讨论,它提供了杰克曼自己为布道1科林斯1–4的准备的内观.

最后的章节提供了对传道者实际上有用的核对表,附录中包含了作者自己准备圣经演讲的模板. 初学者和老练的传道人和教师都将受益于这本书。 David Jackman,《从文字到教学:准备圣经会谈指南》,Matthias Media,2021年。

甚至老练的传教士有时也需要回到基础,被刷新. 类似地,开始的人需要教书,有人教他们如何操作这款工艺。 最有帮助的教师往往是经验丰富的教师。 更好的是,如果这种传道者也花大量时间训练其他人传道。

理想的情况是,传教士/教官对材料有如此高的指挥力,他能够将自己的见解和咨询意见提炼成一本紧凑可读的书。 在大卫·杰克曼的"从文字到教学"一书中,我们得到了这样的礼物。 在92页里,杰克曼为初学者和老练的传道者提供了一生的智慧.

正如他在导言中所解释的,他正在讨论(如标题所证明的)《圣经》教学的技巧更普遍,而不仅仅是传道。 这可能会让那些不认为自己在进行“圣经会谈”的传道者退后,

每当我们打开圣经并在任何背景中从中教导时,我们所能做的事情的分量都得到了杰克曼的正确尊重. 该书首先讨论了“影响艺术与科学”。 如果我们要做得好,就必须坚持艺术和科学两个方面的传道。

将传道视为一种科学,有助于我们理解,我们可以应用一些工具来更好地开展工作。 把它看作是一门艺术,提醒我们,这部作品需要我们关注"圣经"宣言的美. 意义不仅仅是用"圣经"来沟通.

相反,我们的任务是宣扬案文所说的话,即在背景上赋予案文所述的含义,供坐在我们前面的人民使用。 杰克曼的信念对一些人来说是新的,对另一些人来说是共同的,但对所有人都有好处。 1. 编写过程

在这里,杰克曼帮助"圣经"的传道人/老师思考如何将一个信息集中起来. 作为一名培养其他传教士的传教士, 我经常问每周我怎么做, 杰克曼有圣人的建议 他提醒我们,我们应当永远祈祷(准备工作中一个明显但被严重忽略的方面)。

他还明确指出,我们应该从战略角度利用我们的时间。 我们从来没有像我们想要的那样多的时间,我们常常认为我们需要比我们多的时间。 事实是道教经常会因为不具有战略意义而浪费大量时间. 杰克曼建议在一周内留出几块时间(每两到三小时四会).

重要的是,传道者要知道什么对他很有效,并据此规划他的时间安排。 杰克曼随后就如何研究并写出这些时间段内的布道给出了有益的建议,而这个建议对于所有水平的熟练程度的人都是有帮助的. 书中接下来的三章(3–5)是纯金.

基本上,杰克曼邀请我们进入他的书房 在他行走的过程中聆听 他准备了科林斯1 -4的信息。 在这里,我们深入了解他建议的进程如何在实际文本中发挥作用。 这是很多书 关于布道 忽略做,留下的灵性

featured.title_zh: 谁是圣经中的神？
featured.content: According to the Belgic Confession , God reveals himself to us in two “books”: the book of nature (God’s world) and the book of Scripture (God’s written Word). The primary way God reveals himself in the book of Scripture is by proclaiming his name. In this first of two paired lectures from TGC25, Scott Swain considers several of the names whereby God reveals himself in the Bible. Contemplating God’s names provides a deeper understanding of his being and attributes and a firmer foundation for our faith and hope. It also helps us better appreciate the ways God reveals himself to us in Jesus Christ. featured.title: ‘I Play Rocky’ Finds New Inspiration in an Old Story
featured.summary: ‘I Play Rocky’ is the latest pop-culture celebration of storytelling as agency: telling your story in just the way you want it to be told.
featured.summary_zh: “I Play Rocky”是将讲故事作为代理的最新流行文化庆祝活动：以您希望的方式讲述您的故事。
featured.title_zh: 《我扮演洛基》在古老的故事中寻找新的灵感
featured.content: Rocky debuted in theaters 50 years ago, in 1976—a bicentennial-year release that underscored the movie’s profound American spirit. Immediately a blockbuster and critical darling (the highest-grossing movie of 1976 and winner of the Best Picture Oscar), it has since become a pantheon film in American cinema. Rocky ’s Philadelphia setting and underdog, rags-to-riches story captured a hardscrabble American optimism, something that gave needed inspiration in the mid-1970s and resonates still today. Now in 2026—America’s semiquincentennial— Rocky is getting a theatrical rerelease. And a new movie, I Play Rocky (out today in select theaters) is telling the story of the iconic movie’s development, which is an underdog epic of its own. The movie, directed by Peter Farrelly ( Green Book ) and starring Anthony Ippolito in a breakout turn as Sylvester Stallone, is a refreshingly feel-good crowd pleaser. It’s the sort of well-made, intelligent, but also inspiring movie for grown-ups that feels like a dying breed in Hollywood. Movies About Moviemaking I Play Rocky (rated PG-13 for language) follows a well-worn template of a movie about the making of a classic movie. Saving Mr. Banks (2013) was about Walt Disney and the making of Mary Poppins . Hitchcock (2012) was about Alfred Hitchcock and the making of Psycho . Last year’s Nouvelle Vague was about Jean-Luc Godard and the making of Breathless . I Play Rocky is about Stallone and the making of Rocky . Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Hollywood loves making movies about itself: stories about storytelling, movies about moviemaking, actors playing actors. Self-reflexive inspiration goes back more than a century in cinema, perhaps starting with Dziga Vertov’s Man with a Movie Camera (1929). The 1950s produced classics like Sunset Boulevard (1950) and Singin’ in the Rain (1952), but the trend really picked up in the postmodern era in the 1960s and beyond: 8 ½ (1963), Day for Night (1973), Mulholland Drive (2001), Adaptation (2002), The Artist (2011), and Once Upon a Time . . . in Hollywood (2019). The list is long. A hallmark of postmodernity is a metaposture of knowing awareness—storytellers who know they’re storytellers and want the audience to know that they know. As postmodernism has given way to metamodernism , the trend of “movies about moviemaking” has continued, but in a slightly different register. These sorts of films are no longer merely metaexercises in self-awareness. The cerebral, cynical detachment of “films about filmmaking” like Barton Fink (1991), Ed Wood (1994), or even Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988) has given way to metamodern expressions that blend cynicism and sincerity, self-awareness with earnest escapism. Steven Spielberg’s The Fabelmans (2022) is a recent example of a movie in this vein, and I Play Rocky has a similar feel. Even as it lifts the veil on the Hollywood myth factory and mines many laughs out of the fundamentally profit-seeking, money-centric nature of the movie business, it’s full of heart and soul. It has a joyful, hopeful, sincere, perhaps idealistic spirit (“I’d rather be an optimist and be wrong, than a pessimist and be right,” one character says). Refreshing Celebration of Marriage I also like how I Play Rocky celebrates the empowering beauty of marriage. The film opens with Stallone as a broke actor in New York, sometimes sleeping on the streets and at one point accepting a role in an X-rated adult film just to earn some desperately needed money (a dark part of Stallone’s past that the film plays for awkward laughs). He’s a lost soul with bleak prospects. But then he meets Sasha (AnnaSophia Robb), with whom he works at a movie theater. They get married and move to Los Angeles, and things start to turn around for him. As a husband and soon a father, Stallone feels more urgency to provide. featured.title: How the Lord’s Supper Fuels Spiritual Growth
featured.summary: Calvin shows us that the Lord’s Supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time.
featured.summary_zh: 加尔文向我们表明，主的晚餐是灵性成长的燃料，所以我们每次都应该期待地来到餐桌前。
featured.title_zh: 主的晚餐如何促进灵性成长
featured.content: Recently, I (and my peers) have experienced a number of parishioners converting to Catholicism. As I’ve talked to these converts, they’ve consistently brought up the Lord’s Table. They find encouragement in identifying the bread and wine with Jesus’s body and blood. I’ve heard statements such as this: Pastor George, I like the idea that Jesus was talking about the Lord’s supper when he said, “Whoever feeds on my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6:56). My faith just feels more real if I’m literally bringing Jesus into my body on a daily basis. While this phenomenon seems to be happening with greater frequency, it’s not totally new. Years ago, I served alongside a man at an ordination service for another pastor in our city. I hadn’t met this man before; I only knew he had until recently been a professor at a Reformed and evangelical seminary. This man preached a solid message on Jesus’s call for ministers of the gospel, and I thanked him for it. Then, the next day, I saw him being interviewed on TV. I tuned in just as he explained, I needed more realism than my tradition provided, so during lunch I would walk down to the local Roman Catholic parish and take the Eucharist. To unite literally with Jesus’s body and blood was more deeply satisfying to me than the “mystery of union with Christ” my church taught. So, I resigned my post at the seminary and went home to Rome. I could relate other conversations with those who have left the Reformed faith and joined the Roman Catholic, Orthodox, or Anglo-Catholic traditions. A similar theme runs through them all: the desire for a more transformational, sensory reality than what the Reformed view of the Lord’s supper provides. Is this critique valid? How would John Calvin respond to the critique that if you follow the Reformed view of the supper, you’re missing out on its power? Transformed at the Table Sometimes, in an effort to have biblically faithful theology, Reformed Christians speak only of what the communion elements are not . I’m painfully aware of my of shortcomings in this regard. This can inadvertently drive some believers to seek out a more “real” experience in other traditions. We can get caught up in debating the exact nature of the bread and wine and forget to ask the more pressing question: How should this meal change me today? Let’s look back at Calvin’s teachings on communion. When we do, we’ll recover a renewed vision for the table, one that sees it as a divine encounter that motivates a transformed life of profound gratitude and obedience. In short, Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In Calvin’s “ Short Treatise on the Lord’s Supper ,” he writes that the supper fuels the believer’s spiritual growth in at least three ways. 1. The supper assures us of our inheritance in Christ. Calvin teaches that Jesus uses his table to assure us of our inheritance. He doesn’t merely mean that the supper gives us a psychological boost. He means that assurance comes by means of a real union between Christ and the believer, and he means that our experience of this union is expedited by faithfully partaking in the covenant meal. Calvin shows us that the Lord’s supper is fuel for spiritual growth, so we should come to the table expectantly every time. In his commentary on Ephesians, Calvin writes , “Paul says that we are members of his [Christ’s] flesh and of his bones. Do we wonder then, that in the Lord’s Supper he holds out his body to be enjoyed by us, and to nourish us unto eternal life?” Calvin insists that by faith, Christians are made members of Jesus’s fleshly human body, so at communion, we experience all the benefits of spiritual union with him. Christ took on flesh so that in his ascended state, he might be a channel of righteousness to the believer, pouring into him all that Christ’s human life accomplished. 正如他所解释的,我需要比传统更现实的, 所以在午餐期间,我会走进罗马天主教当地的教区, 并带上尤查里会。 比起教会教义的“与基督结合的谜团”, 于是我辞去神学院的职务,回到了罗马.

我可以和那些脱离改革后信仰并加入罗马天主教、东正教或天主教传统的人交谈。 一个类似的主题贯穿于所有这些方面:渴望一个比改革后对主的晚餐提供的看法更具有转型性、感官性的现实。 这种批评有道理吗?

我们将会重新恢复对桌子的憧憬, 简言之,加尔文告诉我们,主的晚餐是精神成长的燃料,因此,我们每次都应该期待地来到餐桌旁。

featured.content: Abstract : Jonathan Leeman highlights the corporate component of conversion, pointing out that God not only reconciles us to himself through Christ but also to one another. While our (vertical) reconciliation to God is foundational and primary, our (horizontal) reconciliation to others is necessarily bound up with our salvation. Conversion makes us part of God’s people, and this corporate aspect of our salvation should compel us to join a local church. Editor’s Note: This article is taken from Church Matters, the 9Marks journal for pastors, in the issue titled Conversion . If your doctrine of conversion is missing the corporate element, it’s missing something essential. Jesus died for a people (see Mark 10:45). He saves us as individuals, and he saves us into a people. Salvation includes a family. If you’re not convinced, jump straight to these parallel statements from Peter: Once you were not a people, but now you are God’s people; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy. (1 Pet. 2:10) If someone asks you how you became a Christian, you probably emphasize the second line in your testimony. You say something like, “I was living in sin apart from God. A friend shared the gospel with me. I recognized who God is and what Christ did in dying and rising again. Therefore, I repented and believed. Praise God, he forgave me and I received his mercy!” What a wonderful testimony. Don’t stop saying that! Widen Your Perspective But notice that Peter widens the aperture of the camera and tells us a little more about what happened in that same moment. In addition to moving from not mercy to mercy, we simultaneously moved from not a people to a people. That means our testimonies could include a little bit more. Like this: “I was living in sin apart from God, and I wanted nothing to do with God’s family, the church. A friend shared the gospel with me. I recognized who God is and what Christ did in dying and rising again. Therefore, I repented and believed. Praise God, he forgave me and I received his mercy! I also realized that—wow!—I was part of a family now, the church.” Do you see what I mean by the “corporate” component of conversion? We’re saved into the universal church. That’s not to say we should put the corporate element out front. One might think of N. T. Wright’s well-known line about justification being “not so much about soteriology as about ecclesiology; not so much about salvation as about the church . ” N.T. Wright, What Saint Paul Really Said (Eerdmans, 20 1 4), 1 1 9. This is a clear example, in Douglas Moo’s almost-as-well-known line, of backgrounding what the New Testament foregrounds, and foregrounding what the New Testament backgrounds (as cited in D. A. Carson, “Faith and Faithfulness,” Ligonier, February 1 , 20 1 0, https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/faith-and-faithfulness). There can be no true reconciliation between humans until individual sinners are first reconciled to God. The horizontal necessarily follows the vertical. Ecclesiology necessarily follows soteriology. Which is to say, the corporate element must not come first, lest we lose salvation altogether. Vertical and Horizontal But it must come. Indeed, the corporate component must remain within the structure of the doctrine of conversion itself. Our corporate unity in Christ is not just an implication of conversion; it’s part of the very thing. Being reconciled to God’s people is distinct from but inseparable from being reconciled to God. These two elements of conversion are wonderfully put on display in Ephesians 2 with two instances of the word “but.” The first comes as Paul narrates man’s rescue from sin and death (vv. 1–10), which hinges on the words “ But God, being rich in mercy . . . ” (v. 4). Those words introduce God’s saving love and the fact that he has “raised us up with [Christ] and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (v. 6). featured.content: What marks Christians attuned to cross-cultural missions? They may not serve as full-time missionaries, but they embrace Great Commission responsibilities. The history of missions reveals little-known senders who used their vocations for strategic gospel advance around the world. Captain Benjamin Wickes (1746–1830) was one such man. ‘Old Captain Wickes’ We meet this early American captain of a merchant vessel unexpectedly at a prayer meeting in 1806. The missionaries in Serampore, India, had gathered to send Henry Martyn to a station on the Ganges River where he would begin his work of translation and evangelism. Martyn recorded that they “met at my pagoda this evening for the purpose of commending me to the grace of God before my departure. My soul never before had such divine enjoyment” ( The Letters of Henry Martyn , 194). I would love to have been there. The meeting included both Baptist missionaries — William Carey, Joshua Marshman, and William Ward — as well as evangelical Anglicans David Brown, Daniel Corrie, and Henry Martyn. It represented a substantial collaboration between these earliest English missionaries for the advance of the gospel in India. Since much of India was controlled by the British East India Company, only Anglican missionaries received official recognition and freedom to travel. Even they, however, could pursue missionary work only when not employed in chaplaincy duties to English people residing in India. Amid such challenges, this prayer meeting of gathered co-laborers was a high point for Martyn and a moment he remembered fondly. To the list of those present, Martyn added “old Captain Wickes.” He mentioned him again in another letter as “the good old Captain Wickes, who has brought out so many missionaries to India” ( Letters , 178). But who was this old American captain so well loved by the English missionaries in India? Missionaries as Risky Passengers Captain Wickes was born to a seafaring family in Maryland in 1746. His older brother, Captain Lambert Wickes, fought and died at sea during the American War for Independence. Benjamin first entered the missionary record in 1799, when the Baptist missionaries Joshua Marshman and William Ward sought passage to India from London. The situation was sensitive. The East India Company had forbidden full-time missionaries from entering, so no English ship would give Marshman and Ward passage. Carey had established his home in the Danish port of Serampore, not far from Calcutta, but no Danish ships were available. Wickes’s American ship, however, could take the risk of transporting missionaries. When he heard about the situation, Wickes wrote to Baptist leader Andrew Fuller, saying that “he had long cherished the hope of being privileged to convey the messengers of the Gospel to the heathen, and that his fondest wish was about to be gratified” ( The Life and Times of Carey, Marshman, and Ward , 110). The privilege came with difficulties. Although American ships were regularly received in East India Company ports, the presence of missionaries complicated their arrival. When Wickes arrived in Calcutta with Marshman and Ward, East India Company officials refused him permission to sail home unless he took the missionaries with him. By God’s grace, Wickes convinced the authorities of the missionaries’ good intentions. When similar circumstances occurred in 1806, he persuaded officials that detaining his American ship might cause an international incident. Each voyage involved protracted negotiations that certainly distracted from his primary trading business. Yet Wickes’s service proved invaluable. Every time the missionaries mentioned him, they affirmed their unbridled thanks for his efforts. William Carey wrote about him in 1805, “I, in common with my dear brethren and sisters here, feel much pleasure in hearing of the safe return to you of our much beloved brother in Christ, Capt. Wickes” ( Evangelical Intelligencer , 1:201). Marshman and Ward called him “th
featured.content_zh:
基督徒如何适应跨文化任务? 他们可能不是全职的传教士,而是承担大委员会的责任。 特派团的历史揭示了鲜为人知的发送者,他们利用自己的使命在世界各地进行战略福音宣传。 Benjamin Wickes上尉(1746–1830)就是这样的人。

威克船长 在1806年的一次祈祷会中,我们意外地遇到了这位早期的美国商船船长. 印度塞兰波尔的传教士们聚集一堂,将亨利·马蒂恩送往恒河上的一个站,在那里他将开始翻译和福音派的工作.

Martyn记录说,他们“今晚在我的佛塔相会,目的是在我离开之前赞扬我受到上帝的恩惠。 我的灵魂从未有过如此神圣的享受”(The Letters of Henry Martyn, 194). 我很想去过那里。

与会的有浸信会传教士威廉·凯里(William Carey),约书亚·马什曼(Joshua Marshman)和威廉·沃德(William Ward)等,还有福音派圣公会教徒大卫·布朗(David Brown),丹尼尔·科里(Daniel Corrie)和亨利·马蒂恩. 它代表了这些最早的英国传教士为在印度推进福音而进行的实质性合作。

由于印度大部分地区被英国东印度公司所控制,只有英国圣公会传教士才得到官方的承认并享有出行的自由. 然而,即使他们也只能在不受雇于居住在印度的英国人担任牧师职务时才能从事传教工作。

在这样的挑战中,这次聚集的同实验室的祈祷会是马蒂恩的高潮,也是他亲切回忆的一瞬. 在出席者名单中,马蒂恩加上了“威克船长”。 他在另一封信中再次提到他,称他为“威克船长,他把这么多传教士带到了印度”(信件,178)。

但这位老美国队长 在印度的英国传教士这么爱谁? 传教士作为"冒险乘客""威克船长"于1746年生于马里兰的一个航海家庭. 他的哥哥,船长兰伯特·威克斯(Lambert Wickes)在美国独立战争中出战并死于海上.

本杰明于1799年首次入传教记录,当时浸信会传教士约书亚·马什曼和威廉·沃德从伦敦寻求通向印度. 情况很敏感。 东印度公司曾禁止全职传教士入道,因此英国船只不会给马什曼和沃德通过.

凯里在离加尔各答不远的丹麦塞兰波尔港建立了他的家,但是没有丹麦船只可供使用. 但威克斯的美国船可能承担运送传教士的风险。

当Wickes听说情况时,他写信给浸信会领袖Andrew Fuller,称“他长期以来一直珍视着有幸将福音信使传达给异教徒的希望,而且他最亲切的愿望即将得到满足”(The Life and Times of Carey, Marshman, and Ward, 110.). 特权带来了困难。

虽然美国船只经常被接收到东印度公司港口,但传教士的到来使其更加复杂. 当威克斯与马什曼和沃德一起到达加尔各答后,东印度公司官员拒绝他出航回家,除非他带着传教士一起. 在上帝的恩典下,威克说服了传教士的善意权威.

当1806年发生类似情况时,他劝说官员们,扣留他的美国船只可能造成国际事件. 每次航行都涉及旷日持久的谈判,当然分散了他的初级贸易业务。 但威克斯的服务证明是宝贵的。 每逢传教士提到他,他们都申明他们无所顾忌地感谢他的努力.

featured.content: Autumn is a season of changes. At our home, as the leaves yellowed and the days shortened, my youngest child started middle school. That means picture books have me feeling a little nostalgia for the past these days, right alongside a lot of excitement for new things to come. Many of these books are about big changes and adjusting to them, like living with a new baby, moving to a new place, or finding a new heart in Christ’s kingdom. But some are also about the little changes happening around us every day, like laughter over a fleeting moment of childhood imagination or settling down to sleep to prepare for a new day. With all these experiences arriving on the horizon and then flying past like interstate billboards, it’s sweet to remember that “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change” (James 1:17). As you hand one of these brand-new books to a young reader or curl up to enjoy it together, let these stories remind you to enjoy the goodness of the moment, even as it is changing to something new, and that God’s goodness is everlasting. 1. God Gives Sleep by Betsy Childs Howard, illustrated by Bethan Welby ( TGC Store | Amazon) When our family was exhausted and planning a big move with four children ages 6 and under, I really could have used this little book from Betsy Childs Howard. God Gives Sleep is a rhyming board book with illustrations of adorable animals (sleeping ladybugs!) and two simple refrains that even very young listeners can repeat or “read” for themselves: “God gives sleep” and “God will keep.” Both reflect promises from God that feel vital to the early days of parenting filled with sweet, sleepy snuggles and long, sleepless nights. The last picture shows the entire family asleep and includes Isaiah 40:31 (“Those who hope in the LORD will renew their strength,” NIV). God Gives Sleep is engaging, gentle, funny, and wise, and I’ve already given it to parents of new babies. 2. Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel by A. A. Milne, adapted by Kevan Chandler and Joe Sutphin ( Amazon ) Full disclosure: I’m a huge Pooh fan. I’ve probably read the original Milne book dozens of times, and I can be a little sniffy about adaptations. But I loved this one. While I missed Milne’s distinctive narration in parts of the storytelling, this graphic novel retains enough of the original language and has such beautiful artwork that it easily justifies its existence. Parents of young independent readers often ask me for recommendations for books complex enough to be engaging but with content and formatting suitable for early elementary school. This version perfectly fits that space where 6-to-9-year-olds can track the story through the pictures but also enjoy the challenge of some complex vocabulary (“Sudden and Temporary Immersion”) and jokes that reward context research (“An ambush is a sort of Surprise.” “So is a gorse-bush sometimes.”). Winnie-the-Pooh: The Graphic Novel is a sweet and worthy tribute to this classic celebration of early childhood in all its imaginative wonder. 3. The Upside-Down, Inside-Out, Can’t-Believe-It Kingdom by Jonathan Landry Cruse, illustrated by Joe Hox ( Amazon ) The adventure begins with a son begging his father to tell him an exciting bedtime story with dragons and knights. The result is this retelling of the gospel as a quest with a king and a prince and a reminder of our humble place in the kingdom. Joe Hox’s illustrations stand out for being traditional and bright, with a dragon that isn’t too fierce for younger readers but also enough detail within the pictures to engage older readers. The story tells us that the good King will “make us be strong with the strength of His might,” a powerful message for young knights who want to do great things for the kingdom. 4. Doing Something New: A Prayer for Beginnings by Mitali Perkins, illustrated by Andrés Landazábal ( Amazon ) Mitali Perkins includes a n

featured.title: How Memorizing the Sermon on the Mount Reorders My Heart
featured.summary: In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount.
featured.summary_zh: 在一个算法捕捉我们的感情并通过我们的渴望在网上引诱我们的世界里，我们可以使用的最有效的抵抗策略之一是学习和背诵圣经，尤其是登山宝训。
featured.title_zh: 背诵登山宝训如何重塑我的心
featured.content: A couple of years ago, two college students challenged me—a woman in her 50s—to memorize the Sermon on the Mount (Matt. 5–7). Inwardly, I balked, but now I know that few things in my 35 years of following Jesus have been more transformative than committing Jesus’s most famous sermon to memory. John Stott wrote that the Sermon on the Mount is “the nearest thing to a manifesto that [Jesus] ever uttered, for it is his own description of what he wanted his followers to be and to do.” After spending the last few years memorizing it, I see with increasing clarity that I need Jesus’s help to live out what he taught. In a world where algorithms capture our affections and lure us online via our cravings, one of the most effective resistance strategies we can employ is to study and memorize Scripture—especially the Sermon on the Mount. Create a New Algorithm The algorithm often knows us better than we know ourselves. Every time we buy something on Amazon or pause to watch a reel on social media, the algorithm chronicles our activities and builds a profile of us. This profile shows our real interests (not just the ones we list in our social media bios) and some of our most private behaviors (the ones we thank God aren’t live streamed). In milliseconds, companies use what the algorithm knows about us to discover the most effective way to get us to buy their products. In the same way that the algorithm learns about us with each post we like and each reel we watch, God’s Word comes alive in us with every command we learn and put into practice, with every verse we ponder, and with every teaching we adopt as a way of life. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Let Scripture Reorder Your Heart Before I started my memorization project, I’d heard many Christians tout Scripture memory as one of the most potent tools for conforming to Jesus, but I didn’t take it seriously. All that changed when I realized algorithms had more access to my life than God’s Word did. By absorbing and obeying Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, we can create a feedback loop that enlarges his kingdom rule over our lives. Like many Americans, I was averaging more than two hours daily scrolling social media and shopping online, and much less time reading the Bible. I’d thought lack of time was my biggest obstacle to memorizing Scripture. But in reality, my affections and priorities were the obstacle. Memorizing and studying the Sermon on the Mount has provided a powerful reset. I’ve noticed two significant changes in my life. 1. My thoughts are increasingly populated by Jesus’s desires for me. Previously, I was easily shaped by what internet influencers said I should be doing and what my heart really wanted to do. Now, Scripture tenderly draws me to Christ’s transforming grace. For example, a few months ago, someone wrote harsh words to me. I couldn’t sidestep what I’d memorized: Pray for those who hurt you (Mt. 5:44) In those difficult interactions, Jesus’s teaching gave me wisdom to stop reacting and start praying for the one lashing out. Pausing to pray breaks down my self-protective stance so I can consider what the log in my eye might be (Mt. 7:5). 2. I see how vastly different God’s kingdom is from the world we live in. I no longer feel as drawn to the shallow version of perfection the algorithm offers me—the beautiful home, the perfectly fit woman charmingly dressed, or the promise of perpetual travel. When I stop to linger over another picture-perfect kitchen, the Sermon on the Mount prompts me to consider where my treasure really is. These chapters have given me a robust lens through which I can view all of God’s Word. After drinking so deeply of Jesus’s sermon , I see it as the hinge on which both the Old Testament and the New Testament hang. 几年前,两个大学生挑战我——一个50多岁的女性——要记住山上赛门(Matt. 5-7). 但现在我知道,在我追随耶稣的35年里, 没有什么事情比把耶稣最出名的布道当作记忆更具有变革性。

约翰·斯托特(John Stott)写道:"山上赛蒙是[耶稣]曾经发表的宣言中最接近的东西,因为这是他自己对追随者所希望的和所要做的事的描述". 我越来越清楚地看到,我需要耶稣的帮助来维持他所教的。

在一个算法捕捉到我们感情并通过我们的渴望来引诱我们上线的世界中,我们可以采用的最有效的抵抗策略之一是学习并记住"圣经"——特别是"山上"的"塞尔门". 创建新算法 算法常常比我们自己更了解我们.

每次我们购买亚马逊或暂停观看社交媒体的片段, 算法记录我们的活动, 以及一些最私人的行为(我们感谢上帝的人不是活生生的)。

在毫秒内,公司利用算法了解我们的情况,发现最有效的方法让我们购买他们的产品. 正如算法用我们所喜欢的每一个帖子和我们所看的每一卷片子来了解我们一样,上帝的言语以我们所学习和运用的每一个命令、我们所思考的每一个诗句和我们所采纳的作为生活方式的每一个教义,在我们中充满活力。

我本以为没有时间是我记起圣经的最大障碍。 但实际上,我的爱和优先考虑是障碍。 纪念并研究了"山上"的"塞尔门"提供了强大的重置. 我注意到我生命中有两个重大的变化。 1. 耶稣对我的渴望使我的思想日益丰富。

5:44 在困难的交往中,耶稣的教导给了我智慧,让我停止反应,开始为那一次狂欢祈祷. 暂停祈祷 打破自我保护的姿势 这样我就可以考虑我的眼中可能是什么(7:5山) 2. 我看到上帝的王国与我们生活的世界大相径庭。

我不再觉得算法能吸引到我的 浅薄的完美版本, 当我停止停留 停留在另一个图片完美的厨房, 山上赛门 促使我考虑 我的宝藏到底在哪里。

featured.title: Five Ways to Pray for Persecuted Christians
featured.summary: Jamie Dean offers a prayer guide for persecuted Christians in Iran, China, North Korea, and other hard to reach nations.
featured.summary_zh: 杰米·迪恩（ Jamie Dean ）为伊朗、中国、朝鲜和其他难以抵达的国家的受迫害基督徒提供了祈祷指南。
featured.title_zh: 为受迫害的基督徒祈祷的五种方式
featured.content: Sunday, Nov. 1, marks the annual International Day of Prayer for the Persecuted Church. It’s a day for believers across the globe to unite in concentrated prayer for Christians suffering for the gospel. Here are a few biblically-based ways to pray for the persecuted, along with a guide to a few specific nations to remember. 1. PRAY FOR THOSE IN PRISON “Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them.” Hebrews 13:3 Iran : In 2025, Christians were sentenced to a combined total of more than 280 years in prison . Pray for those still in jail, and for families enduring separation. China : The Chinese government has continued its crackdown on believers, including several still in prison after a raid on Zion Church last year . Pray for gospel hope and perseverance. Eritrea : As many as 350 believers remained in jails in 2025, including some who have been imprisoned for decades . Pray for endurance and deliverance. 2. PRAY FOR BOLDNESS “And now, Lord, look upon their threats and grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness.” Acts 4: 29 Syria, Pakistan , Libya , Sudan : Danger and threats are a common experience for believers in these nations. Pray for the Lord to protect churches and give them boldness to proclaim Christ, even when it’s difficult. 3. PRAY THAT PEOPLE WILL COME TO KNOW JESUS “I want you to know, brothers, that what has happened to me has really served to advance the gospel.” Philippians 1:12 Afghanistan : In a country where it’s more dangerous than ever to follow Jesus, Afghans are still coming to know him. Pray believers will continue to be a witness, and that unbelievers will find true life in Christ. 4. PRAY FOR GOD’S BLESSING TO THOSE SUFFERING “Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven…Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven.” Matthews 5:10,12 North Korea, Somalia, Yemen: These are among the most difficult places in the world to follow Christ. Pray for the Lord to bless these believers facing severe persecution, and to strengthen them with the hope of heaven. 5. PRAY FOR THE PERSECUTORS “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.” Matthew 5:44 Nigeria: Christians in northern Nigeria have endured kidnappings and violence for years. Pray the Lord will stop their attackers, and use the believers’ witness to draw persecutors to himself. For more ways to pray for the persecuted church, grab a copy of Pray the World , a 31-day devotional for hard to reach nations.

featured.title: Standing with Brothers and Sisters We Cannot See
featured.summary: David Platt shares a powerful story of forgiveness and challenges Christians to support persecuted believers through prayer.
featured.summary_zh: 大卫·普拉特（ David Platt ）分享了一个关于宽恕的强大故事，并挑战基督徒通过祈祷来支持受迫害的信徒。
featured.title_zh: 与我们看不到的兄弟姐妹站在一起
featured.content: I remember the first time I stood at the demilitarized zone, or the DMZ, on the border between North and South Korea. I looked across this dividing line, knowing that on the other side I (and we) have brothers and sisters who are suffering and dying for following Jesus and making him known. I think about Soon Yangown, a pastor in a leper colony during the Japanese occupation of the Korean peninsula many years ago. He refused to worship the shrines that had been set up for the Korean people to worship, so he was arrested and imprisoned. When the Japanese occupation ended, he was released. Years later, his two oldest sons, Tongin and Tongsin, were in middle school when a mob representing the communist party came to their campus. The boys were known to be strong Christians, so the mob brought them out of the school and began to beat them. Eventually, a leader of the mob named Ahn shot and killed both the boys. By the time Pastor Soon heard of his sons’ death, the revolt had been quieted, and his sons’ killer had been apprehended. Upon hearing this news, Pastor Soon immediately sent a messenger to the court to plead for them to spare Ahn. The judge agreed to do so, and Pastor Soon then offered to adopt Ahn as his own son. Years later, communists invaded the leper colony where Pastor Soon was pastoring. He refused to flee and chose to stay with the church. He was arrested, imprisoned, tied up with 75 other followers of Jesus, and executed. I wish these stories were only from the past. Unfortunately, however, suffering, persecution, and martyrdom are present-day realities for our brothers and sisters in North Korea. So what can we do for them? For starters, we can remember them and learn about what they are experiencing. In the words of Hebrews 13:3: “Remember those who are in prison, as though in prison with them, and those who are mistreated, since you also are in the body.” We can take time to listen to and learn the story of our family in North Korea as if we were with them in North Korea. (Radical’s documentary Hard to Reach: North Korea is a good place to start.) As you remember our brothers and sisters in North Korea and other hard lands , I invite you to pray for them. Let your prayers be guided by Paul’s exhortation in Ephesians 6:18–20 for the church to pray for him while he was in prison: “To that end, keep alert with all perseverance, making supplication for all the saints, and also for me, that words may be given to me in opening my mouth boldly to proclaim the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains, that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak.” Finally, let’s join them. They’re giving their lives to share the gospel with people around them. If you’re reading this, the likelihood is that your life is not at stake in the same way as theirs. But you can still give your life to what they’re giving their lives to: speaking the gospel and sharing God’s love in Jesus with the people you and I interact with today. Let’s lock arms with our brothers and sisters in North Korea , following Jesus and making him known no matter what it costs, because we know that he is our reward. This article first appeared in The Commission , Radical’s biweekly newsletter featuring global gospel stories and encouragement from David Platt and others to help you follow Jesus and make him known. featured.content_zh: 我记得我第一次站在非军事区,即位于南北朝鲜边境的非军事区。 我越过了这个分界线,知道在另一边,我(和我们)有兄弟姐妹,他们因追随耶稣并让他出名而受苦受难并死去. 我想起在多年前日本占领朝鲜半岛期间,一个麻风病殖民地的牧师Soon Yangown。 他拒绝为朝鲜人民所崇拜而设置的神社,于是被捕入狱. 日本占领结束后被放出. 多年后,他的两个最年长的儿子通仁和通辛在中学就读,当时一个代表共产主义政党的暴徒来到了他们的校园. 男孩们已知是坚固的基督徒,于是暴徒将他们从学校带出并开始殴打他们. 最终,一个暴徒的领袖命名 安开枪打死了两个男孩 在Sonon牧师听到他儿子的死讯时,叛乱已经平息,杀害他儿子的凶手已被逮捕。 在听到这个消息后,索恩牧师立即派使者去朝廷恳求他们放过安. 法官同意这样做,而索恩牧师随后提出收养安为自己的儿子. 多年后,共产主义分子入侵了"索恩牧师"正在作牧师的麻风病人聚居地. 他拒绝出逃,选择留在教堂. 他被逮捕,入狱,被绑起与另外75名耶稣追随者,被处死. 我希望这些故事只是从过去。 然而,不幸的是,对我们北朝鲜的兄弟姐妹来说,痛苦、迫害和殉道是当今的现实。 我们能为他们做什么? 首先,我们可以记住他们,了解他们正在经历的一切。 用希伯来人13:3的话来说:“记住那些在狱中的人,好像在狱中一样,以及那些受到虐待的人,因为你也是在身体里。” 我们可以花时间聆听和学习我们家在朝鲜的故事,就像我们在朝鲜与他们在一起一样. (Radical的纪录片"难去难去":朝鲜是个好起点. ) 我邀请你为他们祈祷。 保罗在《以弗所书6:18-20》中劝告教会在狱中为他祈祷:“为此,请全心全意地为所有圣人祈祷,也为我祈祷,愿为我大胆地开口宣讲福音之谜,因为我是一个被锁住的大使,让我大胆地宣示福音之谜。 最后,让我们加入他们。 他们献出生命与周围的人分享福音。 如果你读到这个, 你的生命可能与他们的生命不同。 你仍然可以把生命献给他们所付出的:说出福音,与你我今天交往的人分享上帝对耶稣的爱。 让我们和朝鲜的兄弟姐妹们握起手来, 这篇文章首次刊登在委员会的双周通讯《激进》上, 今日订阅.

featured.title: How Missionaries Should Serve Where Churches Already Exist
featured.summary: Brian Pate explains how missionaries can equip national churches to mature, reproduce, and plant healthy churches for generations.
featured.summary_zh: 布莱恩·佩特（ Brian Pate ）解释了传教士如何让国家教会成熟、繁殖和种植健康的教会。
featured.title_zh: 传教士应该如何在教会已经存在的地方服务
featured.content: I’m a missionary in Brazil , and I’m surrounded by churches—Baptist, Presbyterian, Nazarene, Assembly of God—the list goes on and on. Brazil has a rich history of missionaries who left a legacy of churches that are now sending missionaries to other countries. This raises a question: Should we send missionaries to countries where churches already exist? Shouldn’t we consider those regions “reached” and send our resources into more needy areas of the world? It’s a fair question, and worth exploring. Before we land on an answer, here are a few factors to consider: REMEMBER THE EXAMPLE OF PAUL Didn’t Paul say his mission was to reach those who had never heard the gospel (Rom 15:20)? Yes, a significant part of Paul’s ministry was as a church-planting missionary. But he did not abandon these newly planted churches. Paul was also a church-strengthening missionary. He revisited the churches he planted (Acts 14:21–23; 15:36; 18:22–23). He wrote letters to these churches because there was more that he needed to teach them (1 Thess 3:10). He even sent out his own missionary workers to areas he had previously reached: Tychichus to Ephesus and Colossae, Titus to Corinth, Crete, and Dalmatia, and Timothy to Ephesus and other cities. Surprisingly, we don’t have any record of Paul sending missionaries to unreached areas, but only to areas he had already reached. Paul creates helpful categories for us. We see Romans 15 pioneer missions, but we also see Acts 14 church-strengthening missions. Should we send missionaries where churches already exist? Paul shows us there is a biblical category for missions like this . In fact, Paul did it. CONSIDER THE HEALTH OF THE CHURCHES As I have trained pastors over the years, I have encountered alarming situations: churches that tolerate immorality, pastors who fail to understand the simple gospel message, and church leaders who unknowingly regurgitate heresy to their congregation. In my denomination, many churches are either embracing prosperity theology or depending on pragmatism to fulfill the Great Commission . Yes, I’m surrounded by “churches”, but when we only consider truly evangelical churches, the list is much smaller. And if we want to further whittle it down to healthy churches, the number gets very slim. Consider the health of the churches. If we neglect “reached” fields, we run the risk of creating new unreached people groups in just a few generations. UNDERSTAND THE NEEDS OF GOSPEL INFRASTRUCTURE So, what is the role of a missionary in a “reached” country? It is helpful to consider the missionary’s role in the big picture of what God is already doing in that country. This is where the rubric of gospel infrastructure is so helpful. Think of it this way: A city needs to put certain structures in place (such as road networks, water supply, and energy grids), so that it can continue to exist and thrive in the future. Similarly, the Great Commission requires far more than initial evangelism. For a national church to grow and reproduce, it will need to have “gospel infrastructure” in place. This begins with evangelism, Bible translation, and planting healthy churches, but also includes Christian literature, local pastor training, local worship music, and seminaries. The missions task involves everything a national church needs, so they can continue planting healthy churches for generations to come. When sending missionaries to areas that already have churches, we need to ask where the missionary’s gifts and the national church’s needs intersect. For example, Brazil probably does not need missionaries to plant more churches, but there are still great needs in the areas of seminaries and local pastor training. MISSIONS WHERE CHURCHES ALREADY EXIST? Should we send missionaries where churches already exist? Based on Paul’s own example, the answer is yes. We should continue sending Great Commission workers anywhere there is the need for healthy churches and gospel infrastructure. May we joyfully serve in
