featured.title_zh: 想要帮助消除贫困吗？这里有五种方法可以开始
featured.content: In the mid-2000s, Ate Tina was working long hours at a factory in the Philippines and supporting her household alone. Ate is Tagalog for older sister, and it’s a title of respect. Seven months after her wedding, her husband developed a serious medical condition, which made her the only breadwinner. When she became pregnant, the factory’s demands stayed the same. “I ended up giving birth at home because I wasn’t allowed to leave work,” she recalls. Two months after her daughter was born, she was back on the factory floor and her daughter was in the care of others. Tina began to notice changes in her daughter’s behavior that worried her. She says she prayed in desperation for a livelihood that would let her provide for her family and be present with them. In 2008, she connected with the Center for Community Transformation, a partner of HOPE International in the Philippines. Her first loan was $80. She repaid it, kept meeting with staff and fellow borrowers, and by her third loan, $800, she bought three sewing machines and rented an apartment to start a sewing business. “Because of that trust, I was able to start a business I can call my own,” she says of the organization that lent to her. The business has since grown into an online clothing company with around 70 employees. Tina trains them, encourages them to save and points them toward the same support she found. The loan mattered. So did the parts of her story that cost nothing: people who trusted her, a group of borrowers who met with her, a prayer life she kept returning to and a skill she kept sharpening. If your budget has no room for a monthly gift, that list is still within reach. Here are five places to start: Watch the way you talk about poverty. Poverty is more than a shortage of money. Material need is real, and it sits inside a larger brokenness that reaches into relationships, communities and a person’s sense of who they are. Talking about poverty that way changes who is in the story. Everyone knows what a broken relationship feels like, so the distance between you and the person asking for help on the corner gets shorter. You make eye contact instead of looking away. You ask a name. You find out what the person actually needs before you decide what to offer. Protect the dignity of the people you want to help. Tina put the turning point in terms of trust. The lender believed she would repay, and she did, and the business that followed was hers. That makes a useful test for any help you offer: does it treat a person as someone with ideas and work of their own, or as someone to be rescued? Giving things away freely is the right call in a crisis. Outside a crisis, it can turn people into recipients in their own community. The better question is how to meet someone’s needs as a whole person while protecting their dignity. Do your job well. You don’t have to work for a nonprofit to fight poverty at work. Vocation is one of the main ways Christians answer the call to love their neighbors, which means many of us are already doing some of that work without noticing. Tina’s sewing business now supports around 70 employees, which is vocation doing exactly this. A barista pours coffee grown by farmers in developing countries. Someone in telecommunications works in an industry that provides cell-phone access in impoverished nations. A worker on an oil field produces fuel that keeps a stranger warm at night. A recruiter connects a person to a job that person badly needs. Pray about where you’ve been placed, do the work well, and think of it as a way to serve people you will probably never meet. Spend your time where the need already is. Poverty has an address close to home, too. Food pantries, tutoring programs and church benevolence ministries run on volunteers, and they tend to need people who show up on a schedule. A standing weeknight shift usually builds more trust than a one-time service day, because the people on the other side get to know your name as well. If you have

featured.content: Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham told Theo Von on his podcast that nothing a person does or doesn’t do can separate them from God’s love, after Von said he wishes his connection with God were stronger. The conversation is in episode No. 692 of This Past Weekend . Von said his prayer connection with God is the part of his life he likes most, but that when he gets too busy it can feel disconnected. “I wish my connection was stronger,” he said. Cunningham answered, “Dude, I feel you,” and said she was saying it for other people listening too: “There’s nothing that you can or can’t do that’s going to separate you from God’s love and grace and forgiveness. Like that’s why Jesus came and died on the cross because he already knew everything you were going to do.” She added that what comes next is up to the person, who can “educate yourself and read the Bible,” but that “you’re already forgiven.” She also said she feels most connected when she is “prayed up,” a phrase Von said he likes and hears from a friend all the time. Earlier in the conversation, Cunningham said she relies on her faith because of what she does for a living. “You get a lot of hate, you get a lot of praise,” she said. Faith keeps her stable and “who I am,” she said, and she doesn’t care what people’s opinions are about her “because I’m not living for their praise.” Von later asked whether the media is unfair to Christians. Cunningham said that depends on perspective, but that she loves seeing more people say they are believers. “I feel like there’s a revival happening,” she said. She said it can be scary to speak up because people have had bad experiences with church, and that she likes seeing athletes with big platforms be “bold and courageous and come out about Jesus.” Von said more athletes he has gotten to know in the past four years seem to have faith, and that more of his friends are trying to learn about it too. “We want to have some more religious figures on to talk about stuff on here,” he said.

featured.title_zh: “我的上帝需要一点肉汁” ：柯克·富兰克林的新双专辑是他对33年评论家的回答
featured.content: Kirk Franklin’s new album I Am What I Am , his first double album, is out Oct. 30, and he says it is partly an answer to the people who have been questioning his choices for decades. At a listening party in Atlanta , he joked about the whole idea: “I need a little gravy on my God.” The album has 14 songs across two discs, seven studio recordings on the first and seven recorded live on the second. It is Franklin’s 14th studio album, according to the Associated Press, which reports that he is tired of defending his musical decisions. He told the AP he prayed with Chris Brown and Usher before a concert because they asked him to, a moment that drew criticism on social media. “We as believers sometimes become judge and jury,” he said. He also stands by working with GloRilla, whose music is explicit, on the single “This Time.” The song extended his record to 10 No. 1s on Billboard’s Hot Gospel Songs chart, the AP reports. “You start trying to play in other people’s sandboxes, it is going to come with scrutiny,” Franklin said. At the listening party he put it more plainly: “I’ve been trying to explain myself for the last 33 years. This felt like the right opportunity to let people know that I listen and I hear everything that is being said. I am aware. This is my humanity.” Jelly Roll opens the record on “Free Me Tonight,” a spoken-word track the AP says nods to Phil Collins’ “In the Air Tonight.” Franklin reflects on his imperfections and his public criticism on it. Franklin told the AP the song was cathartic and that he once worried it would end his career. “Gospel music is able to handle the raw, unfiltered truth about how ugly and difficult life can be,” he said. On “It Gets Better,” with Tobe Nwigwe, Franklin said at the listening party: “That song was my attempt to find a space to talk about mental health. I’ve had my own journey with anxiety and depression.” He also said, “Living up to the religious standards can create psychological trauma,” and recalled that in his childhood church, young women could be publicly shamed for getting pregnant while the men involved faced no comparable accountability. “Can you imagine the trauma?” he asked. Davido is on “Hope In You,” and Karen Clark Sheard of the Clark Sisters is on the live “Thank You for Everything.” The AP singles out the live “Welcome In,” in which Franklin describes feeling forgotten by God at times while expressing gratitude for God’s steadfast presence. He said the sound of Black church music changed while he was making the album. “The Black church culture changed,” he said. “The church got rid of their choirs and the music was in a space that was not my strength.” Franklin, who is 56 and a 20-time Grammy winner, has no plans to slow down. “The hole that I came from was so deep that whenever I’m around light, I never get tired of feeling the sunlight,” he told the AP.

featured.content: Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs says the celebration that set off social media after his latest touchdown was a tribute to a gospel song, not a joke about his recent arrest. In the second quarter of the Packers’ 27-19 win over the Carolina Panthers, Jacobs scored on a 1-yard run and briefly put his hands behind his back while teammates congratulated him. Some viewers watching on television thought he was pretending to be handcuffed. Jacobs said he was modeling the moment after a gospel song called “Break Every Chain.” “The guys did it with me,” he said. “I didn’t think it was going to be a thing that can be perceived a certain type of way. But it’s 2026, and it is what it is.” It was Jacobs’ second game of the season. He had spent time on the NFL’s commissioner’s exempt list after charges were filed against him in August over a May altercation with his then-girlfriend, who said he threw her to the ground. Last month he pleaded no contest to misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal damage to property. He was taken off the list last week and returned to the field, though the league’s investigation is still ongoing. Jacobs said he talked with receiver Savion Williams and other teammates before his season debut, and they planned two celebrations. After his first touchdown of the season, in a 20-17 loss at Detroit, he went to his knees and raised his arms to thank God. The “Break Every Chain” moment was meant for the next one. He also said the broadcast cut away early. “It was more to it than that,” Jacobs said. “They stopped showing the celebration after that.” The NFL’s investigation of Jacobs remains open.

featured.title_zh: 皮尤： 23至26岁的美国人是该国宗教信仰最少的成年人，而18至22岁的人参加教会的比率高于任何人
featured.content: If you’re 25, the Gen Z church revival you keep hearing about may not describe you. Pew Research Center’s newest report on American religion finds that adults ages 23 to 26 are actually the least religious age group in the country on the core measures it tracks, including how often they pray, how much religion matters to them and whether they identify with a religion. But the group just below them looks very different. Among adults 18 to 22, 41% say they attend a church, synagogue, mosque or other house of worship at least once or twice a month. That is higher than the 33% for the U.S. public as a whole, and higher than adults born in the 1990s, 1980s, 1970s and 1960s. Among adults 23 to 26, the number is 27%, one of the lowest of any age group. Pew calls the overall picture “complicated,” and the report is careful about what the younger figure can carry. Outside of attendance, the youngest adults are less distinctive. They pray and identify with a religion at lower rates than many older groups. They are no more religious than people that age were in 2014, and by Pew’s measures of prayer, religion’s importance and religious identification, both young groups are significantly less religious than their counterparts in 2007. That said, Pew’s sample is small. The 18-to-22 findings rest on 443 respondents from Pew’s 2025 and 2026 surveys, with a margin of error of plus or minus 5.7 percentage points. Applied to the 41% figure, that is a range of roughly 35% to 47%. Split the group by gender or party and the margins widen further. Pew also notes that this has happened before. In its 2014 Religious Landscape Study, 18-to-22-year-olds attended services at a rate 6 points higher than 23-to-26-year-olds. What is new is that the 2025 and 2026 surveys are the first in which the youngest group is significantly more religious than the next group up on all four of Pew’s core indicators. When the youngest adults have looked more religious in the past, Pew says, the effect has tended to fade with time. It adds that the bump may partly reflect a rebound from the pandemic, and that scholars of religion tend to study change over decades. Some of the details cut against the usual storyline about who is showing up. Young men now attend more often than young women, which Pew says it has not seen before, but 35% of the youngest women attend at least monthly, about the same as women born from the 1950s through the 1980s. Among the youngest Republicans, 55% attend monthly. The youngest Democrats also attend at relatively high rates compared with other Democrats, so Pew says it cannot call this an exclusively Republican phenomenon. Across all ages, Pew finds religion holding steady. The shares who identify with a religion, pray daily, call religion very important and attend monthly have been flat since 2020, and 34% of U.S. adults said in a June survey that they had attended services in person in the previous month, the highest since Pew began asking in 2020. Pew says it has no way of knowing whether the youngest adults will follow the old pattern or break it, and describes the open question as “a turning point or a blip.” If it is a revival, it belongs so far to the very youngest adults in the survey.
featured.content_zh: 若你25岁, 皮尤研究中心关于美国宗教的最新报告发现,23-26岁的成年人实际上是该国在追踪的核心衡量标准上最不信奉宗教的年龄组,包括他们的祈祷次数、宗教对他们的重要性以及他们是否认同某一宗教。 但是他们下面的人群看起来很不一样。 在18至22岁的成年人中,41%的人说,他们每月至少去一次或两次教堂、犹太会堂、清真寺或其他礼拜场所。 这比整个美国公众的33%高,也比1990年代,1980年代,1970年代和1960年代出生的成年人高. 在23至26岁的成年人中,这一数字为27%,是任何年龄组中最低的。 皮尤称总体情况“复杂”,报告对年轻人物能够携带什么十分谨慎。 除了出勤外,最年轻的成年人也不太特别. 他们祈祷和认同宗教的比例低于许多老年群体。 他们的宗教程度不比2014年那个年龄的人多,根据皮尤的祈祷、宗教的重要性和宗教认同措施,2007年,这两个青年群体的宗教程度明显低于同龄人。 皮尤的样本很小。 18至22分的调查结果取自皮尤2025年和2026年调查的443个答卷人,误差幅度为上下5.7个百分点。 适用于41%的数字,约为35%至47%。 按性别或政党划分,差额进一步扩大。 Pew也指出,这以前发生过。 在其2014年的"宗教景观研究"中,18至22岁的青少年参加服务,比23至26岁的青少年高6分. 新情况是,2025年和2026年的调查是第一次最年轻的群体比皮尤所有四个核心指标的下一批群体宗教程度高得多。 当最年轻的成年人在过去看起来更加宗教化时,皮尤说,这种效果往往随着时间逐渐消退. 它还说,这一起伏可能部分反映了该流行病的反弹,宗教学者往往研究几十年来的变化。 一些细节与通常的故事情节相对应, 青年男子现在比青年妇女更经常参加,皮尤说以前从未见过这种活动,但最小的妇女中35%至少每月参加,大约与1950年代至1980年代出生的妇女相同。 在最年轻的共和党人中,有55%每月参加. 与其他民主党人相比,最年轻的民主党人也以相对较高的比率参加,因此皮尤称这不能称之为纯粹的共和党现象. 在所有年龄,皮尤发现宗教是稳定的。 认同某种宗教,每日祷告,呼唤宗教非常重要并每月出席的股份自2020年以来一直是平平的,34%的美国成年人在6月的调查中表示,他们上个月曾亲自参加过各种服务,是皮尤自2020年开始询问以来最高的. Pew说,它无法知道最年轻的成年人是否会遵循旧模式或打破旧模式,并形容这个尚未解决的问题是“一个转折点或一滴一滴地”。 如果是复兴,它迄今为止属于调查中最年轻的成年人。

featured.title_zh: 破碎的系统保护贩运者，而不是女孩
featured.content: I’m often asked about the night I spent in a Southeast Asian jail alongside three young girls who had been exploited by sex traffickers. But the primary question isn’t about why I was in jail. Rather, why were those three girls in jail to begin with? Why them, and not the traffickers who had taken them from their families and sold them repeatedly for sex, turning their lives into a brutal nightmare? Why not the woman who had put tape over the mouth of the young girl so that the man who was raping her would not be disturbed by her screams. The system failed them. The brothel keeper was tipped off about their rescue operation, allowed to hide her crime, and told to dump the girls at a nearby bus stop. The police who should have rescued them instead arrested them on immigration charges. The trafficker walked free, while the girls were treated as criminals. As I sat with them that night, I longed for those girls to have never been taken to jail, much less a brothel. I wanted them to have always been at home with their families, going to school, and playing with their friends. I wanted them to have never been harmed in the first place. But the reality is, like millions of women and girls in our world today, they suffered the consequences of a broken justice system. And so, the reason I stayed with the girls is simply that the alternative was just too horrible. I preferred to be arrested myself rather than leave them vulnerable to further assault. But there’s an important detail to clarify: in the end, I did not need to stay the full night. Once it was clear I was not going away, the jailer himself took on the responsibility of assuring their safety. In a broken system, when even just one agent uses their authority for good, the door to justice begins to open. Shifting Power The very next day, my colleagues at International Justice Mission (IJM) and I were able to bring the girls to safety and long-term holistic aftercare. I continued to visit the girls for years, witnessing their healing as they moved into new lives of freedom. But nearly 25 years after that night in jail, the fight remains the same; we must not leave until those with governing power wield their power to protect the most vulnerable. If we fail to intervene for the women and girls being brutalized by violent criminals, including intimate partners and family members, the alternative is unconscionable. But when we do show up, we get to be part of shifting the levers of power. Entire systems – even the most corrupt and unjust – begin to change for good. In the 21st century, we must reckon with the reality that millions of women and girls are still not any more safe from violence than they have been in any previous era. It is still true, as it has been for decades, that one in three women will experience physical or sexual violence in their lifetime. Today, and in fact, every day, 140 women will be killed by their partners or family members. But far too often, law enforcement and other government actors appear to be on the side of violent perpetrators and other abusers, rather than those who are suffering violence. Whether it’s taking bribes to protect traffickers, criminalizing women and children who are being exploited, or allowing them to be intimidated into not reporting the abuse, agents of the law bear tremendous responsibility and opportunity to change the systemic violence they have enabled to perpetuate. Violent crime thrives on opportunity, and the argument for countering this could not be more clear: strengthening justice systems deters violence. When laws are enforced and traffickers and other abusers are held accountable, other perpetrators of violence are discouraged from committing similar crimes. I think of this as flipping the fear equation. When violent abusers begin to fear the consequences of law, women and children begin to live free from fear. In my work with IJM, I’ve helped build a model that has proved this theory of change. We’ve meticulously m
featured.content_zh: 我经常被问及在东南亚监狱度过的夜晚, 但首要问题并不在于我为何入狱。 相反,为什么这三个女孩要入狱? 为什么是他们,而不是那些从家人那里夺走他们,并反复出卖他们的性生活,把他们的生活变成残酷的噩梦的人? 为什么不让那个把录音带放入年轻女孩口中的女人 让强奸她的男人不会被她尖叫所打扰 系统失败了 妓院老板被告知他们的营救行动,允许她隐瞒罪行,并说要把女孩们扔到附近的一个公交站。 本应救出他们的警察却以移民指控逮捕了他们。 贩卖者走得自由,而女孩则被当作罪犯对待. 当晚我和她们坐在一起时,我渴望那些女孩从来没有被关进监狱,更不用说妓院了。 我希望他们总是和家人一起在家,上学,和朋友一起玩. 我希望他们从一开始就没有受到伤害。 但是,现实是,同我们当今世界上数百万妇女和女童一样,她们遭受了司法制度被打破所造成的后果。 所以,我和女孩们在一起的原因 就是另一种选择太可怕了。 我宁愿自己被捕,而不是让他们受到进一步的攻击。 但有一个重要的细节需要澄清:最后,我不需要过夜。 一旦我明白我不会离开, 看守自己承担了保证他们安全的责任。 在一个破碎的体系中,即使只有一个特工善用权威,正义之门也开始打开. 正在移动电源 第二天,我在国际司法特派团(正义团)的同事和我得以使这些女孩安全地得到长期的全面照顾。 多年来,我继续探访这些女孩,目睹她们进入自由新生活时愈合。 但是,在狱中当晚近25年之后,这场战斗依然如故;我们决不能离开,直到那些拥有统治权的人行使权力保护最脆弱群体。 如果我们不能干预暴力罪犯,包括亲密伴侣和家庭成员对妇女和女孩的残暴行为,那么,另一种选择是不合理的。 但是,当我们出现时, 我们就会成为改变权力杠杆的一部分。 整个系统 — — 甚至最腐败和最不公正的系统 — — 开始永远改变。 在21世纪,我们必须考虑这样一个现实:数百万妇女和女童仍然比以往任何时代都更无法免遭暴力。 几十年来,每3个妇女中就有1个在一生中遭受身体或性暴力。 今天,事实上,每天都有140名妇女被其伴侣或家庭成员杀害。 但是,执法部门和其他政府行为者似乎往往站在暴力肇事者和其他施虐者一边,而不是那些遭受暴力的人一边。 无论是收受贿赂来保护被剥削的妇女和儿童,还是让他们受到恐吓来不报告虐待,法律工作者都肩负着巨大的责任和机会来改变他们得以延续的系统性暴力。 暴力犯罪依靠机会而兴起,打击暴力的论据再清楚不过了:加强司法系统可以阻止暴力。 当法律得到实施,贩运者和其他施虐者被追究责任时,其他暴力行为的犯罪人就被劝阻不犯下类似的罪行。 我认为这是在改变恐惧的等式。 当暴力虐待者开始害怕法律的后果时,妇女和儿童开始免于恐惧地生活。 在与IJM的合作中, 我帮助建立了一个模型, 我们非常谨慎

The scientist, Khosrow Bakhtar, is a veteran U.S. defense scientist and the inventor of the BakhtarRadar system used at the site, according to the project’s…
featured.summary_zh: 一名在土耳其东部船形编队工作的雷达科学家说，他的扫描显示里面有组织的图案、腔室和走廊，这些特征不是天然岩石。根据该项目的说法，科学家Khosrow Bakhtar是一位资深的美国国防科学家，也是现场使用的BakhtarRadar系统的发明者。
featured.title_zh: 研究人员说，雷达显示土耳其船形编队内的房间和走廊，有些人认为是诺亚方舟
featured.content: A radar scientist working at a boat-shaped formation in eastern Turkey says his scans show organized patterns, chambers and corridors inside it, and that those features are not natural rock. The scientist, Khosrow Bakhtar, is a veteran U.S. defense scientist and the inventor of the BakhtarRadar system used at the site, according to the project’s release. He reported the preliminary results from inside the Durupınar Formation, a roughly 515-foot structure near Mount Ararat that Ark hunters have studied since 1959. Bakhtar said the radar was set to mask natural geological signals, so a purely natural anomaly would not have shown up in the processed images. He called it “the most significant finding of 45 years of my career.” Prof. Cenker Atila of Sivas Cumhuriyet University, who oversees the permitted project, reviewed and confirmed the preliminary results, the release says. He added that the radar also shows a structure with three levels, which he compared to the three levels of the Ark in “our Holy Books.” The findings were presented at a symposium in Turkey, and the group, Noah’s Ark Scans, announced them this week. The group also reports recovering charred wood from almost 30 feet down inside the formation, and says the condition of the wood is what makes it interesting. Genesis describes the Ark coated in pitch, which burns easily, so the release suggests someone may have tried to set the Ark on fire long ago. Charring slows decomposition in soil, often to well under 1% a year, so “what was meant to destroy it may have actually preserved it,” the release says. The group also says the wood is not recent surface debris and was not carried in by mudflow, because it came from deep within the formation. The release allows other explanations for the charring, including lightning or volcanic activity. Founder Andrew Jones said the wood could be the charred remains of the Ark or the remains of a campfire a shepherd lit while using it for shelter centuries ago. The wood has been sent for carbon-14 dating and species identification, and the team says no firm conclusions should be drawn until the results are published. Dating would give the wood’s age and identification would show what kind of tree it came from, but neither result would by itself show that it came from a boat. Everything here comes from the group itself. The radar results are preliminary, the masking is the team’s own processing, and none of it has been through independent peer review. A 1996 study by geologist Lorence Collins and Ark hunter David Fasold concluded that Durupınar is a natural rock formation. Noah’s Ark Scans also sells guided tours and merchandise, is running a GiveSendGo fundraiser for more core drilling, and its release asks for donations and points readers to a gold dealer and a preparedness retailer. More radar processing and reporting is expected in the coming months, and Jones has said initial lab results are expected over the winter. Atila has said photos of the wood will be released in the near future.
featured.content_zh: 一位在土耳其东部的船形编队工作的雷达科学家说,他的扫描显示它内部有条理的图案,室室和走廊,这些特征不是天然岩石. 科学家Khosrow Bakhtar是一位美国资深国防科学家, 他报告了Durupınar Formation公司内部的初步结果,这是Ararat山附近一个约515英尺高的结构,由Ark猎人自1959年以来研究。 巴赫塔尔说,雷达是用来遮掩自然地质信号的,因此在经过处理的图像中不会出现纯粹的自然异常. 他称之为“我45年职业生涯中最重要的发现”。 师曰. Sivas Cumhuriyet大学的Cenker Atila监督了许可的项目,审查并确认了初步结果。 他补充说,雷达还显示一个具有三个级别的结构,他与方舟子在“我们的圣书”中的三个级别相比。 调查结论在土耳其的一次研讨会上发表, 剧组还报告从形成地近30英尺下方取出烧焦的木头,并说木头的状况使得它很有趣. "创世记"描述了被涂入花筒的"方舟",这很容易被烧伤,因此发行表明有人可能早就想放出"方舟"了. 碳化物在土壤中的分解速度慢了,每年的分解率往往不到1%,因此“破坏它的意图可能是实际保存下来的”。 剧组还称该木不是近代地表出土出土的地表出土出土后被泥流所承载,因为它出土出土了形成地深. 释放后可以对焦炭进行其他解释,包括闪电或火山活性. 创始人安德鲁·琼斯(Andrew Jones)说,木头可能是"方舟"被烧焦的遗骨,也可能是数百年前在使用时被牧羊人点燃了的营火的遗骨. 该木被送去进行碳-14约会和物种鉴定,队伍表示在结果公布之前不应得出确定的结论. 约会可以说明木材的年代, 这里的一切来自团体本身. 雷达结果初步,口罩是团队自己的处理方式,没有经过独立的同行评审. 1996年由地质学家洛伦斯·柯林斯和方克猎人大卫·法拉尔德进行的一项研究得出结论,杜鲁普纳尔是天然岩层. 诺亚方舟扫描公司也出售导游和商品, 预计未来几个月会有更多的雷达处理和报告,琼斯表示预计冬季会有初步的实验室结果. Atila表示, 木头的照片将在不久的将来发布。

featured.title_zh: 盖洛普： 30岁以下美国人的生活水平比2010年低20个百分点
featured.content: A 25-year-old in 2026 is starting adult life in worse shape than a 25-year-old in 2010, at least by their own account. Gallup’s newest wellbeing report finds that 44% of U.S. adults ages 18 to 29 are “thriving” so far this year, down from a high of 64% in 2010. Gallup counts someone as thriving if they rate their current life a 7 or higher on a zero-to-10 ladder and expect to rate their life an 8 or higher five years from now. Most of the drop came recently. About two-thirds of the total decline has happened since 2019. Gallup is careful about causes, saying a set of factors “may explain” the decline among young adults. It points to a rise in depression, weaker close relationships, less daily enjoyment and less feeling active and productive each day. It also lists lower satisfaction with living standards, with leaders who create enthusiasm about the future and with progress toward personal goals. Among adults 30 to 44, it says the share currently having or being treated for depression is up 15 points since 2019, to 37%. Beyond those measures, Gallup names loneliness, which it says has been particularly acute among younger men, along with housing affordability and fear of losing jobs to AI. About half of adults 18 to 49 doubt Medicare and Social Security will be available in 10 years, far more than other age groups. Just 14% of adults 18 to 34 say they are “extremely proud” to be American, down 10 points since 2025. The numbers follow people as they age. Adults now 34 to 46 are at 46%, compared with 64% when they were the 18-to-29 group in 2010, so their ratings fell as they got older while the young adults behind them are starting from a lower place. Adults 30 to 44 are at 45%, down from a high of 62% in 2016 and 2017. Adults 45 to 64 are at 46%, which matches their low from 2008. The estimates come from three Gallup Panel surveys in February, May and August 2026 with 15,156 U.S. adults in total.
featured.content_zh: 2026年出道的25岁少年开始的成人生活状况比2010年出道的25岁少年更糟糕,至少是靠他们自己的说法. 盖洛普最新的福利报告发现,今年到目前为止,美国44%的18至29岁的成年人在“抢走”,低于2010年的64%。 盖洛普认为,如果把目前的寿命定在7至10个梯子上,并期望从现在起将生命定在8至10个梯子上,那么,盖洛普就认为某人是繁荣的。 大部分的货最近才来 约三分之二的总下降发生在2019年以来. 盖洛普对原因很谨慎,说一系列因素“可以解释”年轻人的下降。 这表明抑郁症的上升,亲密的关系更弱,日常的享受减少,每天的活跃和生产的感觉也更差. 它还列出了对生活水平、对未来产生热情的领导人以及在实现个人目标方面取得进展的低满意度。 在30至44个成年人中,它说,目前接受或正在接受抑郁治疗的比例自2019年以来上升了15分,达到37%. 除了这些措施外,Gallup还称孤独,这在年轻男子中尤其严重,而且住房负担不起,担心会失去AI的工作。 大约一半的18至49个成年人怀疑在10年内将可获得医疗保健和社会保障,远远多于其他年龄组。 18至34岁的成年人中只有14%说,他们“非常自豪”是美国人,自2025年以来下降了10分。 数字跟随人们老去。 成人目前为34至46人,占46%,而2010年是18至29人组的64%,因此他们的收视率随着年龄的增长而下降,而背后的青壮年则从更低的地方开始。 成年人30至44人占45%,低于2016年和2017年的62%。 成年人45至64人的比例为46%,与2008年的水平相匹配。 估计数来自2026年2月,5月和8月的三起盖洛普小组调查,共计15,156名美国成年人.

featured.title_zh: 今年圣经应用程序中搜索次数最多的是诗篇91篇。“焦虑”、“希望”和“治愈”并不落后。
featured.content: The search bar in a Bible app works like any other, which means it shows what people are worried about before they’ve said it out loud to anyone. YouVersion says “Psalm 91” was the single most-searched term in the app this year. In its newest release , the company also says “anxiety,” “hope” and “healing” were among the year’s most searched terms. YouVersion describes Psalm 91 as a psalm that encourages readers to turn to God for refuge and comfort in difficult times. The psalm runs 16 verses. Together, YouVersion says, the searches offer a glimpse into the personal questions and hopes people are bringing to Scripture. Daily use of the Bible App grew by more than 13% compared with 2025, reaching 18.5 million people a day. It also says it added more than 160 million new installs across its family of apps in 2026, after celebrating one billion installs last November. Daily engagement grew faster than installs, which the company reads as a sign that people are returning to the app and not only downloading it. Some of the highest engagement is outside the U.S. YouVersion says it sees some of the highest levels of Bible App engagement in Sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East and Southeast Asia, and it is building regional hubs in places including the United Kingdom, Brazil, Kenya and Mexico. Its apps offer 3,800 versions of the Bible in 2,400 languages, and it works with a network of more than 45,000 churches and partners. Bobby Gruenewald, YouVersion’s founder and CEO, said in the release that the company has been encouraged by “how many people are turning to Scripture for answers to their questions.”

featured.title: Fear Itself
featured.summary: Widow's Bay  and the Trolley Problem of Life   The post  Fear Itself  appeared first on  Mockingbird .
featured.summary_zh: 寡妇湾和生活的手推车问题帖子Fear Itself首先出现在Mockingbird上。
featured.title_zh: 恐惧自身
featured.content: W hat is your biggest fear? Spiders? That’s a classic. Deranged clowns? Sure! Maybe you prefer the more existential variety? How about never fully realizing your potential or dying alone? All of the above? Similar to the What superpower would you choose? question, it is hard for me to select only one. I am a fearful person. I have a way of collecting fears as I go about my life. Alpha-gal, something I did not know existed until two days ago, is the flavor of the week. But my fear of dying alone is more like a longtime, trusted companion. The world is a scary place. At any moment, our identities could be hacked. Our phones could ring with dreadful news. Our brains could suffer an aneurysm. Swimming in a bottomless sea of insecurity, we are meagerly equipped with our basic survival instincts: fight, flight, freeze, and appease. These impulses may help keep us safe from spiders and clowns (answer for both: flight!), but what do we make of the dangers that are harder to pin down? What if the dangers are not only without but within? Leave it to this year’s hit TV series to explore these questions. If you’re looking for a spooky show to get into this weekend, it’s Widow’s Bay. The Emmy-sweeping, genre-bending, horror-comedic series is a triumph for a number of reasons. For starters, it muddles the black-and-white worlds Hollywood has created (e.g., horror movies without humor, comedies without any depth), reminding us that life can be both scary and funny. The show has all the irresistible horror tropes (the harbinger who warns everyone of impending doom, the suspenseful music, the jump scares) but, along with its crowd-pleasing antics, it dives deeper than surface-level fears. Its anthropology is refreshingly low. This is not a match between good people and evil monsters. Yes, sometimes the enemy is a chainsaw-wielding fiend. Much scarier, however, is when the enemy is yourself. Take Tom Loftis, for instance, the ambitious new mayor who wants to transform the cursed island town of Widow’s Bay into the next Martha’s Vineyard. He is, from every angle, a secular man. For Tom, God is no more real than ghosts. The only higher power that exists is the one you achieve by climbing the ladder. He resents how the locals tolerate the town’s haunted reputation. For too long, people have been resigned to the rumors that the hotel is haunted, the church is cursed, and the bay isn’t safe for a swim. For Tom, the only thing to fear is fear itself. Like any mayor with a messiah complex, he sets out to do something about it. As Loftis sees things, the real problem with the place is not that it is demonically possessed. The real problem is bad branding . In his eyes, Widow’s Bay is simply misunderstood. When visiting Widow’s Bay to write a piece for the New York Times travel section, a reporter asks Loftis about a framed article in the historical society titled “Cannibalism in God’s House.” Loftis tries to water it down. “These stories get so exaggerated over time,” he says. “Was there a deadly storm in 1786? Yes. Did a group of people get trapped inside a church? Apparently so. Did they immediately turn to cannibalism? No, that took four days !” See? That’s not so bad, right? Loftis’ PR campaign is like slapping new siding on a haunted mansion. He is convinced that the plight of Widow’s Bay can be solved by installing a proper cappuccino machine in the local coffee shop. Cappuccino machines are great at making a proper latte but pretty useless when up against the occult. Before long, Loftis’ denial of the curse over the island town is just as dangerous as the curse itself. The first step to keeping the forces at bay is to admit they exist. There is a scene in which Loftis speaks to another character about the Trolley Problem, an ethical thought experiment in which there is a runaway trolley barreling down the tracks toward a crowd of people. In this hypothetical setup, there is a lever that would switch the trolley to a different track with only one
featured.content_zh: 帽子是你最大的恐惧? 蜘蛛吗? 这是经典。 疯狂的小丑? 当然! 也许你更喜欢生存的品种? 永远不能充分发挥你的潜力 或孤独地死去怎么样? 所有这一切? 类似于你选择的超级大国? 问,我很难只选一个 我是一个害怕的人。 我有办法收集恐惧 当我去我的生活。 Alpha -gal,我两天前才知道的东西 是这个星期的口味 但我害怕孤独地死去 更像是长期 值得信赖的同伴 世界是个可怕的地方。 我们的身份随时可能被黑入 我们的电话可能会传出可怕的消息 我们的大脑可能会有动脉瘤 在一个不安全的无底海中游来游去,我们装备了我们的基本生存本能:战斗、出逃、冻结和安抚。 这些冲动也许可以帮助我们远离蜘蛛和小丑(回答:飞行!),但我们如何应对那些更难消除的危险? 如果危险不仅是没有危险,而且是内部危险呢? 让今年的电视连续剧来探讨这些问题。 如果你想要一个恐怖的节目进入这个周末, "艾美扫地"(英語:Emmy-sweating, genre-bending),"恐怖喜剧"(英語:Description-comed)系列,由于多种原因,是一场胜利. 首先,它搅乱了好莱坞所创造的黑白世界(例如没有幽默感的恐怖电影,没有任何深度的喜剧),提醒我们生活既会恐怖又会搞笑. 该节目拥有所有不可抗拒的恐怖颤抖(预告会警告所有人即将来临的末日,悬疑的音乐,跳跃的惊吓等),但连同其人群取悦的焦虑,其潜入比地表恐惧更深. 它的人类学水平低得惊人 这不是好人和邪恶怪物的对决 是的,有时敌人是一个 链锯的恶魔。 然而,更可怕的是当敌人是你自己的时候。 以汤姆·洛夫蒂斯(Tom Loftis)为例, 他,从每个角度来说,都是世俗的人. 对汤姆来说,上帝不比鬼更真实. 唯一高的电能是通过攀登梯子实现的. 当地民众如何容忍镇上闹事的名声? 久而久之,人们对旅馆闹鬼、教堂被诅咒、海湾游泳不安全等谣言辞职。 对汤姆来说,唯一害怕的是恐惧本身. 像任何拥有救世主建筑群的市长一样,他开始对此有所行动. 正如洛夫提斯所见 这个地方真正的问题不是 它被恶魔附身 真正的问题是品牌不好 在他眼中,寡妇湾只是被误解了。 当一位记者访问寡妇湾为纽约时报旅行部写出一篇作品时,他问洛夫蒂斯关于历史社会中一篇被设定为“神殿中的食人狂”的文章。 洛夫提斯试图给它浇水 他说,“这些故事随着时间的推移变得如此夸张。” “1786年是否有致命的风暴? 对 一群人被困在教堂里了吗? 显然如此。 他们有没有立即转向吃人? 不,那需要四天时间!” 这还不算太糟吧? Loftis的公关活动就像在闹鬼的豪宅上再拍一拍。 他相信寡妇湾的困境可以通过在当地咖啡店安装适当的卡布奇诺机器来解决。 卡布奇诺机器很擅长做一个正宗的拿铁 但和神秘主义作对时却很没用 不久之后,洛夫蒂斯否认对岛屿城镇的诅咒,与诅咒本身同样危险。 阻止势力存在的第一步是承认它们的存在. 有个场景让洛夫蒂斯向另一个角色讲述了"特罗莱问题"(Trolley Problem),这是一场道德思想实验,其中有一个跑跑的推车管向一行人冲去. 在这个假想的设定中,有一个杠杆,可以把推车换到只有一跑道的另一跑道.

featured.title: A Crazy Train Crying in the Wilderness
featured.summary: Ozzy Osbourne's Plea to Be Heard   The post  A Crazy Train Crying in the Wilderness  appeared first on  Mockingbird .
featured.summary_zh: Ozzy Osbourne的《Pleas to Be Heard》《A Crazy Train Crying in the Wilderness》一文首次出现在《知更鸟》上。
featured.title_zh: 疯狂的火车在荒野中哭泣
featured.content: No matter who won or lost the last big game you attended, chances are, Ozzy Osbourne was there in electronic chains, locked inside a brain-rattling sound system, unnoticed, unnamed, misunderstood, a voice crying in the wilderness of crowded rows of fans desperate for a win, cheering for their heroes while jeering at their opponents, paying too much for unnecessary carbs and calories, possibly on the sabbath day. When Ozzy cried, “All aboard!” you stood with hundreds or thousands of tangential warriors singing along with the fatalistic chorus, air guitaring with the riffs, nodding with the rhythm, but you weren’t there for music. You were there to shout, thump your chest, flex, thrust hands with fingers contorted into symbols of specific allegiance, or claim you’re #1, convinced that the song, the battle cry, and the power behind it all were on your side. The words didn’t matter. Your heroes were fighting for you, to give you hope. You’d fight for them if you could, if you had to, against whoever stands in your way, to win at all costs. But what if that’s not what Ozzy wanted? How do we know what he wanted? He screams, “You’ve got to listen to my words!” Below is a paraphrase of the “Crazy Train” lyrics: “It’s crazy, but it’s always been like this — we’re all living as enemies. But maybe it’s not too late to learn how to love and forget how to hate. We’ve all got mental wounds that aren’t healing. I’m losing it. I’ve listened to everyone — fools, preachers, anarchists. Nothing helps. There’s always a system run by someone who’s a product of the system and has been conditioned to run the system, which is sold to us by rich people who get richer by keeping the system alive. And we buy it, screaming in pain from our open mental wounds. It’s messed up. I’m messed up. We’re all messed up. We inherit each other’s trouble. We’re heirs of unresolved conflict. I keep saying it, but no one listens. You’ve got to listen to my words. I can’t figure out how to feel. The mental wounds don’t heal. I don’t know who to blame, but I know it’s not fair.” I wrote the above paraphrase to read to my senior literature class last Monday morning. Nearly half of the students in the class are varsity football starters chasing championships and full-rides. I prefaced the reading with a white lie, “I got this message from someone you all know over the weekend. I won’t tell you who it is, but I want you to help me think through how to respond.” The starting quarterback, worried, tried to interrupt me. I didn’t look up, held my hand out to pause questions, and continued reading. When I finished, there was a chorus of concern from several voices: That’s a cry for help! Is it from a boy or a girl? You said we know them? Who is it? Did they email you? What did you say? They need help. Who are you going to talk to? Still in character, I said, “I can’t tell you a name, but I’ll play this song.” A few seconds into “Crazy Train,” the students realized what was going on, looked relieved, but then became uncomfortable when I turned down the volume and read out the actual lyrics. In confused silence, their faces said, We weren’t listening . I felt bad. I smiled and apologized for manipulating their emotions, and the air lightened. Someone started singing the chorus, and we moved on. But I’m not sure we should have. “Crazy Train” is the most popular song from the most recognizable sex, drugs, and rock-n-roll villain to ever bite the head off a bat, but it’s also a cry for help from a struggling human admitting personal weakness and claiming no superiority. While suggesting that love is better than hate, he’s doing more than just asking us to love. He’s asking us to LEARN HOW TO. French philosopher and mystic, Simone Weil, who died during World War II in solidarity with residents of German-occupied France, didn’t write how-to books, but she couldn’t stop talking about attention. Her bumper sticker quote, “Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity,” is clippe
featured.content_zh: 不管是谁赢了还是输了你参加的最后一场大赛 Ozzy Osbourne身处电子链中 被锁在脑震荡的音响系统里 无人注意 姓名不明 被误解 在一群挤满的粉丝的荒野中哭泣 渴望获胜 为他们的英雄欢呼 而嘲笑对手 付出了太多钱来换取不必要的卡布和卡路里 可能在安息日 Ozzy呼喊“所有人上船! ”你和数以百计或数以千计的勇士站在一起, 你在那里大叫,打起胸来,放出花花,用手指将手推入具体效忠的象征,或者说你是"一号",深信歌曲,战斗的叫声,以及背后的力量都站在你一边. 这些话并不重要。 你的英雄们为你而战 为了给你带来希望 如果你可以, 如果你不得不, 对抗阻碍你的人, 如果不是奥兹想要的呢? 我们怎么知道他想要什么? 他喊道:「你必须听我的话! 以下是“疯狂火车”歌词的句子:“这很疯狂, 但也许学会爱和忘记恨还不算太晚。 我们都有精神创伤, 我快输了。 我倾听了每个人的声音, 没什么用 总是有一个系统由某个人运行, 而这个人是这个系统的一个产品, 我们买下它, 在痛苦中尖叫 从我们开放的精神创伤。 情况很糟, 我搞砸了, 我们都搞砸了。 我们继承彼此的麻烦。 我们是未决冲突的继承人。 我一直这么说,但没人听 你必须听我的话。 我无法理解如何感受。 精神创伤无法愈合。 但我知道这不公平。 我写了上面的句子 上周一早上给我的高级文学班念 班上学生有近一半是 versity 足球起步者追逐冠军和全程. 我用一个白色的谎言在阅读前作了前言:“我收到了你们周末认识的人的这个信息。 但我希望你帮我思考如何回应。 开始的四分卫担心,想打断我 我并没有抬头, 我完成后,有多个声音关注的合唱: 这是求救的呼声! 是男孩还是女孩送的? 你说我们认识他们? 谁? 他们给你发邮件了吗? 你说什么? 他们需要帮助。 你要跟谁说话? 但我会演奏这首歌。 数秒钟后, 学生们意识到发生了什么, 他们的面孔模糊地沉默, 我觉得很糟。 我笑了起来,为操纵他们的情绪道歉,而空气也随之淡出. 有人开始唱合唱 我们继续 但我不确定我们是否应该这样做。 “疯狂列车”是最受欢迎的一首歌曲, 他不仅要求我们爱, 他要求我们如何学习。 法国哲学家和神秘主义者西蒙·魏尔(Simone Weil)在二战期间为声援被德意志占领的法国居民而死,她没有写如何写作的书,但她不停地谈论注意的问题. 她的保险杠贴纸引用了“注意是最罕见和最纯洁的慷慨形式”,

featured.summary: "... to be restored, our sickness must grow worse."   The post  East Coker and the Cure for Human Inability  appeared first on  Mockingbird .
featured.summary_zh: “......要恢复，我们的疾病必须变得更糟。“《East Coker and the Cure for Human Inability》一文首次出现在《知更鸟》上。
featured.title_zh: East Coker和治疗人类残疾的方法
featured.content: H ow strange that one can read the same poems countless times and discover new things with each visit, like a traveler coming home for Christmas only to find it slightly altered! It is the same for me revisiting T. S. Eliot’s Four Quartets : the end is different than I imagined in the beginning when I first read these words, imagined these places, and attempted to grasp the author’s meaning. Eliot had the same experience. The meaning of the Four Quartets was one thing when he originally envisioned them, another when he wrote them, and still another when the public began analyzing them. He never believed they would be forever linked with the world’s most destructive war. He had not even known there would be four. In the beginning, there was only “Burnt Norton,” written in 1936 and intended to be a one-off. It was generally well received by critics, and the whole business could have been over then. But three years passed, and Eliot found himself with that most common of authorly ailments: not knowing what to write or fearing that he no longer knew how to write properly. Specifically, he had gone for some time without constructing new poems. The world had changed since “Burnt Norton” was published. A growing menace once possible to ignore had exploded into a firestorm of destructive force sweeping through the nations of Europe, consuming all in its path. The bonds that had knit together what remained of Western Christian civilization were snapping with wild abandon, supplanted by ideologies of extermination. Faced with such a crisis, Eliot searched for the one fixed point amid the whirling chaos. He settled on the village of East Coker in Somerset, England. His ancestor Andrew Eliot had left there in 1669, abandoning the historic family home and immigrating to New England. Nearly three centuries later, Thomas Stearns Eliot had become the first member of the family to move back to the motherland, and the family connection held spiritual significance for him. In 1937, he visited St. Michael and All Angels’ Church in East Coker, where his ashes would one day be placed. I know something of Eliot’s experience. I too am the descendant of Englishmen and women whose bones lie buried in every corner of that land, some in tombs I have visited. I too was the first person in my family to return and live in England, if only for a year. It did feel in a sense like returning to my beginning, which is probably why I connect so strongly with the Four Quartets . The secret Eliot discovered at East Coker is one that has transformed my own life as well: we do not possess the power to redeem ourselves or the world and are utterly dependent on the gift of grace. Of all the Four Quartets , this is the most law and gospel poem. The Four Quartets are commonly associated with the four traditional elements of the physical world: air, earth, water, and fire. But as I have noted, Eliot did not begin with a grand plan, so the elemental symbolism becomes stronger in the later poems. Yes, we see the movement of air in “Burnt Norton” disturbing a bowl of rose leaves and carrying the laughter of children, but you would not conclude “This is an air poem” unless you had the other three Quartets to guide you. Likewise, the earth theme is not obvious after the first section of “East Coker,” but once we get to “The Dry Salvages,” we will be drowned in water imagery, and “Little Gidding” will pelt us with fire from beginning to end. Thus, Eliot begins “East Coker” rooted in the earth, in time and place and home. But immediately, the earth is overturned by the machinations of human societies succeeding and supplanting one another, building up to heaven and returning to dust. In my beginning is my end. In succession Houses rise and fall, crumble, are extended, Are removed, destroyed, restored, or in their place Is an open field, or a factory, or a by-pass. featured.content_zh: 奇怪的是,人们可以阅读同名诗作无数次,每次拜访都会发现新的事物,就像一个旅行者回家过圣诞节,只为了发现它略有改变! 我同样重温了T. S. Eliot的四重奏:结局和我最初读到这些话、想象这些地方并试图理解作者含义时所想象的不一样。 Eliot也有同样的经历. 四重奏的意义是他最初设想它们的时候是一回事,他写它们的时候是另一回事,当公众开始分析它们的时候仍然是另一回事. 他从未相信它们会永远与世界上最具破坏性的战争联系在一起。 他甚至不知道会有四个。 一开始只有"伯恩特·诺顿"(Burnt Norton,作于1936年)一作一作一作一想. 它普遍受到批评者的好评,整个业务本来可以到那时结束. 但三年过去了,艾略特发现自己与最常见的作者病症相伴:不知道该写什么,或担心自己不再知道如何正确写作. 具体地说,他已经走了一段时间,没有创作出新诗. 自“Burnt Norton”出版以来,世界发生了变化。 日益严重的威胁一旦可能被忽视,就已演变成一股由毁灭性力量横扫欧洲各国并吞噬其道路的火焰。 将西方基督教文明遗留下来的东西联系起来的纽带,被被灭绝思想所取代而疯狂地抛弃了。 面对这样的危机,埃利奥特在旋转的混乱中寻找一个固定点. 他定居于英格兰萨默塞特的东科克村. 他的祖先安德鲁·埃利奥特于1669年离开那里,放弃了有历史意义的家族家园并移民到新英格兰. 近3个世纪后,托马斯·斯蒂恩斯·埃利奥特成为了第一个搬回祖国的家庭成员,家庭联系对他具有了精神意义. 1937年,他参观了东科克的圣迈克尔和All Angels教堂,在那里有一天他的骨灰会被放置. 我知道Eliot的经验。 我也是英国男人和女人的后人 他们的骨头埋在这片土地的每一个角落, 一些在我的访问过的坟墓。 我也是我家里第一个回到英国生活的人 哪怕只有一年 我确实感觉回到我的开始, 这可能是为什么我如此紧密地与四重奏联系起来。 Eliot在东科克发现的秘密 也改变了我自己的生活: 我们没有拯救自己或世界的能力, 完全依赖恩赐。 在所有四重奏中,这是最有法律和福音的诗. 四重奏通常与物理世界的四大传统元素相通:空气,地,水,火. 但正如我所指出,艾略特并没有从一个宏伟的计划入手,因此元素符号主义在后期诗作中变得更加强大. 是的,我们看到“Burnt Norton”中的空气运动扰乱了一碗玫瑰叶并带了孩子们的笑声,但除非有另外三个四方来指导你,否则你不会得出“这是一首空气诗”的结论。 同样地,在第一部分“东科克”之后,地球主题并不明显,但一旦我们到达“干涸的盐水”,我们将被水上图像所淹没,而“小吉丁”将从头到尾向我们开火。 因此,Eliot开始“东科克”扎根于地球、时间、地点和家园。 但是,立即,人类社会的成功和取而代之的诡计推翻了地球,使地球升入天堂并回到了尘土中。 在我开始的时候,就是我的结局。 房屋的起伏、倒塌、被延长、被拆除、被摧毁、被恢复或取代,都是空地、工厂或旁道。 如果你曾参观过萨利斯伯里平原上古老的巨石阵纪念碑 你知道它坐落在一条相交的公路上

featured.content: Listeners will have a better idea of why The Mockingcast works (or doesn’t) and why they keep tuning in, 11 years later. We included a few such stories at the beginning of the 300 th episode , and the tears I shed were real. But I thought take the opportunity to offer a few observations from behind the curtain about what I personally appreciate about our podcast, what I’m most proud of, and what’s been challenging. No doubt my co-hosts would have other aspects they’d highlight. First, the longevity. It’s worth celebrating, even if it’s both a blessing and a curse. The time has allowed us to develop some pretty priceless chemistry. When I’m picking articles for us to talk about, I know that even if the material falls flat, I can rely on our dynamic to take up the slack. I trust my co-hosts, and it’s been very gratifying to watch us gel in a non-contrived way over the years. We’ve been through a lot together, and it shows, I think. Being around so long (in internet years) means we’ve had the benefit of watching things come and go. Sarah mentioned this recently in relation to the moralization of food in our society. It was super acute about eight years ago, then it retreated a bit with the body-positivity moment, now it’s back again under the guise of #maxxing. But that’s just one example. I could mention radical atheism, or gospel-centered this and that, or mindfulness. We’ve seen cultural fixations take hold and then recede, specific anxieties bubble up and dissipate. The longer view allows for a measure of perspective that I believe lends the show added depth. Longevity can also be a curse. The ebb and flow can foster a degree of detachment that masquerades as superiority. For example, it’s hard to take the latest rebranding of medieval monasticism (or justification by works) seriously when you’ve seen it happen four times under four different (best-selling) names already. Discipline becomes application becomes virtue becomes formation and so on. It’s a challenge to keep listening and paying attention, but a challenge that I’m proud of us for at least trying to live up to. Because beneath every one of the trends we’ve observed are real people with real hopes and dreams and disappointments. The second longevity-related challenge is the same one that afflicts anyone in a public role, especially those in ministry or thought life. It’s the danger of impersonating yourself. Whenever I detect in my voice any sense of “the grace guy needs to say a grace thing now” — it makes my skin crawl. Autopilot is the enemy, along with its cousin repetition. I remember a trusted listener once warning me that we were becoming a podcast about social media. Another said we were talking too much about parenting. These grooves are understandable, but to keep things fresh, especially over the long haul, you have to always be finding fresh vistas, not just in the culture but in yourself. It’s not easy. This leads me to the next observation: over ten years, it’s become notably more difficult to find suitable material for The Mockingcast . One of the things that I hold sacred about our show is its role as a refuge from culture wars. I want listeners to be confident that when they press play, we’re not going to trigger them about the same headlines that trigger them the rest of the day. We haven’t done this perfectly, I realize, but it remains a guiding principle. When the occasional how-dare-you emails come in, folks are usually surprised to hear that they come just as frequently from both sides of the aisle. If they didn’t, I’d try to course correct. Finding stuff that threads the needle of interesting and substantial but not pre-narrativized has gotten more challenging over our tenure. It’s like the ledge we walk has gotten narrower. Not nonexistent, mind you, just narrower. I’m so proud we’ve reached this milestone without, at least in my view, falling into an ideological ditch or becoming (too) predictable. featured.content: “You only work on Sundays, anyway.” One of the go-to jokes of a group of guys I hang out with. I laugh because, well, I just like to please people. But every time the boys say it, I think to myself, “If you only knew what being a pastor feels like sometimes.” An impromptu funeral at the clinic for veterinarians whose colleague committed suicide, scrolling to find an angry email about last week’s sermon or the changing of the carpet color in the narthex, begging financial generosity from people who pay your salary, lunch with a lonely man going through a brutal divorce, restocking the youth fridge with 7,000 Cheerwines, hearing that they’re gossiping about you again, failing yet again to prepare a sermon that marries TikTok and TED Talk, off to the shelter to serve dinner, did I even eat lunch? Did I mention that this was last Tuesday? Ministry is often pure gift. The highs are as high as they get. Pastors bear witness to the most intimate, most raw, most human, most beautiful and terrifying moments of people’s lives. We play at the level of the soul. We get paid to read and write and pray. We have a front-row seat to miracles: the bound freed, the sinner forgiven, the debts paid, the dead resurrected. It’s not lost on me that having a job rife with meaning is a privilege and honor. This is what God has chosen to make of my life, and I am truly grateful. And yet, there’s no way to get away from the fact that ministry is a burden too. Its shape is a cross. Its form is death and resurrection. People bring all their junk to church — and they should. Sunday mornings are not an assembly of the righteous, they are a sanctuary for sinners — hypocrites anonymous, I like to call it. One of the chief problems that has arisen in my ministry is that I find it so hard to be ministered to. Ministers minister, preachers preach, consolers console, but if you’re not careful, a pastor will find herself without a pastor, a preacher will find himself without a preacher. Everyone needs both. Not long ago I burnt out. Years after, I realize the burnout was not the product of overwork. The fire in my soul was extinguished because for years I had offered relief to others without finding ways to receive it myself. What becomes of a healer who forsakes his own wounds? Pay attention when your soul stops singing. And I did. I prayed for God to bring relief, somehow, someway. And then, to quote Morgan Freeman in The Shawshank Redemption , “a beautiful little bird flew into my drab little cage.” That beautiful bird was Mockingbird Ministries. And now for six years I have done what Michael Gershon calls “staking one’s life on the rumors of grace.” As the 300th of the Mockingcast draws near, I thought it fitting to say what Mbird has been for me: My theological home: Pastors in the mainline will tell you that our denominations are fracturing. It’s tempting to give in to extremes and to weaponize politics toward ecclesial ends. This has made me feel like I don’t belong anywhere politically, theologically, or pastorally. I know many fellow pastor Mbirders agree because we’ve talked about it. Pastors in the mainline who long for a ministry rooted only in the gospel are like an island of misfit toys. Mbird has become for us a gracious home and a place to be reminded again and again of the gospel of grace. My Preacher: I listen to the Mockingcast on Monday mornings. You pastors out there know Monday’s malaise. Dizzied and frenzied from all of Sunday’s work and pressured by a million regrets about the sermon or the attendance, I find sweet relief in the words of RJ, Sarah, and Dave. “That’s right,” I think. “This is what ministry about.” God may not speak to us all through an audible voice in our heads, but God does speak through the words of a sermon. featured.content_zh: “不管怎样,你只在星期天工作。” 我和一群人一起玩的笑话 我笑是因为我喜欢取悦别人 但是,每当男孩们说,我想,“如果你知道牧师有时会是什么感觉。 ” 在诊所为兽医举行即兴葬礼, 其同事自杀, 滚动寻找愤怒的电子邮件, 有关上周的布道或地毯颜色的改变, 我有提到这是上周二吗? 礼部常为纯礼. 高取相如来相. 牧师见证了人们生活中最亲密、最生动、最人性化、最美丽和最恐怖的时刻。 我们在灵魂的层面演奏。 我们得到报酬读写祈祷. 我们有一个前排的座位 奇迹: 束缚的释放者, 罪人原谅, 债务偿还, 死人复活。 工作充满意义, 这是上帝选择 使我的生活, 我真的很感激。 然而, 也没有任何办法可以摆脱这个事实, 其形状为十字. 它的形式是死亡和复活. 人们把他们所有的垃圾都带到教堂,他们应该这样做。 星期天早晨不是善人集会,而是罪人的避难所——伪君子匿名,我想称之为. 在我部里出现的主要问题之一是,我感到很难处理。 但是如果你不小心, 牧师会发现自己没有牧师, 每个人都需要两者。 不久前我烧焦了 多年之后,我意识到 燃烧不是过度劳累的结果。 我灵魂中的活火被扑灭了,因为多年来我一直向其他人提供救济,但没有找到自己接受的方法. 一个抛弃了自己伤口的医护人员会怎样? 你的灵魂停止唱歌时要注意 我这样做了。 我祈求上帝带来解脱,不知何故,某种方式。 然后,引用摩根·弗里曼(Morgan Freeman)在"肖申克救赎"(The Shawshank Resemption)中的话,“一只美丽的小鸟飞入了我的小兔子笼子。” 那美丽的鸟是鸟类部 而现在,六年来,我做了迈克尔·格申所说的“用恩典的谣言夺走自己的生命 ” 。 随着"摩克活人"第300期的到来,我认为应该说出Mbird对我的意义: 我的神学家:主线的牧师会告诉你,我们的教派正在分化. 将政治武器化, 这让我觉得自己不属于政治、神学或牧业的任何地方。 我知道许多牧师都同意, 主线的牧师渴望一个只植根于福音的部,就像一个不适应玩具的岛屿. featured.content: 1. At his Substack, Tim Kreider eulogizes the model shops where he dithered in Covid times and the other quirky, abrasive, irreplaceable businesses that are ever more quickly dwindling in Manhattan. There are few things as authentic feeling as genuine indifference to your presence (or antagonism to it). Kreider describes what’s been lost in our frictionless contemporary world: You find the thing you want, you click on it; a day or two later, the thing you wanted arrives. It’s true you don’t have any discomfiting encounters with misanthropes or wackos, but you also don’t come home with any stories. […] The trip to the model shop, including the weird quirks of the owner, used to be as much a part of making a model as sanding or painting it. But for a lot of increasingly timid, introverted consumers, not having to interact with any human beings when they need something is the whole point of the internet. Which is why Jeff Bezos got to rent Venice for his wedding, and one reason people now seem so grotesquely maladjusted to interacting with each other, or living in a society. […] Look: I am as ambivalent as you about Other People. Other People are problematic, impossible. I don’t want to get too sentimentally nostalgic about the lost joys of real-life encounters with crazy, abrasive human beings. I did not enjoy being treated like a contemptible dilettante or a simpleton when all I wanted was to buy some glue. […] But we need the brush and abrasion of Other People, including — maybe even especially — annoying and difficult ones. Because look at the world we’ve constructed to avoid it. If it’s a choice between awkward conversations with eccentrics and cranks or this infinite blank impenetrable wall of corporate contempt we all now face daily — the constant, soul-eroding hassle of creating an account with a unique username and novel password including capital and lowercase letters plus at least one numeral and symbol for every single transaction or errand, scanning a QR code, downloading the app […] accidentally clicking on a popup and scrambling to close the blaring garish page it opens, being asked to take a moment to fill out a brief survey to rate your experience! and Let Them Know How They’re Doing, briefly explain your reason for cancelling, and having to delete one last “We’re Sorry to See You Go!” email — I know which world I choose. Shopping used to be one of the few things that forced us to engage with others, in ways that abrade us but also give to us. Give what? It’s intangible, but maybe just a sense for a reality beyond ourselves. I’m reminded of a quote from Thomas de Zengotita’s brilliantly prophetic Mediated , that “the opposite of real isn’t phony or illusional or fictional — it’s optional.” I think part of what he’s getting at is that anything optional is, once chosen, something that you constructed, something you are responsible for, whose existence depends on your own. What feels real is the thing that exists outside of you — that bracing feeling you get on a mountain or at McSorley’s that the world exists utterly apart from you and will go on existing apart from anything you do. It’s those sorts of encounters, given rather than constructed, arising naturally from a human soul rather than private equity market modeling and focus groups, that seem to get lost in today’s world. Maybe our 2027 NYC Conference will finally be my year for a platza. 2. On Tuesday, journalist Calum Marsh published a history of CrossFit , which seems like a gold mine for tracing the seculosity of fitness in our culture, at least if this week’s profile in UnHerd is anything to go by. Apparently CrossFit pioneered the model, common today, of pricey subscriptions to a high-intensity exercise program that function not just for health but as an arena in which one can pursue personal excellence. At the time, the metrics were revolutionary, and the idea that an adult would pay to be yelled at seemed fantastical. The eccentric visionary who star
featured.content_zh: 1. 在他的Substack,Tim Kreider赞美了他在科维德时代抖动的模范店铺,以及曼哈顿日益迅速倒闭的其他奇特、粗糙和不可替代的企业。 很少有像真正漠不关心你的存在(或对你的敌意)那样真实的感觉。 Kreider描述了在当代世界失去的东西: 你找到你想要的东西,你点击它; 一两天后,你想要的东西到达。 确实,你没有遇到任何不愉快的人类或疯子, 模特店之行,包括店主的怪怪怪之行,曾是制作"模特"同"打砂"或"作画"一样的重要一环. 但对于许多越来越胆小的、内向的消费者来说, 当他们需要东西时, 不需要与任何人互动是互联网的整个点。 这就是为什么杰夫·贝佐斯不得不租给威尼斯参加他的婚礼, 这也是人们现在看起来如此怪异的不适应 彼此互动或生活在一个社会中的原因。 你看:我和你一样对别人充满矛盾。 其他人有问题,不可能 我并不想对现实生活中与疯狂而残忍的人类相遇所失去的欢乐怀念太多。 我并不喜欢被当做一个可鄙的二手货 或简单的人对待 当我只想买些胶水的时候 但我们需要其他人的刷子和磨擦,包括——也许甚至特别——烦人和困难的人。 因为看看我们所构建的世界, 如果在与古怪分子和曲柄的尴尬对话之间做出选择, 或者在这种无限空白的企业蔑视墙上, 我们每天都会面临这种不断的、令人心痛的麻烦, 让他们知道自己在做什么, 简单解释你取消的原因, 并删除最后一封“我们很遗憾看到你走!”电子邮件, 购物曾经是少数迫使我们与他人接触的事物之一,其方式使我们感到愤怒,但也给了我们。 给什么? 但也许只是对现实的感想, 我还记得托马斯·德·泽戈蒂塔(Thomas de Zengotita)辉煌地预言的“Mediated”的一篇文章,“与真实相反的不是虚构的、幻想的或虚构的,而是可选的。 ” 我认为,他得到的一部分是,任何可选的事物,一旦被选中,都是你构建的,你负责的,它的存在取决于你自己。 感觉真实的是你身外存在的东西 — — 吹嘘地感觉你在山上或在麦克索利的山上,世界的存在与你完全不同,并且会与你所做的一切相去甚远。 在今天的世界中,似乎迷路的是那些自然产生于人的灵魂而不是私人股权市场模型和焦点团体的交会。 也许我们2027年的纽约公会 终于能成为我的一年了 2. 记者Calum Marsh星期二发表了"CrossFit"(CrossFit)的历史, 显然,CrossFit开创了一种模式, 即今天常见的, 一个高强度的锻炼计划, 它不仅为健康运作, 并且是一个可以追求个人卓越的舞台。 当时的度量衡是革命性的,一个成年人会付出代价去被骂的想法看起来是奇幻的. 怪异的想象力谁的明星

featured.title_zh: 邪恶的无形
featured.content: Happy Halloweek, boils and ghouls! Halloween is right around the corner, and so is Michael Myers, back to show everyone why he is the undisputed master slasher! Blaine Grimes, Blake Collier, Caleb Stallings, and I are in our Halloween best and invite you to join us in watching Halloween (2018). Ian : I picked this because it takes me back so vividly to October 2018 and seeing it with my wife, Kristin, and her sister, Anna. Weird as it may sound, this flick lights my heart up like a dozen M-80s in a jack-o’-lantern. I was excited for Michael Myers to return to the big screen and for a new generation to reckon with the horror of The Shape. Caleb : This was the first movie my wife, Aleece, and I ever saw together. Our second date! It’ll always be important to me for that reason alone, but it’s also important to me because it’s a good Halloween sequel! Blake : This movie will forever hold a dear place in my marriage as the first film I took my wife to that caused her to cry and to lose sleep. The first Halloween she watched, she didn’t even bat an eye. This one was just too much for her. Caleb : Wild that we all associate this, for good or for ill, with our wives! Blake : Except Blaine, who just saw it for the first time, right? Blaine : Yeah. I’ve only ever seen the OG and this one. Blake : That is WILD. Caleb : Do you think this one stands out more than others, Ian? Ian : In some significant ways, yes. Halloween (2018) resets the board by proceeding as if there had never been a sequel to the 1978 Halloween . Even titling this film Halloween shows how it positions itself as spiritual successor to the original, and it kind of implicitly announces that nothing with that word and a number after it matters. Caleb : I will admit, I am a sucker for all the various timelines and reboots. But I think this is far and away the best one. Ian : Don’t get me wrong, I enjoy certain sequels before this, but it’s largely in the same way I enjoy the Friday the 13th sequels: schlocky fun. Blake : I don’t hate any of the sequels. But this and its subsequent two films were the first time I felt giddy about being in Haddonfield again. Ian : Halloween (2018) definitely seeks to accomplish something amid its slasher spectacle. I think it wants to go back to basics in showcasing Michael as the evacuated site and vessel of evil: The Shape. Caleb : It’s fascinating how they have to cast the horror of Michael killing five people in 1978 against the larger horror of the subsequent 40 years in American society. Michael isn’t the most prolific serial killer. There have been worse threats than him, but still: he is an avatar of the shapeless Shape of evil. So I think Laurie gets it right later when she talks about how hard and dark the world is. All of us have to be prepared for it. The question is How can we be? Ian : You’re actually approaching something I’m sensing this time around. Although this film officially disavows forty years of sequels, it nevertheless assumes their lore, after a fashion, precisely because the Michael of Halloween (1978) murdered five people, but there’s a mythos to Michael here as though he had carried out everything in those sequels. Caleb : It definitely reckons with its own lore. Laurie’s granddaughter’s friends hear rumors that Laurie was Michael’s sister, which alludes to Halloween 2 (1981). But the truth is much scarier: he’s not related to Laurie at all. His stalking and tormenting her is utterly inscrutable; random. And I think a thesis of this movie is that the world is the same: full of random horror that we can’t ever truly parse out in this life. Michael just happens to be one personification of that. Ian : One of the most satisfying things to me was how the inmates at the asylum chitter and cry out when the mask is presented to Michael, like they sense a power drawing near. That shapeless evil seeks a vessel but also a shape. Michael is at the ready but seeks union with the mask. It’s an anti-wholeness: a complete evac

Blaine Grimes Blake Collier Caleb Stallings 我参加万圣节最佳演出 邀请你加入我们观看万圣节(2018年) 伊恩:我选这个是因为它让我生动地回到了2018年10月,并与我的妻子克莉丝汀和她的妹妹安娜一起看到了它. 这个闪光照亮了我的心, 我很兴奋迈克尔·迈尔斯回到大屏幕上 以及新一代人去考虑"形状"的恐怖 凯勒布: 这是我妻子艾莉丝的第一部电影 我曾经一起看过 我们的第二次约会! 但对我来说也很重要, 因为它是一部很好的万圣节续集。 布莱克: 这部电影将永远占据我婚姻中最珍贵的一席之地,作为我带我妻子去看的第一部电影,她因此哭泣并失眠. 她看的第一个万圣节, 这个对她来说太过分了 凯勒布:我们为了好,为了病,为了我们的妻子,把这件事联系起来,真是疯狂! 布莱克:除了布莱恩,谁刚刚第一次看到它,对不对? 对 我只见过OG和这个。 这是WILD。 你觉得这个比其他人更突出吗,伊恩? 伊恩: 在某些重要方面,是的。 万圣节(2018年)通过程序重放板子, 即使授权这部电影万圣节也展示了它如何将自己定位为原作的灵性接班人,它隐含地宣布了这个词和之后的数字都无关紧要. Caleb:我承认,我对各种时限和重回潮流都是个傻瓜。 但我认为这是最远的 Ian:别误会, 之前我还喜欢一些续集, Blake:我不讨厌任何续集。 但是,这及其之后的两部电影,是我第一次对再次出现在哈德顿菲尔德感到迷茫. Ian:万圣节(2018年)肯定在它的刀锋一现中寻求成就。 我认为它想回到基本点 展示迈克尔 被疏散的地点和邪恶的船:形状。 Caleb : 1978年迈克尔杀死了五个人,而美国社会随后的40年却发生了更大的恐怖。 迈克尔并不是最有实力的连环杀手。 曾经有比他更严重的威胁,但仍然:他是一个无形状的邪恶形状的造型. 所以,我想劳里得到它的权利 稍后,当她谈到 多么艰难和黑暗的世界是。 我们所有人都必须为此做好准备。 问题是,我们怎么能这样? (笑声) 伊恩:你实际上正在接近我这次所感知的东西。 虽然这部电影正式否定了40年的续集,但它仍然假定了他们的神话,在时尚化后,正是因为万圣节的迈克尔(1978年)谋杀了五个人,但迈克尔在这里有一个神话,好像他在那些续集中完成了一切。 凯勒布: 它肯定用它自己的神话来考虑 Laurie的孙女朋友听说Laurie是Michael的妹妹, 但事实更可怕:他与劳里根本不相干。 他跟踪和折磨她完全是不可理喻的,是随意的。 我认为这部电影的一个论点是世界是相同的:充满了随机的恐怖,而我们无法在这样的生活中真正地理解。 迈克尔恰好就是个人物 Ian:我最满意的一件事是 当面具被出示给Michael时, 精神病院的囚犯们哭喊着, 好像他们感觉到力量在接近。 这种无形的邪恶既寻求一种容器,也寻求一种形状。 迈克尔已经准备好了,但寻求与面具结合。 这是一个反整齐:一个完整的撤离

featured.title_zh: 非仪器活动的重要性
featured.content: Here’s something that retired Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin and I have in common: we both have secret hobbies that we don’t talk about. My hobby is houseplants. About two years ago, I decided I needed a hobby that was affordable, indoors, incapable of being monetized, offered zero status, and could be managed while raising two preschool-aged kids. The result was a half-priced money tree purchased off the clearance rack from Lowe’s. It was touch and go at first: two of the four “trunks” braided together on this money tree were dying of root rot, and it took me a while to figure out the right lighting and a good watering schedule. (Did you know that most houseplants don’t die from lack of water but from being overwatered? The more you know!) Once I figured all that out, my money tree stabilized, and a new hobby was born. About twelve years ago, the then head coach of the Pittsburgh Steelers, Coach Tomlin, started playing Minecraft with his two preteen sons. For the unfamiliar, Minecraft is like a digital game of Legos, and while there are competition elements to the game, Coach Tomlin felt the draw of the game’s free-play mode, which allowed gamers to build their own creations out of the game’s various styles of bricks. Earlier this fall, having moved from coaching football to broadcasting, Tomlin disclosed his twelve-year Minecraft hobby to the world, offering a YouTube live stream tour of a city that he had spent more than a decade building from digital bricks. Both gamers and sports fans responded in mutual shock. If you’re not an NFL or sports fan, you might not know that Mike Tomlin is one of sport’s most respected head coaches, famously stringing together nineteen years of coaching without a single losing season. He won the Super Bowl in 2009 and kept the Steelers among football’s most winning franchises. One of his talents was keeping the sport’s most “diva” players in winning form. When top-flight players would leave the Steelers for other teams, many would go on to have public crashouts and exit the league in embarrassing failures. Players uniformly loved Tomlin, and many viewed him as a surrogate father figure. But when the Sunday Night Lights were off, and when the family was cared for, and when the man had some free time, the famous head coach was on his laptop playing Minecraft. This is as unusual as it is amazing. Professional sports of all stripes are marked by an “all-in” mentality. Everything is secondary to the game, whether it’s diet, exercise, sleep, even family and friendships. The money is just too much and the stakes are too high to be anything but 100% focused on preparing for the game ahead. And yet, Coach Tomlin achieved his incredible results while spending a lot of time hanging out in the land of the chicken jockey. Gamers have been just as shocked as the football fans. When Tomlin hosted his YouTube live stream of his city, it garnered universal appreciation from other Minecraft players. It was big, well designed, and orderly down to every last detail and accent. In the great divide between the nerds and the jocks, here was a jock who could keep up with the nerds. Arthur Brooks, the social science good-life guru, had lots to say about Tomlin’s hobby over at the Free Press . He confessed to being “gobsmacked” at the news and took the moment to reflect on his own lack of hobbies. Sparing you the requisite “here’s what a bunch of scholarly studies found about hobbies” bits that populate Brooks’ articles, here’s what stood out: A key element of a hobby that brings happiness is that the rewards must not be extrinsic. By this, I mean the hobby can’t run up your personal or professional scoreboard in terms of money, power, or prestige. The rewards must be intrinsic, involving personal growth, enjoyment, or drawing closer to others. Psychologists have long found a huge happiness difference between these two types of reward. 我和迈克·汤姆林有一个共同点:我们都有秘密的爱好, 我的爱好是家用植物 大约两年前,我决定我需要一种爱好,这种爱好是负担得起的,室内的,无法被货币化,提供零地位,可以在抚养两个学龄前儿童的同时进行管理.

结果是一棵半价钱树从Lowe的清关架上购买。 起初是触摸并去的:在这棵钱树上被捆绑在一起的4个"trunks"中有2个正被根腐烂而死,我花了一阵子才找出正确的照明和良好的取水时间表. (你知道大多数家用植物不是因为缺水而死,

越发知道! ) 一旦我明白了这一切, 我的钱树稳定下来了, 一个新的爱好诞生了。 大约12年前,时任匹兹堡钢人队主教练的汤克林教练开始和他的两个小儿子一起出演"Minecraft".

对于不熟悉的人来说,"Minecraft"就像一款"Legos"的数字游戏,虽然游戏中存在竞争元素,但主教练汤姆林感受到了游戏自由游戏模式的图画,这使得游戏者能够从游戏的各种花砖风格中打造出自己的创作.

今年秋天早些时候,汤姆林从教练足球转向广播,他向世界披露了自己十二年的"Minecraft"爱好,提供YouTube活溪游览一个他用数字砖建造了十多年的城市. 比赛双方球迷和体育迷均在相互冲击下响应.

featured.content: Kirk Franklin did not walk through The Jennifer Hudson Show’s spirit tunnel. He worked it. The Jennifer Hudson Show posted the walk to Instagram with one caption: “Show off those moves @kirkfranklin!” View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Jennifer Hudson Show (@jenniferhudsonshow) He was there to promote his new album, I Am What I Am , which comes out Friday, Oct. 30. It’s his 14th solo album, and he’s a 20-time Grammy winner. His song with Karen Clark Sheard, “Thank You For Everything,” is already out. It made its live TV debut at the 41st Stellar Gospel Music Awards. At a listening party in Atlanta on Oct. 12, according to Hot 100.9, Franklin said, “I’ve never done a double album before.” He described the TobyMac collaboration “It Gets Better” as “my attempt to find a space to talk about mental health,” and added, “I’ve had my own journey with anxiety and depression.” He also talked about changes in the Black church. “The Black church culture changed,” he said. “The church got rid of their choirs and the music was in a space that was not my strength.” He had advice for emerging artists, too. “Start off very true and build your audience slow,” he said. “Don’t ride the trends because you don’t know when they’re coming.”

featured.content: San Antonio Spurs rookie Tarris Reed Jr. got baptized days after making his NBA debut, and he posted the video to Instagram under two words: “Jesus Saves.” Reed, a 23-year-old center, was the No. 26 pick in this year’s draft out of UConn. Denver took him, and San Antonio acquired him in a trade. He debuted on Tuesday, Oct. 20, in a 116-104 loss to the Oklahoma City Thunder. In the caption, Reed wrote that he got home late after his first NBA back-to-back and “got my first real glimpse of just how grueling the 82-game NBA season can be.” On the plane ride, he remembered it was Baptism Sunday at his church. “I texted Pastor Ed, and the rest was history LOL.” “It’s been on my heart for a while now to be baptized,” Reed wrote. “I wanted to publicly signify my union with Christ and what it means to walk in His grace, mercy, and NEWNESS OF LIFE!” He quoted Romans 6:4: “We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too may live a new life.” He also wrote about what he sees coming next. “The Lord has placed me in a unique position to help others come to know Christ and experience His life changing power,” he wrote. “To think that I went from wanting nothing to do with the Lord to now desiring to live for Him is something I never could have imagined. I never would have thought my life would look like this.” View this post on Instagram A post shared by TRJ (@iamtarrisreed) Reed is a St. Louis native who started his college career at Michigan, transferred to UConn after his sophomore year and was the Big East Sixth Man of the Year as a junior. In April, UConn lost the national title game to Michigan, and Reed went to Instagram afterward. “I’ve been wrestling with God about this all day” , he wrote in a post that week. “Losing the biggest game of my entire basketball career hurts,” he said. “I tend to be a perfectionist, but only Jesus was perfect.” He wrote that he felt Jesus put it on his heart to go to an Athletes in Action meeting and speak, even though he didn’t want to. He barely had time to prepare, so he told himself he would let the Holy Spirit speak through him. “That night, two of the women’s basketball players got baptized,” he wrote. “It’s not my will, it’s His.” His October post ended with “All glory to God!”

featured.title_zh: 弗兰妮·卡什（ Franni Cash ）离开家族乐队，首次独唱并在邪教中成长
featured.content: Franni Cash was about 13 when she says the community her family belonged to officially became a cult. She was 17 when her family left it. She told RELEVANT that her parents joined after their marriage hit a rough patch and a friend suggested counseling. The therapist they saw, she said, was “dangerously smart” and used people’s vulnerabilities “to kind of tether loyalty to himself.” Counseling sessions became Bible studies with other families, and then she says they were told they no longer needed church. Eventually the leader declared himself their spiritual father and warned that anyone who broke covenant with him would be cut off, and women who disagreed with their husbands were said to have “the Jezebel spirit.” “It just became so far away from the truth,” Cash said. She kept a diary about how strange it all felt. The leader found it and burned it. She was 14. “From that place I pushed it down,” she said. “I can’t question it and can’t voice this anymore.” Her family left in the middle of her senior year of high school, after an article exposed years of alleged fraud and sexual allegations tied to the leader. She remembers her parents telling the kids in their bedroom. “It was like this weight flew off my shoulders,” she said. Then came a harder year, when she feared the curses and watched her brothers struggle. “I didn’t know if I was gonna make it. I really mean that.” Her parents put the family in therapy immediately. Talk therapy alone didn’t work for her, because she was still so brainwashed she didn’t know what she could say. EMDR and brainspotting did. She has been in consistent therapy for ten years now and says talking about the cult no longer stings. “I’ve had to grieve them being susceptible to something so harmful,” she said of her parents. “But right off the bat, they got themselves in therapy.” She describes her healing journey as medicine and scripture working together. “You can’t just slap a Bible verse on it,” she said. “Scripture is so powerful, but sometimes you don’t know how to absorb it until you can do some surgery.” The family’s first song came a year and a half after they left, and it became We the Kingdom. Cash said the band was a place where she felt understood, because her family were the only people who could laugh at the jokes instead of being horrified. She also says they were trauma bonded, and that she needed to learn who she was on her own. She left the band, and says she and her family are now the closest they’ve ever been, “from a health and respect” place that “doesn’t feel enmeshed.” Her solo debut, Here I Am , takes its title from a lyric she and her father, producer and songwriter Ed Cash, wrote together for the song “The Real Thing”: Here I am, I made it through. The page is burned, but this story is not over. Here I Am was also going to be the title of an album she planned at 16, in the middle of everything. “Now here I am, kind of on the other side of healing,” she said. Getting there meant relearning music. A friend, the writer Paul Duncan, told her she needed to “date music like you would your spouse,” meaning listen to records she loved as a kid with no goal. She was driving on the Pacific Coast Highway when U2’s “Where the Streets Have No Name” came on. “It was like I heard music for the first time,” she said. She has since been listening to Marvin Gaye’s What’s Going On , Al Green, Elton John, Casey Musgraves, John Mayer and Linkin Park’s Hybrid Theory . Her view of God changed too. “I just really thought that God was this angry man upstairs,” she said. She remembers being told to get off the worship stool because she wasn’t “anointed enough.” Then she met what she calls the real Jesus. “He was so loving. And gracious with me,” she said. “It changed everything.” When we asked what she’d say to someone inside a controlling church, her answer was short. “Leave. You’re free to.
