featured.title: Finish the Race: Final Steps in the Transition to a Plurality of Elders
featured.summary: It is easy to get lost in wanting to lead out in change just so we can say we did it, or out of concern to our reputation. But our motivation for change should be to bring greater glory to God and greater health to his church.   The post  Finish the Race: Final Steps in the Transition to a Plurality of Elders  appeared first on  9Marks .
featured.summary_zh: 我们很容易迷失在想要在变革中发挥领导作用，这样我们就可以说我们做到了，或者出于对我们声誉的关注。但我们改变的动机应该是给神带来更大的荣耀，给祂的教会带来更大的健康。“完成比赛：向多元长老过渡的最后步骤”一文首先出现在9Marks上。
featured.title_zh: 完成竞赛：向多元长老过渡的最后步骤
featured.content: Abstract: Zach Kilpatrick encourages pastors who are transitioning to a plurality of elders to finish the process well by addressing some practical questions. Questions concerning how new elders will be identified, how they will be presented to the congregation, and what this will mean for the church’s existing constitution and bylaws—along with a multitude of other practical issues—may feel less important, but, as Kilpatrick reminds us in this third article of a three-part series, they are vital if the congregation is to have confidence in the men who are selected and in the process as a whole. Ultimately, this transition should be aimed at the glory of God and the building up of his people. You finally did it. You talked your wife into letting you turn the basement into a man cave! However, after receiving approval, you still have to do the work. What size TV will you buy? Where will it go? How much furniture will you have? Will you put anything on the wall? Many practical questions remain. Similarly, leading a change from a single-elder polity to a plurality of elders has final steps that are often overlooked. We know we need to educate the body on the biblical model and its practical benefits. We understand the need for discussions and an official vote. But even after all this, we aren’t done yet. Having discussed the evaluation and education phases of this process in previous articles, we will now look at the final step, which is also vital: execution. A Word of Warning: Remember Your First Love In his letter to the church in Ephesus (Rev. 2:1–7), Jesus commends them for their perseverance and discernment. Thomas R. Schreiner, Revelation , in ESV Expository Commentary , v ol. 12 , 570 – 571. They were known for their commitment to sound doctrine and righteous living. Yet they are rebuked because they had abandoned their first love. Schreiner argues that the Ephesians had stopped loving God and others. Sch r einer , Ibid. , 571. These Christians, who were so committed to doing the right thing, had forgotten why they were doing it in the first place. They had orthodoxy and orthopraxy, but they were missing love. Don’t let this be your story. It is easy to get lost in wanting to lead out in change just so we can say we did it, or out of concern to our reputation. But our motivation for change should be to bring greater glory to God and greater health to his church. So don’t lose focus after the vote is taken. See the process through to the end. Finishing Well Check Your Documents One of the first things to do after there is general agreement to move toward a plurality is to consult the church’s governing documents (bylaws, policies, and procedures). You need to determine how to officially adopt the change. Even if all the members are on board and ready, it still has to accord with your governing documents. If your documents do not allow for having a plurality of elders, then you will need to amend or rewrite them. The congregation will then need to vote to accept the amendments or new constitution. As part of this process, you might consider consulting a trusted attorney who has helped like-minded churches deal with these kinds of issues. They might have insights that help prevent you from making a costly mistake. Identify Elder Candidates Once your documents are in order, you will need to identify qualified elder candidates. How this process is handled will have a significant effect on the congregation’s confidence in the transition. One of the most important questions to answer is who will be responsible for nominating the first elders to serve alongside you. The constitution and bylaws of most elder-led congregational churches make the elders responsible for nominating new elders to the congregation. I think this is the best practice. However, since you are the only elder at the time of this change, you will need to decide whether to nominate qualified men yourself or form a one-time committee to help you. Either way, don

Schreiner,《启示录》,载于ESV Expository 评注,v ol. 12, 570–571. 他们以致力于健全的理论和正直的生活而出名。 然而,他们被斥责,因为他们抛弃了初恋。 Schreiner认为以弗所人不再爱上帝等. Sch r einer, 同上,571页。 这些基督徒,他们如此致力于做正确的事情,已经忘记了他们最初这样做的原因. 他们有正统的和正统的,但他们缺少了爱。 不要让这成为你的故事。 我们很容易迷路,想在变革中起带头作用,这样我们可以说我们做到了,或者是出于对我们声誉的关切。 但我们改革的动机应该是给上帝带来更大的荣耀,为他的教会带来更大的健康. 所以不要在投票后失去注意力。 见过程到底. 正在完成您的文档检查 在普遍同意走向多元化之后,首先要做的是查阅教会的执政文件(细则、政策和程序)。 你需要确定如何正式通过修改. 即使所有成员都已经上船并做好了准备,它仍然必须与你的管理文件保持一致。 如果您的文档不允许有多个长者, 您需要修改或改写这些文件 。 随后会众需要投票接受修正案或新宪法. 作为这一过程的一部分,你不妨考虑咨询一位信任的律师,他帮助志同道合的教会处理这些问题。 他们也许有能防止你犯昂贵的错误的洞察力 确定老年人候选人 一旦您的证件齐全,您需要确定合格的长者候选人。 这一进程的处理方式将对教会对过渡的信心产生重大影响。 要回答的最重要的问题之一是,谁将负责提名第一批长老与你们一起服务。 多数长老领导的教会的宪法和章程规定,长老有责任向教会提名新的长老。 我认为这是最佳做法。 然而,由于您是本次变更时唯一一位年长者,您需要自行决定是否提名合格的男性,或者组成一个一次性的委员会来帮助您. 随便你,唐

featured.title_zh: 事工与婚姻：如何成为一个健康的团队
featured.content: Marriages with one or both spouses employed in ministry face unique pressures, challenges, and opportunities. Over the years, we change, our ministries change, and the pressures on us change. How can we navigate these changes in a way that draws us closer to each other instead of driving us apart? In this discussion, recorded at TGC25, Michael and Lucy Aitcheson talk with Jim and Angela Davis about their experiences of seeking to keep their marriage healthy while ministering faithfully. featured.title: Martin Luther in 5 Latin Phrases
featured.summary: Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift.
featured.summary_zh: 耶稣完美的生命和牺牲的死亡对所有信徒都很重要。因此，神的义不仅仅是他的审判。这也是他的天赋。
featured.title_zh: 马丁·路德的5个拉丁短语
featured.content: Martin Luther was born in Eisleben, Germany, on November 10, 1483. He was christened at Saints Peter and Paul Church the next day. At age 7, Luther entered the Mansfeld Latin School. There he learned Latin grammar and prayers, and he memorized Aesop’s Fables . From those early years through his time studying at boarding school in Magdeburg then later at the University of Erfurt, Luther was a diligent student. He kept up with his Latin, and several important Latin phrases appear throughout Luther’s writings. Five of them serve as a good summary of his life and chief theological emphases. 1. Iustitia Dei In July 1505, Luther was caught in a fierce thunderstorm. Panicked and terrified, he bargained with God, promising to become a monk. After entering the monastery, Luther was again overcome by fear. When he led his first mass as a priest, it wasn’t an occasion of joy. Instead, it was filled with trembling. As the service began, Luther took his place at the front of the chapel, and he began to recite the Latin prayers. Luther knew that God is perfect in judgment and completely without sin. So as he thought about iustitia Dei , “the righteousness of God” (Rom. 1:17), terror struck him. Biographer Roland H. Bainton describes the thoughts that plagued Luther’s mind: Who am I that I should . . . raise my hands to the divine Majesty? The angels surround him. At his nod the earth trembles . . . [but] I am dust and ashes. When Luther held up the bread and wine, he shook so badly he almost dropped the cup. During those years growing up in school and at the monastery, Luther only thought of God’s righteousness, or justice, as his active judgment against human sin. He later wrote , Though I lived as a monk without reproach, I felt and knew I was a sinner before God. I had an extremely disturbed conscience. . . . I hated the righteous God who punishes sinners. 2. Extra nos In 1512, Luther became a university professor in Wittenberg. As he studied the Bible for his lectures, he began to see God’s righteousness in a new light. Luther saw how Jesus Christ took on our humanity, how he lived a perfect life and died the painful and shameful death of the cross to take the punishment due for sin. He saw how God raised Jesus from the dead, and how he now justifies Christians by faith. God declares that in his sight, Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift of salvation. Jesus’s perfect life and sacrificial death count for all believers. So God’s righteousness isn’t merely his judgment. It’s also his gift. What happened when Luther made this discovery? Here’s how he described it: “I felt that I was altogether born again and had entered paradise itself through open gates.” After that day, Luther began to teach that God gives Christians his “alien righteousness,” that is, a righteousness that comes extra nos , “from outside of us.” Our righteousness isn’t from us; it doesn’t come from what we do. It can’t be earned by saying a prayer or even by having a good attitude. Our righteousness is ultimately found in and belongs to another, our Savior Jesus Christ. 3. Crux sola est nostra theologia On October 31, 1517, Luther famously posted his Ninety-five Theses on the door of Castle Church. In it, Luther spoke clearly against the money-raising indulgence schemes Pope Leo X and Germany’s own Prince Albert of Brandenburg had sponsored. The next year, in April 1518, Luther defended these views at the Augustinian order’s spring meeting in Heidelberg. Luther walked to the meeting in fear. He expected the leaders there to sternly rebuke him. After all, that’s what the pope had asked them to do. But to Luther’s surprise, the leaders at the meeting welcomed his defense with excitement. featured.content: The older I get, the more convinced I am that a posture of gratitude is key to a life of joy. God’s gifts are constant and abundant—his daily provision of life and breath far more than we deserve. Being alert to the constancy of his gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention . That’s why Thanksgiving is such a great holiday. It’s at least one day dedicated to pausing and taking stock, giving our attention to the Giver of all good gifts. Being alert to the constancy of God’s gracious provision is the epitome of rightly ordered attention. But it’s a shame Thanksgiving is just one day. Because really, we should practice gratitude constantly. What if, as a start, we dedicated the whole month of November to giving thanks? What if we dedicated time each day this month to intentionally naming God’s provision and giving him thanks? To help, I created a new playlist all about giving thanks to God. The playlist has 30 songs (one for each of November’s 30 days) expressing gratitude to God for our salvation in Christ, for the many blessings of marriage and family, and for the beauty of the earth. You can access the playlist now on Spotify and Apple Music . Enjoy! featured.summary: We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners.

featured.title_zh: 殉道者的声音：受迫害者的祈祷
featured.content: “How long, O LORD? . . . Pour out your anger. . . . Let the avenging of the outpoured blood of your servants be known among the nations before our eyes!” (Ps. 79:5–6, 10). As you’re reading through Psalms and you stumble across Psalm 79, you can’t help but wonder what to do with this very Old Testament-sounding prayer. Surely, Asaph needed to be educated in the gospel, right? Revelation 6:9–10 describes the martyrs in heaven who have been slain for their testimony to the gospel and places Psalm 79 on their lips: “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long before you will judge and avenge our blood on those who dwell on the earth?” Scholars agree the prayer of Psalm 79 is the likely background for the prayer of the martyrs, furthering our appreciation of this as a prayer for the church. It’s a prayer of and for the persecuted church. As we stand alongside them, we have divine warrant to pray Psalm 79 on their behalf. Trevor Laurence explains , “The vengeance petition of Rev. 6:9–10 thus supplies a model for the ongoing prayer of Christ’s body on earth.” Rather than being contrary to New Testament ethics, then, Psalm 79 fuels the church’s longing for every wrong to be made right. Nevertheless, you may still wonder, How do I take up a psalm like this in prayer for my persecuted brothers and sisters without falling into vindictive rage and vengefulness? Thankfully, Psalm 79 provides the guidelines needed to answer this question. Pray in Response to Horrific Injustice Verses 1–4 catalog the horrors God’s people suffered at the hands of the Babylonians who destroyed their temple: They defiled God’s holy place, they gave the flesh of God’s faithful ones to the beasts of the earth, they poured out their blood like water and refused them a proper burial, and they were the cause of God’s people becoming a taunt to their neighbors. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. Psalm 79 is not prayed in response to petty grievances but birthed out of horrendous evil. This has two implications. First, these prayers do not give license for us to pray such things against just anyone. Second, if we object to such prayers, they challenge us to ask whether we have ever faced anything close to the agonizing evil that gave birth to this prayer. As Jamie Grant posits , “Perhaps our reluctance to appropriate the psalms of enmity is rooted in the comfort of our lives.” If we knew the kind of horror Psalm 79 speaks of (and that our persecuted brothers and sisters endure daily), perhaps we wouldn’t be so quick to dismiss these psalms. Pray for the Glory of God As psalms like this respond to such evil, they are fundamentally concerned with God’s glory. We see this in Psalm 79:6, where the nations’ refusal to call on God’s name is the motive behind Asaph’s cry. Likewise, verse 9 cites the glory of God’s name and his “name’s sake” as a rationale for God to answer this request. And verse 10 is concerned that, at present, the onlooking nations say, “Where is their God?” So Asaph asks that God’s justice would be made known among the nations (v. 10), and that God’s people might praise him for it (v. 13). The glory of God is the ultimate end of the imprecatory psalms. Or as James Hamilton says , “The glory of God in salvation through judgment is the center of the theology of Psalms.” The same is true of imprecatory psalms like Psalm 79. Their controlling desire is “Hallowed be thy name.” Pray with a Humble Posture The imprecatory psalms are not prayed in a spirit of self-righteousness; those praying them understand their need for God’s grace. They pray for justice from a posture of humility, where they confess that this judgment is what they too deserve apart from God’s grace (vv. 8–9). This is not unlike the widow’s prayer for justice in Luke 18:1–8 being paired with the parable of the Pharisee and tax collector in verses 9–14. We pray for justice, but we do so as forgiven sinners. featured.title_zh: 有效的利他主义者和电子表格福音
featured.content: Over the past decade, an emergent secular philosophy has taken root in Silicon Valley. It now drives many conversations around politics and technology, particularly as its ideas shape how our society approaches artificial intelligence. Known as “effective altruism,” this worldview is having a moment. The Economist recently called the philosophy “this century’s biggest idea” and labeled the movement as “admirable, but dangerous.” Even as this philosophy is moving markets and shaping global debates, many Christians are unfamiliar with it.
